Module 1
Web & Django Fundamentals

Module 1 — Web & Django Fundamentals

We’ll start from zero. By the end of this module, you should be able to explain the basic working of a web application and confidently answer the common viva questions about Django.

1. What is a Website?

A website is a collection of web pages that can be accessed through the internet using a web browser.

Examples:

  • Google
  • YouTube
  • Amazon
  • Wikipedia

A website generally contains:

  • HTML → structure
  • CSS → styling
  • JavaScript → behavior/interactivity
  • Backend → processing and business logic
  • Database → storing information

For example, when you open an online shopping website:

text
You → Browser → Website Server → Database
                       ↓
                    Response
                       ↓
                    Browser

2. What is a Web Application?

A web application is a website that allows users to perform operations and interact with data.

For example:

Simple website

A page that says:

text
Welcome to my website

There may be little or no user interaction.

Web application

An online shopping application allows you to:

text
Register
Login
Search products
Add products to cart
Place orders
Make payments
View previous orders

So:

A web application is an application that runs through a web browser and allows users to interact with data and functionality provided by a server.

Django is mainly used for developing the backend of web applications.

3. Client and Server

This is VERY important for understanding Django.

Client

The client is usually the user's device/browser that sends requests to a server.

For example:

text
Chrome
Firefox
Edge
Safari

Server

The server is a computer/program that receives requests, processes them, and sends responses.

For example, when you type:

text
youtube.com

your browser sends a request to YouTube's servers.

The server processes it and sends information back.

4. Request and Response

The basic communication is:

text
Client
   |
   | Request
   ↓
Server
   |
   | Response
   ↓
Client

Request

The browser says:

"Give me this webpage."

Response

The server says:

"Here is the webpage."

This concept is the foundation of Django.

5. Example of Request-Response

Suppose you visit:

text
example.com/about

The process is approximately:

text
1. Browser sends request
          ↓
2. Server receives request
          ↓
3. Django processes request
          ↓
4. Django determines what should happen
          ↓
5. Django generates response
          ↓
6. Server sends response
          ↓
7. Browser displays webpage

Later, we'll learn exactly how Django performs steps 3–5.

6. What is HTTP?

HTTP = HyperText Transfer Protocol

HTTP is a protocol used for communication between a client and a web server.

It defines how requests and responses are exchanged.

For example:

text
Browser ─── HTTP Request ───→ Server

Browser ←── HTTP Response ─── Server

Common HTTP methods include:

text
GET
POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE

For your Django syllabus, GET and POST are particularly important.

We'll study them deeply in Unit II and Unit IV.

7. GET vs POST — Basic Idea

Don't worry about the details yet.

GET

Generally used to request/retrieve data.

Example:

text
/products
/products/10

POST

Generally used to send data to the server.

For example, submitting a registration form:

text
Name: Aman
Email: aman@example.com
Password: ********

The browser can send that information to the server using POST.

We'll study this properly later.

8. Frontend vs Backend

A web application generally has two major sides.

Frontend

The frontend is what the user sees and interacts with.

Technologies include:

text
HTML
CSS
JavaScript
React
Angular
Vue

Example:

text
+---------------------------+
|       My Website          |
|                           |
| Name: [____________]      |
|                           |
|       [ Submit ]          |
+---------------------------+

That's frontend.

9. Backend

The backend handles things that happen behind the scenes.

For example:

text
User submits login
        ↓
Backend receives username/password
        ↓
Backend checks database
        ↓
Is user valid?
      /    \
    Yes     No
     ↓       ↓
 Dashboard  Error

Backend can handle:

  • Authentication
  • Database operations
  • Business logic
  • Form processing
  • Security
  • APIs
  • Sessions
  • User permissions

Django is a backend web framework.

10. Where Does the Database Come In?

Suppose you create an account.

The information needs to be stored somewhere:

text
Username
Email
Password

A database stores this information.

So a simplified application looks like:

text
                Web Application

Browser
   ↓
Request
   ↓
Django Backend
   ↓
Database
   ↓
Django Backend
   ↓
Response
   ↓
Browser

Django provides tools to communicate with the database.

Later you'll learn something very important called:

ORM — Object Relational Mapping

11. What is a Framework?

Before understanding Django, you need to understand framework.

Suppose you want to build a house.

You could create everything from raw materials yourself:

text
Bricks
Cement
Doors
Windows
Electrical system
Plumbing
etc.

Or you could use an established structure/design that makes construction easier.

A software framework provides a similar advantage.

A framework is a collection of tools, libraries, conventions, and structures that helps developers build applications more efficiently.

12. Why Do We Need Frameworks?

Imagine building a web application completely from scratch.

You would have to handle:

  • URL routing
  • HTTP requests
  • Database connections
  • Authentication
  • Security
  • Forms
  • Sessions
  • Error handling
  • HTML rendering

Doing everything manually would take a lot of time.

A framework provides many of these facilities.

So instead of reinventing everything, you can focus on your application's functionality.

13. What is Django?

Now the main question.

Django is a high-level, open-source Python web framework used for building web applications quickly, securely, and maintainably.

Important keywords for viva:

Django

  • Python-based
  • Web framework
  • Open-source
  • High-level
  • Used for web application development

You should remember this definition.

14. Why is Django Called a Python Web Framework?

Because Django is:

text
Python
   ↓
Django
   ↓
Web Application

You write Django applications primarily using Python.

For example, a very simple Django view can look like:

python
from django.http import HttpResponse

def home(request):
    return HttpResponse("Hello World")

Don't worry if you don't understand this yet.

We'll build this from scratch in later modules.

15. Why Use Django?

Django provides many things out of the box.

1. URL Routing

It helps map URLs to application logic.

Example:

text
/about → about view
/login → login view
/products → products view

2. Templates

Django allows Python-generated data to be displayed in HTML.

For example:

text
Hello, Aman

can be dynamically generated.

3. Forms

Django provides tools for creating and validating forms.

4. Database Support

Django provides an ORM for working with databases using Python.

Instead of writing SQL for everything, you can write:

python
Student.objects.all()

5. Authentication

Django provides built-in support for:

text
Users
Login
Logout
Passwords
Permissions
Groups

6. Security

Django provides protections/features for common web security concerns, including:

text
CSRF protection
SQL injection protection through ORM usage
Clickjacking protection
XSS-related protections
Secure password handling

7. Admin Panel

One of Django's famous features is its built-in admin interface.

You can manage database data through a web interface.

Conceptually:

text
Django Application
       ↓
     Models
       ↓
   Django Admin
       ↓
Manage data

16. Django's "Batteries Included" Philosophy

You may hear this phrase in a viva.

Django is often described as having a "batteries-included" philosophy.

It means Django provides many commonly needed features as part of the framework.

For example:

text
Authentication
Admin
ORM
Forms
Sessions
Security
Templates
URL routing

You don't need to build all of these from scratch.

17. What is MVT?

This is VERY IMPORTANT for your viva.

Django follows an architectural pattern commonly described as:

MVT = Model – View – Template

The three components are:

text
Model
View
Template

Let's understand each.

18. Model

The Model deals mainly with data and database structure.

Suppose you have students.

A model might represent:

text
Student
----------------
id
name
email
age
course

Django can use this model to interact with the database.

Think:

Model = Data + Database logic

19. View

The View contains the logic that processes a request and determines what response should be returned.

For example:

python
def home(request):
    return HttpResponse("Welcome")

Think:

View = Business/request processing logic

20. Template

The Template is generally the presentation layer.

It usually contains HTML with Django Template Language.

Example:

html
<h1>Welcome {{ name }}</h1>

If the name is:

text
Aman

the resulting page can display:

text
Welcome Aman

Think:

Template = Presentation/UI

21. MVT Diagram

Remember this:

text
                 USER
                  |
                  | Request
                  ↓
                URL
                  |
                  ↓
                VIEW
              /      \
             ↓        ↓
         MODEL     TEMPLATE
           |           |
           ↓           ↓
       DATABASE      HTML
             \       /
              ↓     ↓
                VIEW
                  |
                  | Response
                  ↓
                USER

This is a simplified conceptual diagram. Django internally handles some details differently, but this is the useful mental model for your course.

22. Real Example of MVT

Suppose the user visits:

text
/students/

Step 1 — URL

Django sees:

text
/students/

and determines which view should handle it.

Step 2 — View

The view asks the model for student information.

text
View → Model

Step 3 — Model

The model interacts with the database.

text
Model → Database

Database returns:

text
Aman
Rahul
Priya

Step 4 — View

The view sends the data to a template.

text
View → Template

Step 5 — Template

The template generates HTML.

text
Template → HTML

Step 6 — Response

Django sends the generated HTML back to the browser.

text
Django → Browser

The browser displays:

text
Students

1. Aman
2. Rahul
3. Priya

23. Django Request-Response Cycle

This is one of the most important things to understand.

Suppose you enter:

text
http://127.0.0.1:8000/about/

The simplified flow is:

text
Browser
   |
   | HTTP Request
   ↓
Django
   |
   ↓
URL Configuration
   |
   ↓
View
   |
   ↓
Model / Database
   |
   ↓
Template
   |
   ↓
HTTP Response
   |
   ↓
Browser

You will gradually learn every part of this flow throughout the course.

24. What is 127.0.0.1:8000?

When we start Django's development server, you'll commonly see:

text
Starting development server at http://127.0.0.1:8000/

127.0.0.1

This means the local machine (localhost).

8000

This is the port on which Django's development server is listening by default.

So:

text
127.0.0.1:8000

means:

"Access the Django development server running on this computer at port 8000."

25. Django vs Python

A common viva question:

Is Django a programming language?

No.

Django is a web framework written in Python.

Correct relationship:

text
Python
  ↓
Programming Language

Django
  ↓
Python Web Framework

26. Django vs Flask

You may be asked this in an interview/viva.

Both are Python web frameworks.

A simplified comparison:

Django Flask
More batteries-included More minimal
Built-in ORM Doesn't force a specific ORM
Built-in admin No built-in Django-style admin
Built-in authentication tools Usually assembled through extensions/code
More structured More flexible/minimal
Suitable for large structured applications Useful for lightweight/custom applications too

Don't say:

"Django is always better than Flask."

Instead say:

"Both are useful Python web frameworks. Django provides more built-in functionality, while Flask is more lightweight and minimal."

27. Important Django Terminology

Start becoming familiar with these words:

Term Meaning
Django Python web framework
Project Overall Django application/configuration
App Component that performs a particular functionality
View Handles request/application logic
Model Represents/manages data
Template Presentation layer
URL Maps requested paths to views
ORM Allows database interaction using Python objects
Migration Tracks/applies database schema changes
Admin Built-in interface for managing data
Form Handles user input
Session Stores user-specific state across requests
Cookie Small data stored by the browser

We'll study every one of these in detail.

28. Project vs App — Important

Students often confuse these.

Imagine you're building an e-commerce website.

The project could be:

text
E-Commerce Website

Inside it, you could have apps:

text
accounts
products
orders
payments
reviews

Conceptually:

text
                 PROJECT
                    |
       +------------+------------+
       |            |            |
    accounts     products      orders
       |            |            |
    users        products      orders

Project

The overall Django site/application configuration.

App

A component that handles a particular functionality.

We'll learn exactly how to create both later.

29. What You Should Be Able to Explain Now

If your teacher asks:

"What is Django?"

Answer:

Django is a high-level, open-source Python web framework used to develop web applications quickly, securely, and maintainably.

"What is MVT?"

Answer:

MVT stands for Model, View, and Template. Model handles data and database-related operations, View handles request and application logic, and Template handles presentation.

"What is a Model?"

Answer:

A Model is a Python class that represents the structure of application data and provides an interface for interacting with the database.

"What is a View?"

Answer:

A View is responsible for processing a request and returning an appropriate response.

"What is a Template?"

Answer:

A Template is used to define the presentation layer, usually HTML, and can contain Django Template Language for displaying dynamic data.

python

hello(request)

             Django

Module 2
Python Environment & Installation

Module 2 — Python Environment, Virtual Environment & Django Installation

In this module, we'll go from "I have Python installed" → "I have a proper Django development environment ready."

This module is mostly practical, so I'll explain the commands, what they do, why we use them, and viva questions.

1. What do we need before Django?

Django is a Python framework, so we need:

text
Python
   ↓
pip
   ↓
Virtual Environment
   ↓
Django
   ↓
Code Editor

Usually you'll use something like:

  • Python
  • VS Code
  • Terminal/Command Prompt
  • Django

2. What is Python?

Python is a high-level, interpreted programming language.

Django is built using Python, so your Django code will primarily be written in Python.

For example:

python
def hello():
    print("Hello")

Django adds web-development functionality on top of Python.

3. Check Whether Python Is Installed

Open Command Prompt / PowerShell / VS Code Terminal.

Run:

bash
python --version

You may see:

text
Python 3.x.x

On some systems, especially Windows, this may also work:

bash
py --version

Viva question

Q: How do you check the Python version?

Answer:

We can use python --version or, on Windows, py --version.

4. What is pip?

You will frequently see:

bash
pip install django

So what is pip?

pip is Python's package installer.

It allows us to install Python packages.

For example:

bash
pip install django

means:

Install the Django Python package.

You can check pip using:

bash
pip --version

5. What is a Python Package?

A package is reusable code that can be installed and used in your Python programs.

For example:

text
Django
NumPy
Pandas
Requests
Matplotlib

Instead of writing everything yourself, you can install packages containing functionality written by other developers.

6. Why Do We Need a Virtual Environment?

This is very important.

Suppose you have two Django projects.

Project A

Requires:

text
Django 4.x

Project B

Requires:

text
Django 5.x

If both projects use the same global Python environment, you can run into dependency/version conflicts.

A virtual environment creates an isolated Python environment for a project.

Conceptually:

text
Computer
│
├── Project A
│    └── Virtual Environment
│         └── Django version A
│
└── Project B
     └── Virtual Environment
          └── Django version B

This keeps project dependencies separate.

7. What Exactly Does a Virtual Environment Do?

It creates an isolated environment where you can install Python packages specifically for your project.

Without virtual environment:

text
System Python
    |
    +-- Django
    +-- Package A
    +-- Package B
    +-- Package C

With virtual environments:

text
System Python
     |
     +----------------+
     |                |
   Project A        Project B
     |                |
     ↓                ↓
   venv A           venv B
     |                |
  Django A          Django B

This is one of the most important reasons virtual environments are used.

8. Creating a Virtual Environment

Suppose you create a folder for your Django work:

text
DjangoCourse

Open the terminal inside that folder.

Run:

bash
python -m venv venv

Let's understand this command.

text
python

Runs Python.

text
-m

Tells Python to run a module.

text
venv

Python's built-in module for creating virtual environments.

text
venv

The name we're giving our virtual environment.

So:

bash
python -m venv venv

means:

Use Python's venv module to create a virtual environment named venv.

9. Can We Give the Environment Another Name?

Yes.

For example:

bash
python -m venv myenv

or:

bash
python -m venv django_env

But you'll commonly see:

bash
python -m venv venv

10. Activating the Virtual Environment

Creating it isn't enough.

You need to activate it.

Windows — Command Prompt

cmd
venv\Scripts\activate

Windows — PowerShell

powershell
.\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

After activation, you may see something like:

text
(venv) C:\Users\...\DjangoCourse>

The:

text
(venv)

indicates that the virtual environment is active.

11. Why Do We Activate It?

Because we want commands such as:

bash
pip install django

to install Django into the project's virtual environment rather than relying on the global environment.

So:

text
Activate venv
       ↓
pip install django
       ↓
Django installed in venv

12. Installing Django

Once your virtual environment is activated:

bash
pip install django

pip downloads and installs Django and its required dependencies.

After installation, check:

bash
django-admin --version

You should get a Django version number.

You can also use:

bash
python -m django --version

13. django-admin vs python -m django

You'll encounter both.

django-admin

Django's command-line utility.

For example:

bash
django-admin startproject myproject

python -m django

Runs Django through the currently selected Python interpreter.

For example:

bash
python -m django --version

Using python -m django can be useful when you want to make sure you're using Django associated with the Python environment you're currently working in.

14. Why Is python -m Useful?

Suppose your computer has multiple Python installations or environments.

Running:

bash
python -m pip

or:

bash
python -m django

ties the command to the Python interpreter represented by python.

For example:

bash
python -m pip install django

is often a reliable alternative to:

bash
pip install django

because it makes the Python environment relationship explicit.

15. Verify Django Installation

Run:

bash
django-admin --version

or:

bash
python -m django --version

If it returns a version, Django is installed.

Example:

text
5.x.x

The exact version you see may differ from examples in your college material.

16. Installing VS Code

You can use any suitable editor, but we'll use VS Code throughout this course.

You'll generally want the:

Python extension

installed in VS Code.

Later, VS Code will help with:

  • Syntax highlighting
  • Autocomplete
  • Error detection
  • Running code
  • Terminal
  • Django project editing

17. Selecting the Correct Python Interpreter

This is a very common beginner problem.

Suppose your project has:

text
DjangoCourse/
│
└── venv/

Your VS Code should ideally use the Python interpreter from that virtual environment.

In VS Code:

text
Ctrl + Shift + P
       ↓
Python: Select Interpreter
       ↓
Select your venv Python

On Windows it will typically be something similar to:

text
venv\Scripts\python.exe

The exact path depends on where your project is located.

18. Why Does the Interpreter Matter?

Imagine:

text
Python A
   ↓
No Django installed

Python B
   ↓
Django installed

If VS Code uses Python A, you might get an error such as:

text
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'django'

even though you installed Django.

Why?

Because you installed Django in one Python environment, while VS Code is using another.

That's why:

text
Virtual Environment
        +
Correct Interpreter

is important.

19. Typical Project Setup

A clean setup can look like:

text
DjangoCourse/
│
├── venv/
│
└── project/

Eventually, after creating the Django project, you'll have more files and folders.

Don't worry about the exact project structure yet—we'll cover it in Module 4.

20. The Complete Setup Process

For your practical exam, remember this sequence:

Step 1

Create a folder:

text
DjangoCourse

Step 2

Open terminal in it.

Step 3

Create virtual environment:

bash
python -m venv venv

Step 4

Activate it:

bash
venv\Scripts\activate

Step 5

Install Django:

bash
pip install django

Step 6

Check Django:

bash
django-admin --version

Step 7

Open the folder in VS Code.

Step 8

Select the virtual environment's Python interpreter.

Now your Django environment is ready.

21. Important Commands to Memorize

These are worth memorizing:

Purpose Command
Check Python python --version
Check pip pip --version
Create venv python -m venv venv
Activate venv — Windows CMD venv\Scripts\activate
Install Django pip install django
Check Django django-admin --version
Check Django through Python python -m django --version
Deactivate venv deactivate

22. Deactivating the Virtual Environment

When you're finished working:

bash
deactivate

The:

text
(venv)

prefix disappears.

Important:

Deactivating the environment does not delete it.

It simply stops using that virtual environment in the current terminal session.

You can activate it again later.

23. Common Mistake #1 — python Not Recognized

You might get something like:

text
'python' is not recognized...

Possible causes include:

  • Python isn't installed
  • Python isn't on PATH
  • Terminal needs to be restarted
  • Windows Python launcher may be available as py

Try:

bash
py --version

24. Common Mistake #2 — Django Not Found

You run:

bash
django-admin --version

and get an error.

Check:

bash
python -m django --version

Also check whether your virtual environment is active:

text
(venv)

Then:

bash
python -m pip show django

This can help determine whether Django is installed in the Python environment you're currently using.

25. Common Mistake #3 — VS Code Uses Wrong Python

You installed Django successfully but your Python file says:

text
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'django'

Check the selected interpreter.

You may have:

text
VS Code → Global Python

while Django is installed in:

text
VS Code → venv Python

Select:

text
venv\Scripts\python.exe

26. Common Mistake #4 — PowerShell Execution Policy

Sometimes Windows PowerShell can block activation scripts.

You may see an execution-policy error.

Don't panic. This is a Windows shell configuration issue, not a Django issue.

For your college practical, you can also use Command Prompt and activate with:

cmd
venv\Scripts\activate

We'll troubleshoot such errors if you encounter them while actually setting up your environment.

27. Viva Questions

Now let's make this viva-ready.

Q1. What is pip?

Answer:

pip is Python's package installer used to install and manage Python packages.

Q2. Why do we use a virtual environment?

Answer:

A virtual environment creates an isolated Python environment for a project, allowing project-specific packages and versions without interfering with other projects.

Q3. How do you create a virtual environment?

Answer:

bash
python -m venv venv

Q4. How do you activate a virtual environment in Windows?

Answer:

For Command Prompt:

cmd
venv\Scripts\activate

For PowerShell:

powershell
.\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Q5. How do you deactivate it?

bash
deactivate

Q6. How do you install Django?

bash
pip install django

Q7. How do you check the Django version?

bash
django-admin --version

or:

bash
python -m django --version

Q8. Why should we use a virtual environment for Django?

A strong answer:

We use a virtual environment to isolate the dependencies of a Django project. This prevents package and version conflicts between different projects.

Q9. What is django-admin?

django-admin is Django's command-line utility used to perform administrative tasks such as creating projects and other Django-related operations.

Q10. What does python -m venv venv mean?

It runs Python's built-in venv module and creates a virtual environment named venv.

28. Viva Trap Question ⚠️

Teacher:

"If I deactivate my virtual environment, is Django deleted?"

Wrong:

Yes.

Correct:

No. Deactivation only stops using the virtual environment in the current terminal session. The environment and its installed packages remain on the system until they are explicitly deleted.

29. Another Viva Trap

Teacher:

"Can I install Django globally without a virtual environment?"

Answer:

Yes, technically Django can be installed globally, but using a virtual environment is recommended because it isolates project dependencies and avoids version conflicts.

That's a much better answer than simply saying "No."

30. Practical Question

Your teacher may say:

"Set up Django and verify that it is installed."

Your answer/action sequence should be:

bash
python --version
bash
python -m venv venv
bash
venv\Scripts\activate
bash
python -m pip install django
bash
python -m django --version

If the version appears, Django is installed.

🧠 Module 2 — What You Should Remember

The complete chain:

text
Python
  ↓
Virtual Environment

Activate

Install Django

Verify Django

Select correct VS Code interpreter

Most important commands:

bash
python -m venv venv
venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install django
python -m django --version
deactivate

And understand this distinction:

text
Python
   ↓
Programming language

pip
   ↓

   ↓

   ↓

Module 3
Creating Your First Django Project

Module 3 — Creating Your First Django Project

Now we start actual Django development.

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

  • Create a Django project
  • Understand django-admin
  • Understand manage.py
  • Start the Django development server
  • Open your project in a browser
  • Understand what happens when Django starts
  • Answer common viva questions
  • Create a project in an exam from scratch

1. What is a Django Project?

A Django project is the overall configuration and collection of settings for a Django website/web application.

For example, imagine you're making a college management system:

text
College Management System

That can be your Django project.

Inside it, you might later create apps such as:

text
students
teachers
courses
attendance
accounts

So remember:

Project = overall Django website/application configuration
App = a specific functionality/component inside the project

We'll explore this distinction much more in Module 5.

2. Before Creating a Project

Make sure your virtual environment is active.

You should see something like:

text
(venv)

For example:

text
(venv) C:\DjangoCourse>

If it isn't active:

cmd
venv\Scripts\activate

Then verify Django:

bash
python -m django --version

3. Creating a Django Project

There are two common approaches.

Using django-admin

bash
django-admin startproject myproject

Using Python

bash
python -m django startproject myproject

Both create a Django project.

For learning, understand the second form too because it explicitly uses the current Python environment.

We'll use:

bash
python -m django startproject myproject

4. Understanding the Command

Look carefully:

bash
python -m django startproject myproject

Break it down:

python

Use Python.

-m django

Run Django as a Python module.

startproject

Django command that creates a new project.

myproject

The name of your project.

So:

python -m django startproject myproject creates a new Django project named myproject.

5. What Happens After Running It?

Suppose your folder initially contains:

text
DjangoCourse/
│
└── venv/

After:

bash
python -m django startproject myproject

you'll get:

text
DjangoCourse/
│
├── venv/
│
└── myproject/
    │
    ├── manage.py
    │
    └── myproject/
        ├── __init__.py
        ├── settings.py
        ├── urls.py
        ├── asgi.py
        └── wsgi.py

Don't worry about each file yet.

Module 4 is dedicated to understanding this structure.

For now, focus on what was created.

6. Why Are There Two myproject Names?

This confuses almost every beginner.

We have:

text
myproject/
│
├── manage.py
│
└── myproject/
    ├── settings.py
    ├── urls.py
    └── ...

The outer myproject is basically the project directory.

The inner myproject is the Python package containing the project's configuration.

So:

text
outer folder
     ↓
myproject/

inner package
     ↓
myproject/

This will become much clearer when we study the project structure.

7. What is manage.py?

This is one of the most important files in Django.

manage.py is a command-line utility provided for interacting with your Django project.

It allows you to execute commands related to your project.

For example:

bash
python manage.py runserver
bash
python manage.py startapp students

Later:

bash
python manage.py makemigrations
bash
python manage.py migrate
bash
python manage.py createsuperuser

So remember:

manage.py is a command-line utility used to perform administrative tasks for a specific Django project.

8. django-admin vs manage.py

Very important viva question.

django-admin

A general Django command-line utility.

Example:

bash
django-admin startproject myproject

manage.py

A project-specific command-line utility.

Example:

bash
python manage.py runserver

A useful way to remember:

text
django-admin
      ↓
Django-level commands

manage.py
      ↓
Specific project's commands

Technically, manage.py sets up the project environment/settings before delegating to Django's command machinery.

9. Starting the Development Server

Move into the project directory:

bash
cd myproject

Then run:

bash
python manage.py runserver

You may see output similar to:

text
Watching for file changes with StatReloader
Performing system checks...

System check identified no issues.

Starting development server at
http://127.0.0.1:8000/

Congratulations.

Your first Django development server is running.

10. Open the Browser

Open:

text
http://127.0.0.1:8000/

You should see Django's default welcome page.

Something conceptually like:

text
🎉 Congratulations!

It worked!

The exact page can vary with Django versions.

11. What is the Development Server?

When you execute:

bash
python manage.py runserver

Django starts a development server on your computer.

It allows you to test your application locally.

The default address is generally:

text
127.0.0.1:8000

12. Understanding 127.0.0.1

127.0.0.1 refers to your own computer through the loopback interface.

It's commonly called:

localhost

So these generally refer to the same local machine:

text
127.0.0.1
localhost

You can typically open:

text
http://localhost:8000/

as well.

13. Understanding Port 8000

A computer can run multiple network services.

A port helps identify which service/network endpoint you're communicating with.

Django's development server commonly uses:

text
8000

So:

text
127.0.0.1:8000

means:

text
Computer: 127.0.0.1
Port:     8000

14. Can We Change the Port?

Yes.

For example:

bash
python manage.py runserver 8080

Now Django will typically run at:

text
http://127.0.0.1:8080/

You can also specify an address and port:

bash
python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000

We'll discuss what this means later when networking becomes relevant.

15. Stopping the Server

When the server is running in your terminal, press:

text
CTRL + C

This stops the development server.

16. Why Does Django Have a Development Server?

Because during development you need to repeatedly test your application.

Instead of configuring a production web server every time, Django provides a lightweight development server.

You can:

text
Write code
   ↓
Run server
   ↓
Open browser
   ↓
Test
   ↓
Modify code
   ↓
Refresh

This makes development convenient.

Important:

Django's development server is intended for development/testing, not production deployment.

This is a good viva point.

17. Automatic Reloading

When the development server is running, Django can detect many code changes and reload the development server automatically.

For example:

text
You modify views.py
        ↓
Save
        ↓
Django detects change
        ↓
Reloads

This is one reason development is convenient.

18. The runserver Command

The basic command:

bash
python manage.py runserver

means:

Start Django's development server.

A teacher may ask:

"How do you run a Django project?"

Answer:

bash
python manage.py runserver

Then access the local server in your browser.

19. Creating a Project in a Specific Directory

You can also specify where Django creates the project.

For example:

bash
django-admin startproject myproject .

Notice the:

text
.

The dot means:

Create the project in the current directory.

This is extremely useful because it changes the resulting structure.

20. Normal vs Dot Method

Method 1

bash
django-admin startproject myproject

Structure:

text
current/
└── myproject/
    ├── manage.py
    └── myproject/

Method 2

bash
django-admin startproject myproject .

Structure:

text
current/
├── manage.py
└── myproject/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── settings.py
    ├── urls.py
    ├── asgi.py
    └── wsgi.py

The second method is often convenient when you've already created a folder for the project.

21. Which One Should You Use in College?

Both are valid.

For a beginner, I recommend:

bash
python -m django startproject myproject

Then:

bash
cd myproject

Then:

bash
python manage.py runserver

This makes the project structure easy to understand.

Later, you'll become comfortable with:

bash
django-admin startproject myproject .

22. What Happens When You Visit /?

Suppose your browser requests:

text
http://127.0.0.1:8000/

The browser sends a request to Django.

Django checks the project's URL configuration.

Initially, Django has a default URL configuration that leads to the default welcome page.

Conceptually:

text
Browser
   |
   | GET /
   ↓
Django
   |
   ↓
URL configuration
   |
   ↓
Response
   |
   ↓
Browser

We'll learn exactly how URL mapping works in Unit II.

23. What Does startproject Actually Create?

The command:

bash
python -m django startproject myproject

creates the basic files needed for a Django project.

The important ones are:

text
manage.py
settings.py
urls.py
asgi.py
wsgi.py

For now, just know their broad purposes:

File Purpose
manage.py Project command-line utility
settings.py Project configuration
urls.py URL routing configuration
asgi.py ASGI deployment interface
wsgi.py WSGI deployment interface

We'll study them properly in Module 4.

24. Important: Project ≠ App

At this point, you have created a:

text
PROJECT

You have not yet created an app.

Later you'll run:

bash
python manage.py startapp students

and get:

text
students/

So:

text
startproject
     ↓
Creates project

startapp
     ↓
Creates app

This distinction is extremely important.

25. Complete Practical — Create Your First Project

If your teacher gives you a blank computer and says:

"Create and run a Django project named College."

You should be able to do:

Step 1 — Create folder

text
DjangoCourse

Step 2 — Open terminal

Step 3 — Create virtual environment

bash
python -m venv venv

Step 4 — Activate

cmd
venv\Scripts\activate

Step 5 — Install Django

bash
python -m pip install django

Step 6 — Create project

bash
python -m django startproject College

Step 7 — Enter project

bash
cd College

Step 8 — Run server

bash
python manage.py runserver

Step 9 — Open browser

text
http://127.0.0.1:8000/

That's a complete basic Django project setup.

26. Common Errors

Error 1 — Wrong directory

Suppose you run:

bash
python manage.py runserver

and get:

text
can't open file 'manage.py'

Likely you're not inside the directory containing manage.py.

Check:

bash
dir

on Windows.

You should see:

text
manage.py

Then run:

bash
python manage.py runserver

27. Error 2 — Django Not Installed

You might get:

text
No module named django

Check:

bash
python -m django --version

If it doesn't work, activate your virtual environment and install Django:

bash
python -m pip install django

28. Error 3 — Port Already in Use

You might see an error indicating that port 8000 is already in use.

Use another port:

bash
python manage.py runserver 8001

Then visit:

text
http://127.0.0.1:8001/

29. Viva Questions

Now the important part.

Q1. What command is used to create a Django project?

Answer:

bash
django-admin startproject project_name

or:

bash
python -m django startproject project_name

Q2. What is manage.py?

Answer:

manage.py is a project-specific command-line utility used to perform administrative tasks for a Django project.

Q3. What command starts the Django development server?

bash
python manage.py runserver

Q4. What is the default port of Django's development server?

8000

Q5. What is 127.0.0.1?

It is the loopback address that refers to the local machine.

Q6. What is localhost?

Localhost refers to the current/local computer. 127.0.0.1 is a commonly used IPv4 loopback address for it.

Q7. How do you stop the Django development server?

Press Ctrl + C in the terminal running the server.

Q8. Is Django's development server suitable for production?

No. It is intended for development and testing, not production deployment.

Q9. What is the difference between startproject and startapp?

startproject creates the structure of a Django project, while startapp creates an application within a Django project.

Q10. What is the purpose of settings.py?

settings.py contains configuration settings for the Django project.

Q11. What is the purpose of urls.py?

urls.py contains URL configuration used to map URL patterns to views or other URL configurations.

30. Viva Trap Question ⚠️

Teacher:

"Does python manage.py runserver create a Django project?"

Answer:

No. runserver starts the development server for an existing Django project. A project is created using startproject.

31. Another Trap Question

Teacher:

"Is manage.py the Django framework?"

Answer:

No. manage.py is a command-line utility generated for a specific Django project. Django itself is the Python web framework.

Module 4
Django Project Structure

Module 4 — Django Project Structure

Now we're going to open the Django project and understand every important file.

This module is extremely important because teachers love asking:

"What is the purpose of settings.py?"
"What does manage.py do?"
"What is urls.py?"
"Why are there two __init__.py files?"
"What is WSGI?"
"What is ASGI?"

By the end, you should be able to look at a Django project and understand what every file is doing.

1. Our Django Project

Suppose we created:

bash
python -m django startproject College

The structure is:

text
College/
│
├── manage.py
│
└── College/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── settings.py
    ├── urls.py
    ├── asgi.py
    └── wsgi.py

Let's understand it one file at a time.

2. Outer College Folder

The outer folder:

text
College/

is simply the directory containing your Django project.

It contains:

text
manage.py
College/

Think of it as the container for your project.

3. manage.py

We've already seen this.

text
College/
│
├── manage.py

manage.py is a command-line utility for interacting with your particular Django project.

For example:

bash
python manage.py runserver
bash
python manage.py startapp students
bash
python manage.py migrate
bash
python manage.py makemigrations
bash
python manage.py createsuperuser

So:

manage.py provides a convenient way to execute Django management commands for a specific project.

4. Inner College Folder

Now:

text
College/
│
└── College/

This inner folder is the Python package containing the project's configuration.

It contains:

text
__init__.py
settings.py
urls.py
asgi.py
wsgi.py

This is where the main Django project configuration lives.

5. __init__.py

You'll see:

text
__init__.py

This is a Python package file.

Its presence historically tells Python that the directory should be treated as a package. In modern Python, namespace packages can exist without it, but Django's generated project structure includes it.

For your Django course, the important point is:

__init__.py marks/helps define the directory as a Python package and allows package-related Python imports.

Usually, you don't need to modify it.

6. settings.py

This is one of the most important files in Django.

It contains the configuration of your Django project.

For example:

python
DEBUG = True
python
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
]
python
MIDDLEWARE = [
    ...
]
python
ROOT_URLCONF = 'College.urls'
python
DATABASES = {
    ...
}

We'll study these settings throughout the course.

Think:

settings.py = project configuration

7. What Kind of Things Are Configured in settings.py?

Many things.

Installed applications

python
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
]

Middleware

python
MIDDLEWARE = [
    ...
]

Templates

python
TEMPLATES = [
    ...
]

Database

python
DATABASES = {
    ...
}

Static files

python
STATIC_URL = 'static/'

Time zone

python
TIME_ZONE = 'UTC'

Debug mode

python
DEBUG = True

And many other settings.

8. DEBUG

You'll see:

python
DEBUG = True

during development.

When something goes wrong, Django can show detailed debugging information.

For example:

text
Traceback
File
Line number
Error message

This is useful while developing.

But:

You should not run a production deployment with DEBUG = True.

Why?

Because detailed error pages can expose sensitive information.

We'll discuss this more when we reach debugging and deployment concepts.

9. INSTALLED_APPS

Another extremely important setting:

python
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
]

It tells Django which applications are installed/enabled in the project.

Later, when we create an app:

bash
python manage.py startapp students

we'll need to make Django aware of the app, commonly by adding its configuration to INSTALLED_APPS.

We'll cover this carefully in Module 5.

10. DATABASES

You will find something similar to:

python
DATABASES = {
    'default': {
        'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.sqlite3',
        'NAME': BASE_DIR / 'db.sqlite3',
    }
}

This configures the database.

The default Django project uses:

SQLite

for development.

Later, your syllabus has an entire topic on:

Database configuration

We'll study:

text
SQLite
MySQL
PostgreSQL

later.

11. TEMPLATES

settings.py also contains template configuration.

Conceptually:

text
Django
  ↓
Template configuration
  ↓
HTML templates

Later, when we create HTML templates, this setting becomes important.

12. urls.py

Now we come to another extremely important file.

text
College/
└── College/
    └── urls.py

This file contains the project's URL configuration.

For example, conceptually:

python
urlpatterns = [
    ...
]

Django uses URL patterns to determine what should happen when a user visits a URL.

For example:

text
/about/

could be connected to:

text
about()

and:

text
/students/

could be connected to:

text
students()

We'll learn this in detail in Unit II.

13. Why Is urls.py Important?

Suppose the browser requests:

text
/students/

Django needs to determine:

"Which code should handle /students/?"

The URL configuration helps answer that question.

Conceptually:

text
/students/
     ↓
urls.py
     ↓
students view

14. ROOT_URLCONF

Inside settings.py, you'll see something similar to:

python
ROOT_URLCONF = 'College.urls'

This tells Django where the root URL configuration is located.

In this case:

text
College.urls

means:

text
College package
     ↓
urls.py

So Django knows where to start looking for URL patterns.

15. wsgi.py

Now we have:

text
wsgi.py

WSGI stands for:

Web Server Gateway Interface

It is a standard interface between Python web applications/frameworks and web servers.

You don't need to master deployment yet.

For your current level, remember:

WSGI provides a standard interface for running Python web applications with WSGI-compatible web servers.

You'll often see:

python
application = get_wsgi_application()

inside the file.

16. asgi.py

ASGI stands for:

Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface

It is a newer interface designed to support asynchronous Python web applications and broader communication patterns.

Django provides an ASGI application through:

text
asgi.py

You'll see something conceptually like:

python
application = get_asgi_application()

For now:

text
WSGI → traditional synchronous Python web deployment

ASGI → supports asynchronous capabilities

Don't worry about deployment details yet.

17. WSGI vs ASGI

This can be a viva question.

WSGI ASGI
Web Server Gateway Interface Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface
Traditionally synchronous Supports asynchronous applications
Older Python web interface Newer interface
Suitable for traditional request-response apps Supports async and broader connection patterns

Viva answer

WSGI is a standard interface for deploying Python web applications, traditionally focused on synchronous request handling, while ASGI extends this model to support asynchronous applications and communication.

18. Complete Project Structure

Now put everything together:

text
College/
│
├── manage.py
│
└── College/
    │
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── settings.py
    ├── urls.py
    ├── asgi.py
    └── wsgi.py

Remember:

text
manage.py
   ↓
Commands

settings.py
   ↓
Configuration

urls.py
   ↓
URL routing

__init__.py
   ↓
Python package

wsgi.py
   ↓
WSGI deployment interface

asgi.py
   ↓
ASGI deployment interface

19. Where Is the Database?

After you run migrations, you may see:

text
db.sqlite3

So eventually your project can look like:

text
College/
│
├── manage.py
├── db.sqlite3
│
└── College/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── settings.py
    ├── urls.py
    ├── asgi.py
    └── wsgi.py

db.sqlite3 is the SQLite database file used by the default development configuration.

20. Where Are Apps?

After creating an app:

bash
python manage.py startapp students

you'll get:

text
College/
│
├── manage.py
│
├── College/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── settings.py
│   ├── urls.py
│   ├── asgi.py
│   └── wsgi.py
│
└── students/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── admin.py
    ├── apps.py
    ├── models.py
    ├── tests.py
    ├── views.py
    └── migrations/
        └── __init__.py

We'll create and understand this in Module 5.

21. Project Structure — Big Picture

Eventually, think of it like this:

text
                   Django Project
                        |
        +---------------+---------------+
        |                               |
 Project Configuration              Apps
        |                               |
   +----+----+                    +-----+-----+
   |    |    |                    |     |     |
settings urls  ...              views models templates

The project controls the overall configuration.

Apps contain specific functionality.

22. Very Important: Don't Confuse These

settings.py

Configuration.

urls.py

URL routing.

views.py

Application/request logic.

models.py

Database/data representation.

templates/

HTML/presentation.

This gives us:

text
URL
 ↓
View
 ↓
Model
 ↓
Template
 ↓
Response

We'll build this architecture step-by-step.

23. How Does Django Know Which Settings to Use?

When you run:

bash
python manage.py runserver

Django needs to know which settings module belongs to your project.

manage.py sets the appropriate environment configuration for the project.

The project settings are then loaded.

This is one reason manage.py is more than just a random Python file—it is specifically generated for your project.

24. What Does manage.py Actually Contain?

You'll see something roughly like:

python
import os
import sys

def main():
    os.environ.setdefault(
        'DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE',
        'College.settings'
    )

    from django.core.management import execute_from_command_line
    execute_from_command_line(sys.argv)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Don't memorize this code.

Understand the important idea:

text
manage.py
   ↓
Sets Django settings module
   ↓
Loads Django management system
   ↓
Executes the command you typed

For example:

bash
python manage.py runserver

The command is passed to Django's management system.

25. Why Do We Need DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE?

This environment variable tells Django:

"Which settings module should I use?"

For our project:

text
College.settings

means:

text
College/
   ↓
settings.py

So conceptually:

text
DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE
          ↓
College.settings
          ↓
settings.py

This is a more advanced detail, but knowing it can impress in a viva.

26. Viva Questions — Project Structure

Q1. What is manage.py?

It is a project-specific command-line utility used to execute Django management commands.

Q2. What is settings.py?

It contains the configuration settings of a Django project.

Q3. What is urls.py?

It contains the URL configuration used to map URL patterns to views or other URL configurations.

Q4. What is __init__.py?

It is a Python package initialization file. Django includes it in project and app packages.

Q5. What is WSGI?

WSGI stands for Web Server Gateway Interface and provides a standard interface between Python web applications and compatible web servers.

Q6. What is ASGI?

ASGI stands for Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface and provides an interface supporting asynchronous Python web applications and communication patterns.

Q7. What is DEBUG?

DEBUG controls whether Django runs in debug mode and provides detailed debugging information. It should not be enabled in production.

Q8. What is INSTALLED_APPS?

It is a setting containing the applications enabled in a Django project.

Q9. What is DATABASES?

It is the Django setting used to configure database connections.

Q10. What is ROOT_URLCONF?

It specifies the Python module containing the root URL configuration of the Django project.

27. Viva Tricky Question ⚠️

Teacher:

"Where do we write database queries?"

A beginner might say:

settings.py

❌ Not normally.

settings.py configures the database connection.

Database interaction is typically performed through:

text
models
   +
Django ORM

So:

settings.py tells Django which database/how to connect, while models and the ORM are used to work with the data.

28. Another Tricky Question ⚠️

Teacher:

"Where do we write HTML?"

The basic answer:

In templates.

For example:

text
templates/
   home.html

We'll study templates extensively in Unit III.

29. Another Tricky Question

Teacher:

"Does urls.py contain the HTML page?"

No.

urls.py defines URL routing.

It can connect a URL to a view:

text
URL
 ↓
View

The view can then render a template:

text
View
 ↓
Template

Module 5 — Creating a Django App

This is where we'll start writing our first actual Django application code. We'll create an app, understand views.py, models.py, admin.py, apps.py, tests.py, the migrations folder, register the app, and then connect our first app to the project.

Module 5
Creating a Django App

Module 5 — Creating a Django App

This is a very important module because from here we'll start building actual Django applications.

By the end, you'll understand:

  • Project vs App
  • Why Django uses apps
  • How to create an app
  • startapp
  • App folder structure
  • views.py
  • models.py
  • admin.py
  • apps.py
  • tests.py
  • migrations/
  • __init__.py
  • INSTALLED_APPS
  • How a newly created app connects to the project

1. Project vs App — First Understand This Properly

This is one of the most frequently asked Django viva questions.

Suppose we're building:

College Management System

The complete website/application is the project.

Inside it, we might have:

text
College Management System
│
├── Students
├── Teachers
├── Courses
├── Attendance
└── Accounts

Each of these can be a Django app.

So:

text
PROJECT
   │
   ├── App 1
   ├── App 2
   ├── App 3
   └── App 4

Easy analogy

Think about a college.

The college is the:

Project

Different departments are:

Apps

For example:

text
College
│
├── CSE Department
├── ECE Department
├── Mechanical Department
└── Civil Department

Each department performs a particular function but belongs to the same college.

Similarly:

text
Django Project
│
├── accounts
├── students
├── courses
└── attendance

2. What is a Django App?

A Django app is a Python package that provides a specific functionality within a Django project.

For example:

text
accounts → user-related functionality
products → product functionality
orders → order functionality

A project can contain multiple apps.

An app can also potentially be reusable across different projects.

3. Why Does Django Use Apps?

Imagine you create a huge application containing:

text
Users
Products
Orders
Payments
Reviews
Notifications

If all code is placed together, the project becomes difficult to maintain.

Instead:

text
accounts/
products/
orders/
payments/
reviews/
notifications/

Each app has a specific responsibility.

This follows an important software engineering idea:

Separation of concerns

4. Creating an App

Suppose our project is:

text
College

First enter the directory containing manage.py:

bash
cd College

Then run:

bash
python manage.py startapp students

This creates an app named:

text
students

5. Understanding the Command

bash
python manage.py startapp students

Break it down:

text
python

Use Python.

text
manage.py

Use the project's management utility.

text
startapp

Django command for creating an app.

text
students

Name of the app.

Therefore:

python manage.py startapp students creates a Django application named students.

6. What Does Django Create?

After running:

bash
python manage.py startapp students

your structure becomes approximately:

text
College/
│
├── manage.py
│
├── College/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── settings.py
│   ├── urls.py
│   ├── asgi.py
│   └── wsgi.py
│
└── students/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── admin.py
    ├── apps.py
    ├── models.py
    ├── tests.py
    ├── views.py
    │
    └── migrations/
        └── __init__.py

Now let's understand every file.

7. views.py

This is one of the most important files.

text
students/
└── views.py

Views contain code that handles requests and returns responses.

For example:

python
from django.http import HttpResponse

def home(request):
    return HttpResponse("Welcome to Students App")

Here:

text
home()

is a view function.

The basic idea is:

text
Browser
   ↓
Request
   ↓
View
   ↓
Response
   ↓
Browser

We'll spend a lot of time on views in Module 6.

8. models.py

This file is used to define models.

Models represent application data.

Suppose our students app needs student information.

We might eventually write:

python
from django.db import models

class Student(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    age = models.IntegerField()

This model represents student data.

Conceptually:

text
Student
----------------
id
name
age

Django can use this model to interact with the database.

We'll study models in great detail in Unit V.

9. admin.py

This file is used to configure/register models with Django's admin interface.

For example, later we might write:

python
from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Student

admin.site.register(Student)

Then the Student model can be managed through Django Admin.

Conceptually:

text
Model
  ↓
admin.py
  ↓
Django Admin
  ↓
Manage Data

We'll study this in Unit V.

10. apps.py

This file contains the configuration class for the app.

For example, Django generates something similar to:

python
from django.apps import AppConfig

class StudentsConfig(AppConfig):
    default_auto_field = 'django.db.models.BigAutoField'
    name = 'students'

This tells Django about the app's configuration.

You generally won't need to modify it much at the beginner level.

11. tests.py

This file is intended for tests for your app.

For example:

python
from django.test import TestCase

You can create test cases to verify that your application behaves correctly.

Example concept:

text
Test:
"Does the home page return HTTP 200?"

We'll cover Django testing later.

12. migrations/

You will see:

text
migrations/

This directory stores migration files related to database schema changes.

Initially:

text
migrations/
└── __init__.py

Later, after creating models and running:

bash
python manage.py makemigrations

you may see something like:

text
migrations/
├── __init__.py
└── 0001_initial.py

Migrations are extremely important in Django.

We'll dedicate a full module to them.

13. __init__.py Inside the App

Just like the project package:

text
students/
└── __init__.py

This is related to Python package structure.

You normally don't need to modify it.

14. Does Creating an App Automatically Activate It?

No.

This is a very important point.

You run:

bash
python manage.py startapp students

Django creates the app files.

But you also need to tell the project that the app is installed.

15. Registering the App

Open:

text
College/settings.py

Find:

python
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
]

Add your app.

You can use:

python
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    'students',
]

or, commonly:

python
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    'students.apps.StudentsConfig',
]

The exact generated app configuration class depends on the app name.

For our app:

text
students

Django generates:

text
StudentsConfig

in:

text
students/apps.py

So:

python
'students.apps.StudentsConfig'

tells Django to use that app configuration.

16. Why Is INSTALLED_APPS Important?

It tells Django:

"These applications are part of my project."

Django uses this information for various framework functionality, including models, migrations, admin integration, and app configuration.

Conceptually:

text
Project
   ↓
settings.py
   ↓
INSTALLED_APPS
   ↓
students
   ↓
Django knows about students app

17. Common Beginner Mistake

You create:

bash
python manage.py startapp students

Then you create a model:

python
class Student(models.Model):
    ...

Then run:

bash
python manage.py makemigrations

but Django doesn't detect the model as expected.

One common reason is that the app hasn't been added to:

python
INSTALLED_APPS

So always remember:

text
startapp
   ↓
Create app
   ↓
Add app to INSTALLED_APPS

18. App Structure — Memorize This

For an app named students:

text
students/
│
├── __init__.py
├── admin.py
├── apps.py
├── models.py
├── tests.py
├── views.py
│
└── migrations/
    └── __init__.py

Remember the core files:

text
views.py
→ Views

models.py
→ Models

admin.py
→ Admin

apps.py
→ App configuration

tests.py
→ Tests

migrations/
→ Database schema-change history

19. Let's Create Our First View

Now we'll write our first actual Django code.

Open:

text
students/views.py

Write:

python
from django.http import HttpResponse

def home(request):
    return HttpResponse("Hello from Students App!")

Let's understand this.

20. from django.http import HttpResponse

python
from django.http import HttpResponse

We're importing Django's HttpResponse class.

It allows us to create an HTTP response.

21. def home(request)

python
def home(request):

We're creating a Python function called:

text
home

Django passes the HTTP request to this function.

The parameter:

text
request

contains information about the incoming HTTP request.

We'll study the request object deeply in Unit II.

22. return HttpResponse(...)

python
return HttpResponse("Hello from Students App!")

This creates an HTTP response containing:

text
Hello from Students App!

So the basic flow is:

text
Request
   ↓
home(request)
   ↓
HttpResponse
   ↓
Browser

23. But Will This Work Yet?

Not yet.

Why?

Because Django doesn't know that:

text
/students/

should call:

text
home()

We need to connect a URL to our view.

We'll do that properly in the next module.

For now, understand:

text
View exists
     ↓
Need URL mapping
     ↓
URL → View

24. Project URL vs App URL

Eventually, Django applications commonly have URL configurations at both levels.

For example:

text
College/urls.py

and:

text
students/urls.py

The project-level URLs can include the app's URLs.

Conceptually:

text
College/urls.py
       ↓
students/urls.py
       ↓
students.views.home

We'll build this in Module 6/7.

25. Why Separate urls.py for an App?

Django doesn't automatically create urls.py when you run startapp.

You can create it yourself.

For example:

text
students/
├── views.py
├── models.py
└── urls.py

This helps keep URL patterns belonging to the app organized.

For a large project:

text
College
│
├── accounts
│   └── urls.py
│
├── students
│   └── urls.py
│
├── courses
│   └── urls.py
│
└── orders
    └── urls.py

This is much easier to maintain.

26. Complete Structure So Far

Our project now looks like:

text
College/
│
├── manage.py
│
├── College/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── settings.py
│   ├── urls.py
│   ├── asgi.py
│   └── wsgi.py
│
└── students/
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── admin.py
    ├── apps.py
    ├── models.py
    ├── tests.py
    ├── views.py
    │
    └── migrations/
        └── __init__.py

27. Project-Level vs App-Level Files

This distinction is useful:

Project

text
College/
├── settings.py
├── urls.py
├── asgi.py
└── wsgi.py

App

text
students/
├── admin.py
├── apps.py
├── models.py
├── tests.py
├── views.py
└── migrations/

So don't confuse:

text
College/urls.py

with:

text
students/urls.py

The first is project-level URL configuration.

The second is an app-level URL configuration that you create when needed.

28. Can a Project Have Multiple Apps?

Yes.

Example:

text
College/
│
├── accounts/
├── students/
├── teachers/
├── courses/
└── attendance/

All of them can belong to the same project.

29. Can an App Be Used in Multiple Projects?

Yes, if designed appropriately.

This is one reason Django's app-based architecture is useful.

For example, a reusable accounts app could potentially be used in multiple Django projects.

30. Viva Questions — Very Important

Q1. What is a Django app?

A Django app is a Python package that provides a specific functionality within a Django project.

Q2. What command creates an app?

bash
python manage.py startapp app_name

Q3. Does startapp create a project?

No.

It creates an app inside an existing Django project context.

Q4. What is the difference between project and app?

A project is the overall Django application/configuration, while an app is a component that provides a specific functionality within the project.

Q5. What is views.py?

views.py contains view functions or classes that handle requests and produce responses.

Q6. What is models.py?

models.py is used to define Django models that represent application data and interact with the database through the ORM.

Q7. What is admin.py?

admin.py is used to configure the Django admin interface, including registering models with the admin site.

Q8. What is apps.py?

apps.py contains the configuration class for the Django app.

Q9. What is tests.py?

tests.py is used to define automated tests for the application.

Q10. What is the migrations folder?

It stores migration files that describe changes to the database schema.

31. Tricky Viva Question ⚠️

Teacher:

"I ran python manage.py startapp students. Is my app now available to Django?"

Best answer:

The app files have been created, but the app should be added to INSTALLED_APPS in the project's settings so Django recognizes it as an installed application.

32. Tricky Viva Question

Teacher:

"Where do you write database configuration?"

Don't answer:

models.py

The better answer is:

Database connection configuration is specified in settings.py, while database models and database operations are handled through models and Django's ORM.

33. Tricky Viva Question

Teacher:

"Can I put all functionality into one Django app?"

Technically:

Yes, but it is generally better to divide a sufficiently large project into apps based on functionality and responsibility.

For example:

text
Bad organization for a large system:

everything/

Better:

text
accounts/
products/
orders/
payments/

34. Practical Coding Question

Question:

Create a Django app called students.

Answer:

bash
python manage.py startapp students

Then add:

python
'students',

to:

python
INSTALLED_APPS

35. Practical Coding Question

Question:

Create a view that returns "Welcome Students".

Answer:

python
from django.http import HttpResponse

def home(request):
    return HttpResponse("Welcome Students")

This is the first Django view code you should know.

36. Practical Coding Question

Question:

Create a view that returns "Hello World".

python
from django.http import HttpResponse

def hello(request):
    return HttpResponse("Hello World")

Notice:

text
hello

is simply the Python function name.

It could be:

python
def home(request):

or:

python
def welcome(request):

The name itself isn't special. What matters is how you connect the view to a URL.

37. Important Concept — Function-Based View

Our view:

python
def home(request):
    return HttpResponse("Hello")

is called a:

Function-Based View (FBV)

because the view is implemented as a Python function.

Later you'll encounter:

Class-Based Views (CBVs)

We'll focus on function-based views first because they make Django's fundamentals easier to understand.

38. The Django App Lifecycle — Basic Understanding

When you create an app:

text
startapp
   ↓
App files created
   ↓
Add app to INSTALLED_APPS
   ↓
Create views/models/etc.
   ↓
Connect URLs
   ↓
Run application

This is the workflow you'll repeatedly use.

The most important distinction:

text
PROJECT
   ↓
Overall Django application/configuration

APP
   ↓
Specific functionality

Create app:

bash
python manage.py startapp students

Core app files:

text
students/
│
├── admin.py       → Admin configuration
├── apps.py        → App configuration
├── models.py      → Models/data
├── tests.py       → Tests

│

And:
