Module 11
Error Handling in Django

Module 11 — Error Handling in Django

This is the last topic of Unit II.

Error handling is very important for both viva and practical coding, because your teacher can easily ask:

  • What happens when a URL doesn't exist?
  • What is a 404 error?
  • Difference between 404 and 500?
  • What is Http404?
  • What is get_object_or_404()?
  • Why should DEBUG=False be used in production?

Let's start from zero.

1. What Is an Error?

An error occurs when the application cannot complete the requested operation normally.

For example:

text
User requests:
    /student/999/
          ↓
Django
          ↓
Student doesn't exist
          ↓
404 Not Found

Or:

text
View contains a programming error
          ↓
Django cannot execute it
          ↓
500 Internal Server Error

2. HTTP Error Status Codes

You've already seen status codes in Module 8.

The important error codes are:

Code Meaning
400 Bad Request
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error

For Django URL/view error handling, 404 and 500 are particularly important.

3. 404 — Not Found

A 404 means:

The requested resource could not be found.

For example:

text
http://127.0.0.1:8000/hello/

If there is no matching URL pattern, Django returns:

text
404 Not Found

4. What Happens When a URL Doesn't Match?

Suppose your urls.py contains:

python
urlpatterns = [
    path('home/', views.home),
]

User requests:

text
/about/

Django checks:

text
/about/
   ↓
Does it match home/?
   ↓
No
   ↓
No other matching pattern
   ↓
404 Not Found

5. DEBUG=True

During development, Django normally has:

python
DEBUG = True

When an error occurs, Django displays a detailed debugging page.

For example, if your Python code contains an error:

python
def home(request):
    print(x)

where x doesn't exist, Django can show a detailed traceback.

This is extremely useful during development.

6. Why Is DEBUG=True Dangerous in Production?

Because the detailed error page can reveal sensitive technical information, such as:

  • File paths
  • Code details
  • Configuration information
  • Stack traces
  • Environment information

Therefore:

python
DEBUG = True

is for development.

Production should generally use:

python
DEBUG = False

7. Http404

Django provides:

python
from django.http import Http404

You can explicitly raise a 404 error.

Example:

python
def student(request, id):

    if id != 1:
        raise Http404("Student not found")

    return HttpResponse("Student found")

If the ID isn't 1, Django raises a 404.

8. What Does raise Http404 Mean?

This:

python
raise Http404

means:

Stop processing this view and tell Django that the requested resource was not found.

You can also provide a message:

python
raise Http404("Student not found")

9. Example With a List

Suppose:

python
students = [
    "Aman",
    "Rahul",
    "Rohit"
]

We can write:

python
from django.http import Http404, HttpResponse

def student(request, id):

    if id < 1 or id > len(students):
        raise Http404("Student not found")

    return HttpResponse(
        students[id - 1]
    )

Now:

text
/student/1/

returns:

text
Aman

while:

text
/student/10/

raises a 404.

10. get_object_or_404()

One of the most important Django shortcuts is:

python
get_object_or_404()

Import it:

python
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404

It is commonly used with Django models.

Suppose we have a model:

python
class Student(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)

We could write:

python
student = get_object_or_404(
    Student,
    id=id
)

If the student exists:

text
Student object

is returned.

If it doesn't exist:

text
404 Not Found

is raised.

11. Why Is get_object_or_404() Useful?

Without it, you might write:

python
try:
    student = Student.objects.get(id=id)
except Student.DoesNotExist:
    raise Http404("Student not found")

That's valid.

But Django provides:

python
student = get_object_or_404(
    Student,
    id=id
)

which is much cleaner.

12. What Does It Do Internally?

Conceptually:

text
get_object_or_404(Student, id=25)
              ↓
Try to get Student with id=25
              ↓
        ┌─────┴─────┐
        ↓           ↓
      Found       Not Found
        ↓           ↓
 Return object   Raise 404

This is why the function has that name:

Get object OR return a 404 response.

Technically, it raises Django's Http404 exception.

13. Important Coding Example

Suppose:

python
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404
from django.http import HttpResponse

def student_detail(request, id):

    student = get_object_or_404(
        Student,
        id=id
    )

    return HttpResponse(
        student.name
    )

URL:

python
path(
    'student/<int:id>/',
    views.student_detail
)

Request:

text
/student/25/

Django:

text
id = 25
   ↓
Search Student with id=25
   ↓
Found?
   ├── Yes → display student
   └── No → 404

14. Student.objects.get() vs get_object_or_404()

Suppose:

python
Student.objects.get(id=25)

If the object doesn't exist, Django raises:

text
Student.DoesNotExist

You would have to handle it.

With:

python
get_object_or_404(Student, id=25)

Django converts the missing-object situation into a 404 response.

15. 404 vs DoesNotExist

This distinction is useful for viva.

ORM:

python
Student.objects.get(id=25)

If missing:

text
Student.DoesNotExist

Shortcut:

python
get_object_or_404(Student, id=25)

If missing:

text
Http404

Therefore:

get_object_or_404() is convenient when a missing database object should result in an HTTP 404 response.

16. 500 — Internal Server Error

A 500 means:

Something went wrong on the server while processing the request.

For example:

python
def home(request):
    result = 10 / 0
    return HttpResponse(result)

This causes:

text
ZeroDivisionError

and Django will generally return a:

text
500 Internal Server Error

response.

17. 500 Is Usually a Programming/Server Problem

Examples:

text
SyntaxError
NameError
TypeError
Database error
Unexpected exception

can result in server errors depending on the circumstances.

For example:

python
def home(request):
    print(student_name)

If student_name isn't defined, Django encounters:

text
NameError

18. 400 — Bad Request

A 400 generally means:

The server cannot process the request because the request is invalid.

For example:

python
return HttpResponse(
    "Bad request",
    status=400
)

You can explicitly return a 400 response when appropriate.

19. 403 — Forbidden

403 generally means:

The server understood the request but refuses to allow the requested action.

Example:

text
User tries to access an admin-only operation
             ↓
Permission denied
             ↓
403 Forbidden

We'll study permissions later.

20. 401 — Unauthorized

401 generally indicates:

Authentication is required or the authentication attempt failed.

Don't confuse:

text
401 → authentication
403 → authorization/access refusal

This distinction is commonly asked in interviews.

21. Custom 404 Page

Django allows you to create a custom:

text
404.html

For example:

html
<h1>Page Not Found</h1>
<p>Sorry, the requested page doesn't exist.</p>

When Django handles a 404 in production, it can use the custom template.

22. Custom 500 Page

Similarly:

text
500.html

can be used for server errors.

Example:

html
<h1>Something went wrong</h1>
<p>Please try again later.</p>

23. Important: DEBUG

For development:

python
DEBUG = True

For production:

python
DEBUG = False

With:

python
DEBUG = True

Django displays detailed debugging information.

With:

python
DEBUG = False

users should see a friendly error page instead of the detailed traceback.

24. Why Custom Error Pages?

Imagine a real website showing:

text
Traceback:
File "/home/server/project/app/views.py", line 47...

to a normal user.

That's bad UX and potentially a security problem.

Instead:

text
Oops!
Something went wrong.
Please try again later.

is better.

25. Handling Exceptions With try/except

Python's exception handling can also be used in Django.

Example:

python
def divide(request):
    try:
        result = 10 / 0
        return HttpResponse(result)

    except ZeroDivisionError:
        return HttpResponse(
            "Cannot divide by zero",
            status=400
        )

Here the Python exception is handled explicitly.

26. But Don't Catch Everything Blindly

Avoid doing:

python
try:
    ...
except:
    return HttpResponse("Something went wrong")

without understanding the problem.

Why?

Because it can hide genuine programming errors.

Better:

python
except ZeroDivisionError:

when you specifically expect that exception.

27. Http404 vs try/except

Suppose an object isn't found.

You could write:

python
try:
    student = Student.objects.get(id=id)
except Student.DoesNotExist:
    raise Http404("Student not found")

Or simply:

python
student = get_object_or_404(
    Student,
    id=id
)

The second is cleaner.

28. Error Handling Flow

A useful mental model:

text
                    Request
                       ↓
                    Django
                       ↓
                    View
                       ↓
              ┌────────┴────────┐
              ↓                 ↓
           Success             Error
              ↓                 ↓
          200 response       Handle error
                                ↓
                       ┌────────┼────────┐
                       ↓        ↓        ↓
                      400      404      500

29. URL 404 vs Object 404

This is a very important distinction.

Case 1 — URL doesn't exist

Request:

text
/abcxyz/

No URL pattern matches.

Django returns:

text
404

Case 2 — URL exists but object doesn't

Request:

text
/student/999/

URL pattern matches, but student 999 doesn't exist.

Your view can use:

python
get_object_or_404()

and return:

text
404

So both can produce a 404, but for different reasons.

30. Complete Example

urls.py

python
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        'student/<int:id>/',
        views.student_detail
    ),
]

views.py

python
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404
from django.http import HttpResponse

def student_detail(request, id):

    student = get_object_or_404(
        Student,
        id=id
    )

    return HttpResponse(
        f"Student: {student.name}"
    )

If student exists:

text
Student: Aman

If student doesn't exist:

text
404 Not Found

31. Common Mistake

Beginners sometimes write:

python
student = Student.objects.get(id=id)

if student is None:
    raise Http404

This doesn't work as expected.

Why?

objects.get() doesn't return None when nothing is found.

It raises:

text
Student.DoesNotExist

Therefore either use:

python
try:
    student = Student.objects.get(id=id)
except Student.DoesNotExist:
    raise Http404

or preferably:

python
student = get_object_or_404(Student, id=id)

32. Common Mistake — DEBUG=True in Production

Never think:

python
DEBUG = True

should remain enabled because it helps you see errors.

It's useful during development, but production should normally have:

python
DEBUG = False

and proper production error handling/logging.

33. Common Mistake — Returning 500 for User Mistakes

Suppose a user submits invalid data.

Don't automatically do:

python
status=500

A 500 generally indicates an unexpected server-side failure.

For invalid client input, an appropriate response might be:

text
400 Bad Request

depending on the application.

34. Viva Questions

Q1. What is a 404 error?

A 404 Not Found response indicates that the requested resource could not be found.

Q2. What is a 500 error?

A 500 Internal Server Error indicates an unexpected error occurred while processing the request on the server.

Q3. What is Http404?

Http404 is a Django exception that can be raised when a requested resource does not exist.

Q4. What is get_object_or_404()?

It retrieves an object and raises Http404 if the object does not exist.

Q5. Why use get_object_or_404()?

It provides a concise way to convert a missing database object into an HTTP 404 response.

35. Important Viva Question

Teacher:

What's the difference between Student.objects.get() and get_object_or_404()?

Strong answer:

Student.objects.get() raises the model's DoesNotExist exception when no object is found, whereas get_object_or_404() catches the missing-object situation and raises Django's Http404, which results in a 404 HTTP response.

36. Important Viva Question

Teacher:

What's the difference between 401 and 403?

Answer:

401 Unauthorized generally indicates that authentication is required or has failed, while 403 Forbidden indicates that the server understands the request but refuses to authorize the requested action.

37. Important Viva Question

Teacher:

Why should DEBUG be False in production?

Answer:

Because Django's debug output can expose sensitive technical information such as stack traces, file paths, and configuration details. Production applications should not expose this information to users.

38. Coding Question

Question:

Write a view that raises a 404 if id is less than 1.

python
from django.http import Http404, HttpResponse

def student(request, id):

    if id < 1:
        raise Http404("Student not found")

    return HttpResponse(
        f"Student ID: {id}"
    )

39. Coding Question

Question:

Write a view that returns a 400 response.

python
from django.http import HttpResponse

def test(request):
    return HttpResponse(
        "Bad Request",
        status=400
    )

40. Coding Question

Question:

Retrieve a student or return 404.

python
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404

def student_detail(request, id):

    student = get_object_or_404(
        Student,
        id=id
    )

    return HttpResponse(
        student.name
    )

This is one of the most useful patterns to remember for future Django CRUD applications.

404:

text
Resource not found

500:

text
Unexpected server-side error

Explicit 404:

python
raise Http404

Object or 404:

python
get_object_or_404(Student, id=id)

Development:

python
DEBUG = True

Production:

python
DEBUG = False

Important status codes:

text
400 → Bad Request
401 → Authentication required/failed
403 → Forbidden
404 → Not Found
500 → Internal Server Error

Module 12
Introduction to Templates

Module 12 — Introduction to Django Templates

Now we start Unit III: Templates, Debugging and Testing.

Until now, our views have mostly returned:

python
return HttpResponse("Hello World")

That works for simple responses, but imagine building a real website with:

  • headings
  • buttons
  • navigation bars
  • tables
  • forms
  • images
  • CSS
  • dynamic data

Putting all of that HTML inside Python would become a mess.

That's exactly why Django Templates exist.

1. What Is a Template?

A Django template is usually an HTML file containing the structure of a webpage and special Django Template Language (DTL) syntax for dynamic content.

For example:

html
<h1>Welcome to my website</h1>
<p>Hello {{ name }}</p>

The HTML defines the page structure, while:

text
{{ name }}

allows Django to insert dynamic data.

2. Why Do We Need Templates?

Without templates:

python
def home(request):
    return HttpResponse(
        "<html>"
        "<body>"
        "<h1>Hello Aman</h1>"
        "<p>Welcome</p>"
        "</body>"
        "</html>"
    )

This becomes difficult to maintain.

With templates:

Python:

python
def home(request):
    return render(request, 'home.html')

HTML:

html
<h1>Hello Aman</h1>
<p>Welcome</p>

Much cleaner.

3. MVT Connection

Remember Django's MVT architecture:

text
Model
  ↓
Data

View
  ↓
Logic

Template
  ↓
Presentation

So:

Template is primarily responsible for presentation/UI.

The view decides what data should be sent to the template.

The template decides how that data should be displayed.

4. Basic Template Flow

The flow becomes:

text
Browser
   ↓
URL
   ↓
View
   ↓
Template
   ↓
HTML Response
   ↓
Browser

For example:

text
/students/
     ↓
students.urls
     ↓
views.home()
     ↓
home.html
     ↓
Browser

5. Creating a Template

Let's assume our project looks like:

text
College/
│
├── manage.py
│
├── College/
│   ├── settings.py
│   └── urls.py
│
└── students/
    ├── views.py
    ├── urls.py
    └── ...

There are multiple ways to organize templates.

A common beginner-friendly approach is to create:

text
templates/

inside the app:

text
students/
├── templates/
│   └── students/
│       └── home.html
├── views.py
└── urls.py

The extra students directory helps avoid template-name collisions between apps.

6. Create home.html

Create:

text
students/templates/students/home.html

Put:

html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Students</title>
</head>
<body>

    <h1>Welcome to Students App</h1>
    <p>This is my first Django template.</p>

</body>
</html>

7. How Does Django Find This Template?

Django's template system needs to know where templates are located.

If you're using the common app-template structure:

text
students/templates/students/home.html

make sure your app is included in:

python
INSTALLED_APPS

in settings.py.

For example:

python
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    'students',
]

Django can then discover templates inside installed apps when APP_DIRS is enabled.

8. APP_DIRS

Look at the default template configuration in settings.py:

python
TEMPLATES = [
    {
        'BACKEND': 'django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates',
        'DIRS': [],
        'APP_DIRS': True,
        ...
    },
]

The important part for our app template structure is:

python
APP_DIRS = True

This tells Django's template engine to look for templates inside installed apps.

9. Rendering a Template

Now go to:

text
students/views.py

Import:

python
from django.shortcuts import render

Then:

python
def home(request):
    return render(request, 'students/home.html')

That's it.

10. What Is render()?

The render() shortcut combines several operations for you.

Conceptually:

text
render()
   ↓
Find template
   ↓
Process template
   ↓
Generate HTML
   ↓
Return HttpResponse

So:

python
return render(
    request,
    'students/home.html'
)

means:

Render this template and return the generated HTML as an HTTP response.

11. render() Syntax

The basic syntax is:

python
render(request, template_name)

For example:

python
return render(
    request,
    'students/home.html'
)

Later we'll use:

python
render(
    request,
    'students/home.html',
    context
)

to send dynamic data.

12. Complete Example

students/views.py

python
from django.shortcuts import render

def home(request):
    return render(
        request,
        'students/home.html'
    )

students/templates/students/home.html

html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Students</title>
</head>
<body>

    <h1>Welcome to Students App</h1>

</body>
</html>

students/urls.py

python
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.home, name='home'),
]

Project College/urls.py

python
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('students/', include('students.urls')),
]

Now visit:

text
http://127.0.0.1:8000/students/

and Django renders:

text
Welcome to Students App

13. What Actually Happens?

Let's follow the complete request:

text
Browser
   |
   | GET /students/
   ↓
College/urls.py
   |
   | students/
   ↓
students/urls.py
   |
   | ''
   ↓
views.home(request)
   |
   ↓
render(request, 'students/home.html')
   |
   ↓
Django Template Engine
   |
   ↓
home.html
   |
   ↓
HTML response
   |
   ↓
Browser

This flow is extremely important.

14. Template vs View

A common viva question:

What should go in a view?

Usually:

  • request handling
  • application logic
  • retrieving data
  • deciding which response to return

What should go in a template?

Usually:

  • HTML
  • presentation
  • displaying data
  • template logic such as loops and conditions

For example:

View:

python
def student(request):
    students = [...]
    return render(
        request,
        'students.html',
        {'students': students}
    )

Template:

html
<h1>Students</h1>

{% for student in students %}
    <p>{{ student }}</p>
{% endfor %}

The view obtains/prepares the data.

The template displays it.

15. Dynamic Templates

The real power of templates is that they're not static.

Suppose your view has:

python
def home(request):
    name = "Aman"

    return render(
        request,
        'students/home.html',
        {'name': name}
    )

The third argument is called the context.

16. What Is Context?

Context is the data passed from a view to a template.

Example:

python
context = {
    'name': 'Aman',
    'age': 21
}

Then:

python
return render(
    request,
    'students/home.html',
    context
)

The template can access those values.

17. Displaying Context Data

In:

text
home.html

write:

html
<h1>Hello {{ name }}</h1>

<p>Age: {{ age }}</p>

Django replaces:

text
{{ name }}

with:

text
Aman

and:

text
{{ age }}

with:

text
21

The browser receives the final HTML, not the template syntax.

18. Important Template Syntax

Django Template Language has several important forms.

Variable:

text
{{ variable }}

Tag:

text
{% tag %}

Comment:

text
{# comment #}

These three are extremely important.

19. Variables

Example:

html
<h1>{{ name }}</h1>

If the context is:

python
{'name': 'Aman'}

Django produces:

html
<h1>Aman</h1>

20. Why Are There Double Curly Braces?

Django uses:

text
{{ }}

to indicate that it should evaluate and display a template variable.

For example:

html
<p>{{ username }}</p>

means:

Display the value of username.

21. Template Tags

Tags use:

text
{% %}

Example:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}
    <p>Adult</p>
{% endif %}

Unlike variables, tags generally control template behavior.

We'll study them in detail in the next modules.

22. Template Comments

Django has:

html
{# This is a comment #}

It won't appear in the rendered HTML.

For multi-line comments, Django provides:

html
{% comment %}
This is a
multi-line comment.
{% endcomment %}

23. Template Variables Can Be Dictionary Values

Suppose your view sends:

python
student = {
    'name': 'Aman',
    'age': 21,
    'course': 'CSE'
}

return render(
    request,
    'student.html',
    {'student': student}
)

Template:

html
<h1>{{ student.name }}</h1>
<p>{{ student.age }}</p>
<p>{{ student.course }}</p>

Output:

text
Aman
21
CSE

Django's dot syntax can access dictionary keys and other supported attributes/methods.

24. Template Variables With Objects

Later, when we learn models, you'll have:

python
student.name
student.age

In a template you can write:

html
{{ student.name }}
{{ student.age }}

This is one reason templates are so useful with Django models.

25. What If a Variable Doesn't Exist?

Suppose template contains:

html
<p>{{ xyz }}</p>

but xyz wasn't supplied in the context.

Django generally renders an empty string rather than raising a normal Python NameError.

So it might display:

text
[blank]

This can sometimes make template bugs harder to notice.

26. Context Dictionary

You can directly pass a dictionary:

python
return render(
    request,
    'students/home.html',
    {
        'name': 'Aman',
        'course': 'Django'
    }
)

Template:

html
<h1>{{ name }}</h1>
<p>Course: {{ course }}</p>

27. Better Practice — Named Context Variable

You can also create:

python
context = {
    'name': 'Aman',
    'course': 'Django'
}

return render(
    request,
    'students/home.html',
    context
)

This is easier to read when you have lots of data.

28. render() vs HttpResponse()

This is a common viva question.

HttpResponse

python
return HttpResponse("Hello")

Directly returns content.

render

python
return render(
    request,
    'home.html'
)

Loads and processes a template, then returns an HTTP response.

So:

text
HttpResponse
    ↓
Direct content

render()
    ↓
Template
    ↓
HTML response

29. Does render() Return an HTTP Response?

Yes.

Conceptually:

python
response = render(
    request,
    'home.html'
)

returns an HttpResponse object.

This is an excellent viva point.

30. Template Folder Structure

A recommended app-based structure:

text
students/
│
├── migrations/
├── templates/
│   └── students/
│       ├── home.html
│       ├── list.html
│       └── detail.html
│
├── views.py
├── models.py
└── urls.py

Why:

text
templates/students/

instead of simply:

text
templates/

?

Because different apps might have templates with the same filename.

For example:

text
students/templates/students/home.html
teachers/templates/teachers/home.html

Then they don't conflict.

31. Template Namespacing

Suppose both apps have:

text
home.html

If you use:

text
templates/home.html

in multiple apps, Django can encounter ambiguity depending on template search order.

Instead:

text
students/templates/students/home.html
teachers/templates/teachers/home.html

Then:

python
render(request, 'students/home.html')

and:

python
render(request, 'teachers/home.html')

are clearly separated.

32. Project-Level Templates

Another common approach is a project-level directory:

text
College/
├── manage.py
├── College/
├── students/
└── templates/
    └── home.html

Then configure:

python
TEMPLATES = [
    {
        ...
        'DIRS': [BASE_DIR / 'templates'],
        ...
    }
]

This tells Django to look in that project-level templates directory.

33. App Templates vs Project Templates

App templates

text
students/templates/students/home.html

Useful for templates belonging specifically to an app.

Project-level templates

text
templates/home.html

Useful for templates shared across the project.

Both approaches are valid.

34. Important Settings

Look at:

python
TEMPLATES = [
    {
        'BACKEND':
            'django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates',

        'DIRS': [],

        'APP_DIRS': True,

        'OPTIONS': {
            'context_processors': [
                ...
            ],
        },
    },
]

For now, remember:

BACKEND

Specifies Django's template backend.

DIRS

Specifies additional template directories.

APP_DIRS

Allows Django to search installed apps' template directories.

35. Common Error — TemplateDoesNotExist

Suppose your view says:

python
return render(
    request,
    'students/home.html'
)

but the file isn't where Django expects it.

You may see:

text
TemplateDoesNotExist

Possible reasons:

  • wrong filename
  • wrong folder
  • app not installed
  • incorrect DIRS
  • APP_DIRS=False
  • typo in template path

36. Example of Wrong Path

Actual file:

text
students/templates/students/home.html

Correct:

python
render(
    request,
    'students/home.html'
)

But if you write:

python
render(
    request,
    'home.html'
)

Django may not find the template depending on your configured template locations.

37. Common Error — App Not Installed

Suppose you have:

text
students/
└── templates/
    └── students/
        └── home.html

but forgot to add:

python
'students'

to:

python
INSTALLED_APPS

With app-directory template discovery enabled, Django won't discover the app's templates as expected.

38. Complete Dynamic Example

Let's create a real example.

views.py

python
from django.shortcuts import render

def home(request):

    context = {
        'name': 'Aman',
        'course': 'Django',
        'age': 21
    }

    return render(
        request,
        'students/home.html',
        context
    )

home.html

html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Student</title>
</head>

<body>

    <h1>Hello {{ name }}</h1>

    <p>Course: {{ course }}</p>

    <p>Age: {{ age }}</p>

</body>
</html>

Output:

text
Hello Aman
Course: Django
Age: 21

39. What Happens Before the Browser Sees It?

The browser does not receive:

html
<h1>Hello {{ name }}</h1>

Instead Django processes the template first.

Conceptually:

text
Template:
<h1>Hello {{ name }}</h1>

        ↓ Django

Final HTML:
<h1>Hello Aman</h1>

        ↓

Browser

This is important.

40. Template Engine

The component responsible for processing Django templates is the Django template engine.

It:

  1. Loads the template
  2. Receives context
  3. Evaluates template syntax
  4. Produces final HTML
  5. Returns it as part of the response

41. Very Important Distinction

Django template language is not Python.

For example:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}

looks somewhat like Python, but template syntax has its own rules.

Don't assume you can write arbitrary Python code inside a template.

Django intentionally limits template logic so presentation doesn't become a full programming environment.

42. Should We Put Business Logic in Templates?

Generally, no.

Bad design:

text
Template
   ↓
Huge complicated application logic

Better:

text
View
   ↓
Prepare/process data
   ↓
Template
   ↓
Display data

Templates should primarily focus on presentation.

43. Viva Questions

Q1. What is a Django template?

A Django template is typically an HTML file containing presentation markup and Django Template Language syntax for displaying dynamic data and controlling presentation.

Q2. Why are templates used?

Templates separate presentation logic from Python application logic and make HTML easier to maintain.

Q3. What is render()?

render() is a Django shortcut that loads a template, combines it with context data, and returns an HTTP response.

Q4. What is context?

Context is the data passed from a view to a template.

Q5. What does {{ variable }} mean?

It is Django Template Language syntax used to display a variable's value.

Q6. What does {% ... %} represent?

It represents a Django template tag used for template operations such as conditions and loops.

44. Very Important Viva

Teacher:

What is the difference between {{ }} and {% %}?

Answer:

{{ }} is used primarily to display or resolve variable values, while {% %} is used for template tags that perform operations such as conditions, loops, and template inheritance.

45. Another Viva

Teacher:

Does render() directly return HTML text?

Better answer:

render() loads and renders a template using the supplied context and returns an HttpResponse containing the rendered content.

46. Coding Question

Question:

Create a Django view that sends a student's name and age to an HTML template.

Answer:

python
from django.shortcuts import render

def student(request):

    context = {
        'name': 'Aman',
        'age': 21
    }

    return render(
        request,
        'student.html',
        context
    )

Template:

html
<h1>{{ name }}</h1>
<p>{{ age }}</p>

47. Coding Question

Question:

Display a course name dynamically.

View:

python
def course(request):

    return render(
        request,
        'course.html',
        {
            'course_name': 'Django'
        }
    )

Template:

html
<h1>Course: {{ course_name }}</h1>

Output:

text
Course: Django

48. Exam Question

Explain the flow of data from a Django view to a template.

Strong answer:

The view receives the HTTP request, prepares the required data, and passes that data as a context dictionary to the render() function. Django's template engine loads the specified template, resolves the template variables using the context, generates the final HTML, and returns it as an HTTP response to the client.

That's an excellent long-answer/viva response.

{% if condition %}

context = {

students/

Module 13
Django Template Language (DTL)

Module 13 — Django Template Language (DTL)

Now we move into the core of Django templates.

You already know how to create an HTML template and pass data from a view. Now we need to learn how Django actually works with that data inside the HTML file.

This is called Django Template Language (DTL).

1. What Is DTL?

DTL = Django Template Language

It is Django's template syntax used to:

  • Display data
  • Work with variables
  • Use conditions
  • Use loops
  • Apply filters
  • Include/reuse templates
  • Generate dynamic HTML

For example:

html
<h1>Hello {{ name }}</h1>

If the view sends:

python
{'name': 'Aman'}

Django renders:

html
<h1>Hello Aman</h1>

2. DTL Is Not Python

This is extremely important for viva.

DTL is designed for templates and presentation. It is not simply Python embedded inside HTML.

For example, you cannot normally write arbitrary Python code such as:

python
for i in range(10):

inside a Django template.

Instead, DTL provides its own syntax:

html
{% for i in numbers %}
{% endfor %}

3. Three Main DTL Syntaxes

You should memorize these three.

1. Variable

html
{{ variable }}

Used to display data.

2. Tag

html
{% tag %}

Used for template operations.

Examples:

html
{% if %}
{% for %}
{% url %}
{% block %}

3. Comment

html
{# comment #}

Used for comments.

4. DTL Variable

Suppose your view is:

python
from django.shortcuts import render

def home(request):
    return render(
        request,
        'home.html',
        {'name': 'Aman'}
    )

Template:

html
<h1>Hello {{ name }}</h1>

Output:

text
Hello Aman

5. How Does Django Find name?

The context is:

python
{
    'name': 'Aman'
}

Therefore Django creates a template context containing:

text
name → Aman

When the template encounters:

text
{{ name }}

it resolves the variable and outputs:

text
Aman

6. Multiple Variables

View:

python
def home(request):

    context = {
        'name': 'Aman',
        'age': 21,
        'course': 'CSE'
    }

    return render(
        request,
        'home.html',
        context
    )

Template:

html
<h1>{{ name }}</h1>
<p>Age: {{ age }}</p>
<p>Course: {{ course }}</p>

Output:

text
Aman
Age: 21
Course: CSE

7. Variable Names Are Case-Sensitive

Suppose context contains:

python
{
    'name': 'Aman'
}

Then:

html
{{ name }}

works.

But:

html
{{ Name }}

does not refer to the same context variable.

So be careful with spelling and capitalization.

8. Dictionary Data

Suppose your view contains:

python
student = {
    'name': 'Aman',
    'age': 21,
    'course': 'CSE'
}

return render(
    request,
    'student.html',
    {'student': student}
)

You can access dictionary values using dot notation:

html
<h1>{{ student.name }}</h1>
<p>{{ student.age }}</p>
<p>{{ student.course }}</p>

Output:

text
Aman
21
CSE

9. Important: Dot Notation

Django template syntax uses:

text
{{ object.attribute }}

It can resolve different types of things, including dictionary lookups and attributes.

For example:

html
{{ student.name }}

can resolve the name value from the context object.

This becomes extremely useful when we start using Django Models.

10. Nested Data

Suppose:

python
student = {
    'name': 'Aman',
    'address': {
        'city': 'Phagwara',
        'state': 'Punjab'
    }
}

Pass:

python
{
    'student': student
}

Template:

html
<p>Name: {{ student.name }}</p>
<p>City: {{ student.address.city }}</p>
<p>State: {{ student.address.state }}</p>

Django can traverse the nested structure using dot notation.

11. Lists

Suppose:

python
students = [
    'Aman',
    'Rahul',
    'Rohit'
]

Pass:

python
return render(
    request,
    'students.html',
    {'students': students}
)

A loop can later display the values:

html
{% for student in students %}
    <p>{{ student }}</p>
{% endfor %}

We'll study loops in depth in a later module.

12. Accessing List Elements

Django templates can resolve numeric indexes using dot notation.

Suppose:

python
students = ['Aman', 'Rahul', 'Rohit']

Then:

html
{{ students.0 }}

gives:

text
Aman

And:

html
{{ students.1 }}

gives:

text
Rahul

This is useful to know for viva questions.

13. What If a Variable Doesn't Exist?

Suppose your context is:

python
{
    'name': 'Aman'
}

but template contains:

html
{{ age }}

Since age isn't available, Django generally renders an empty string.

So you may see:

text
[blank]

rather than a Python NameError.

14. DTL Comments

Single-line comment:

html
{# This is a comment #}

It won't be rendered as visible HTML.

For multiple lines:

html
{% comment %}
This is a
multi-line comment.
{% endcomment %}

15. DTL Tags

Tags are written using:

html
{% ... %}

Some important tags are:

html
{% if %}
{% else %}
{% elif %}
{% endif %}

{% for %}
{% endfor %}

{% url %}

{% extends %}
{% block %}

{% include %}

We'll learn each of these throughout the next modules.

16. Variable vs Tag

This is a common viva question.

Variable:

html
{{ name }}

Purpose:

Display/resolve a value.

Tag:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}

Purpose:

Perform a template operation.

Remember:

text
{{ }} → value
{% %} → operation

17. Filters

DTL also provides filters.

Filters modify or process values before displaying them.

Syntax:

html
{{ variable|filter }}

For example:

html
{{ name|upper }}

If:

text
name = Aman

output:

text
AMAN

The pipe:

text
|

means:

Apply this filter to the value.

18. upper Filter

Example:

html
{{ name|upper }}

If:

text
name = Aman

output:

text
AMAN

19. lower Filter

html
{{ name|lower }}

If:

text
name = AMAN

output:

text
aman

20. title Filter

html
{{ name|title }}

For example:

text
hello django world

becomes approximately:

text
Hello Django World

21. length Filter

You can determine the length of a value.

html
{{ name|length }}

If:

text
name = Aman

output:

text
4

For a list:

html
{{ students|length }}

it gives the number of items.

22. default Filter

Suppose:

python
name = ''

You can write:

html
{{ name|default:"Guest" }}

If name is empty, the output is:

text
Guest

This is very useful.

23. Filter Chaining

You can apply multiple filters.

Example:

html
{{ name|upper|length }}

If:

text
name = aman

First:

text
aman
 ↓ upper
AMAN
 ↓ length
4

Output:

text
4

24. safe Filter

Django templates automatically escape potentially unsafe HTML in many normal variable-rendering situations.

Suppose context contains:

python
{
    'message': '<b>Hello</b>'
}

Template:

html
{{ message }}

Django will normally escape the HTML rather than interpret it as markup.

This helps protect against certain XSS attacks.

25. What Does safe Do?

If you intentionally trust the content and write:

html
{{ message|safe }}

Django treats the value as safe HTML for rendering.

For example:

html
{{ message|safe }}

can render:

html
<b>Hello</b>

as bold text.

Important security rule:

Never blindly use:

html
{{ user_input|safe }}

on untrusted user input.

That can introduce Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities.

26. Autoescaping

Django templates generally use automatic HTML escaping.

Suppose:

python
message = '<script>alert("Hello")</script>'

and template:

html
{{ message }}

Django escapes the HTML so the browser doesn't simply execute the supplied markup as HTML.

This is one of Django's built-in security features.

27. Important Viva Question

What is autoescaping?

Strong answer:

Autoescaping is a Django template feature that automatically escapes potentially unsafe HTML characters when rendering variables, helping protect against XSS attacks.

28. Filter vs Tag

Another common viva question.

Filter:

html
{{ name|upper }}

Changes/processes a value.

Tag:

html
{% if user %}

Controls template behavior.

Therefore:

text
Filter → modifies a value
Tag    → performs template operation

29. Built-in Filters You Should Know

For your exam, know at least:

text
upper
lower
title
length
default
safe

Some other useful filters:

text
truncatechars
join
date
add
floatformat
cut

We'll encounter many of them later.

30. truncatechars

Suppose:

text
description =
"This is a very long description of a Django project."

You can write:

html
{{ description|truncatechars:20 }}

to display a shortened version.

The exact output depends on the value and truncation rules.

31. join

Suppose:

python
subjects = ['Python', 'Django', 'SQL']

Template:

html
{{ subjects|join:", " }}

Output:

text
Python, Django, SQL

32. add

Example:

html
{{ age|add:"1" }}

If:

text
age = 21

it can produce:

text
22

Be aware that Django's add filter uses Python-like addition behavior where possible and can also concatenate compatible values.

33. date

If a context variable is a Python date/datetime object:

html
{{ date|date:"d-m-Y" }}

could display:

text
12-09-2026

Date formatting becomes particularly useful when working with models.

34. Filters Use a Colon for Arguments

Some filters accept arguments.

Example:

html
{{ name|default:"Guest" }}

Here:

text
default

is the filter and:

text
"Guest"

is its argument.

Another example:

html
{{ description|truncatechars:20 }}

35. Complete Example

View:

python
from django.shortcuts import render

def home(request):

    context = {
        'name': 'aman',
        'course': 'django',
        'age': 21
    }

    return render(
        request,
        'home.html',
        context
    )

Template:

html
<h1>Hello {{ name|title }}</h1>

<p>Course: {{ course|upper }}</p>

<p>Age: {{ age }}</p>

<p>Name length: {{ name|length }}</p>

Output approximately:

text
Hello Aman
Course: DJANGO
Age: 21
Name length: 4

36. Chained Filter Example

View:

python
context = {
    'name': 'aman'
}

Template:

html
{{ name|upper|length }}

Processing:

text
aman
 ↓
upper
 ↓
AMAN
 ↓
length
 ↓
4

Output:

text
4

37. Template Syntax Error

Suppose you write:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}
    <p>Adult</p>

but forget:

html
{% endif %}

Django will report a template parsing error.

Correct:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}
    <p>Adult</p>
{% endif %}

We'll study conditions much more in Module 14.

38. DTL and Security

Django templates provide several security protections, but you still have to use them correctly.

Important things to remember:

  • Don't blindly mark user input as safe
  • Don't put passwords into templates unnecessarily
  • Don't disable escaping without understanding why
  • Validate data in appropriate application layers
  • Use CSRF protection for forms

We'll study CSRF later in the Forms unit.

39. A Very Important Concept: Template Context

Suppose your view:

python
def home(request):

    context = {
        'username': 'Aman',
        'age': 21
    }

    return render(
        request,
        'home.html',
        context
    )

Think of context as a bridge:

text
Python View
     |
     | context
     ↓
Template

The template can access:

html
{{ username }}
{{ age }}

40. What If You Change the Context?

Suppose you change:

python
'name': 'Aman'

to:

python
'name': 'Rahul'

without changing the template:

html
<h1>Hello {{ name }}</h1>

the output automatically becomes:

text
Hello Rahul

This is the main idea behind dynamic templates.

41. Real-World Example

Imagine an e-commerce website.

The view gets:

python
product = {
    'name': 'Laptop',
    'price': 55000,
    'stock': 10
}

The template can display:

html
<h1>{{ product.name }}</h1>
<p>₹{{ product.price }}</p>
<p>Stock: {{ product.stock }}</p>

The HTML structure remains the same while the data changes.

That's what makes Django templates powerful.

42. Important Viva Questions

Q1. What is DTL?

DTL stands for Django Template Language. It is Django's template syntax for displaying dynamic data and controlling template presentation.

Q2. Is DTL Python?

No. DTL is Django's own template language and does not allow arbitrary Python code in templates.

Q3. What does {{ }} mean?

It is used to resolve and display template variables.

Q4. What does {% %} mean?

It represents template tags used for operations such as conditions, loops, URL generation, and template inheritance.

Q5. What does | mean in a template?

It applies a template filter to a value.

43. Viva — Filters

Q: What is a template filter?

Answer:

A template filter modifies or processes a value before it is displayed in a template.

Example:

html
{{ name|upper }}

Q: What does upper do?

Converts text to uppercase.

Q: What does lower do?

Converts text to lowercase.

Q: What does length do?

Returns the length of a value when applicable.

Q: What does default do?

Provides a fallback value when the variable is empty or otherwise evaluates as false according to the filter's behavior.

44. Important Security Viva

Teacher:

Why does Django escape HTML in templates?

Answer:

Django's automatic escaping helps prevent malicious HTML or JavaScript from being interpreted as markup, reducing the risk of Cross-Site Scripting attacks.

Teacher:

What does safe do?

Answer:

The safe filter marks a value as safe HTML for template rendering, so it should only be used when the content is trusted or has been properly sanitized.

45. Coding Question

Question:

Pass student information from a view and display it in a template.

View:

python
from django.shortcuts import render

def student(request):

    context = {
        'name': 'Aman',
        'age': 21,
        'course': 'CSE'
    }

    return render(
        request,
        'student.html',
        context
    )

Template:

html
<h1>{{ name }}</h1>
<p>Age: {{ age }}</p>
<p>Course: {{ course }}</p>

46. Coding Question — Filters

Given:

python
context = {
    'name': 'aman'
}

Write template code that:

  1. Converts name to uppercase
  2. Displays its length

Answer:

html
<p>{{ name|upper }}</p>
<p>{{ name|length }}</p>

47. Coding Question — Nested Dictionary

Given:

python
student = {
    'name': 'Aman',
    'address': {
        'city': 'Phagwara'
    }
}

Template:

html
<p>Name: {{ student.name }}</p>
<p>City: {{ student.address.city }}</p>

48. Predict the Output

Given:

python
context = {
    'name': 'django'
}

Template:

html
{{ name|upper }}

Answer:

text
DJANGO

Question:

html
{{ name|upper|length }}

Answer:

text
6

because:

text
django
 ↓
DJANGO
 ↓
6

49. Predict the Output

Given:

python
context = {
    'name': ''
}

Template:

html
{{ name|default:"Guest" }}

Output:

text
Guest

50. One Important Correction to Remember

DTL's dot lookup is more powerful than simply saying:

"Dot notation only accesses object attributes."

Django resolves dot lookups through several mechanisms, including dictionary lookup, attribute lookup, list-index lookup, and callable handling according to its template rules.

For beginner coding, you'll most commonly encounter:

html
{{ student.name }}
{{ student.address.city }}
{{ students.0 }}

⭐ Module 13 Cheat Sheet

Variable:

html
{{ name }}

Tag:

html
{% if condition %}

Comment:

html
{# comment #}

Filter:

html
{{ name|upper }}

Filter with argument:

html
{{ name|default:"Guest" }}

Multiple filters:

html
{{ name|upper|length }}

Dictionary/object access:

html
{{ student.name }}

Nested access:

html
{{ student.address.city }}

List index:

html
{{ students.0 }}

Multi-line comment:

html
{% comment %}
comment
{% endcomment %}

🧠 The Most Important Mental Model

Whenever you see:

html
{{ something }}

ask:

What did my view put into the context under the name something?

For example:

python
context = {
    'student': {
        'name': 'Aman'
    }
}

Then:

html
{{ student.name }}

means:

text
context
   ↓
student
   ↓
name
   ↓
Aman

This way of thinking will make the upcoming loops, conditions, dynamic pages, and database templates much easier.

Next → Module 14: Template Tags — if, else, elif, and for

We'll learn how to make templates actually make decisions and repeat HTML:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}
    Adult
{% else %}
    Minor
{% endif %}

and:

html
{% for student in students %}
    {{ student.name }}
{% endfor %}

We'll cover:

  • if
  • elif
  • else
  • comparison operators
  • and, or, not
  • for
  • empty
  • forloop.counter
  • forloop.first
  • forloop.last
  • nested loops
  • real database-style examples
  • coding questions and tricky viva questions.
Module 14
Template Tags: if, else, for

Module 14 — Template Tags: if, else, elif, and for

Now we learn one of the most important parts of DTL.

So far, you've learned how to display:

html
{{ name }}

and apply filters:

html
{{ name|upper }}

But real websites need to make decisions and repeat content.

For example:

If the student is 18 or older, display "Adult".

Or:

For every student, display their name.

Django Template Language provides template tags for this.

1. What Is a Template Tag?

Template tags use:

html
{% ... %}

They allow you to perform operations inside templates.

Examples:

html
{% if %}
{% for %}
{% url %}
{% extends %}
{% block %}

In this module, we'll focus on:

html
{% if %}
{% elif %}
{% else %}
{% for %}

2. if Tag

Basic syntax:

html
{% if condition %}
    ...
{% endif %}

Example:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}
    <p>Adult</p>
{% endif %}

If:

text
age = 21

output:

text
Adult

If:

text
age = 15

nothing inside the if block is displayed.

3. Complete Example

View

python
from django.shortcuts import render

def student(request):

    context = {
        'name': 'Aman',
        'age': 21
    }

    return render(
        request,
        'student.html',
        context
    )

Template

html
<h1>{{ name }}</h1>

{% if age >= 18 %}
    <p>Adult</p>
{% endif %}

Output:

text
Aman
Adult

4. else

If you want another result when the condition is false:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}
    <p>Adult</p>
{% else %}
    <p>Minor</p>
{% endif %}

For:

text
age = 21

output:

text
Adult

For:

text
age = 15

output:

text
Minor

5. elif

You can check multiple conditions.

html
{% if marks >= 90 %}
    <p>Grade A+</p>
{% elif marks >= 80 %}
    <p>Grade A</p>
{% elif marks >= 70 %}
    <p>Grade B</p>
{% else %}
    <p>Needs improvement</p>
{% endif %}

If:

text
marks = 85

output:

text
Grade A

6. How if-elif-else Works

Django checks from top to bottom:

text
marks >= 90?
     ↓
   No
     ↓
marks >= 80?
     ↓
   Yes
     ↓
Grade A
     ↓
STOP

Once one condition is true, the remaining conditions aren't evaluated for that chain.

7. Comparison Operators

DTL supports common comparisons.

You should know:

text
==    equal
!=    not equal
>     greater than
<     less than
>=    greater than or equal
<=    less than or equal

Examples:

html
{% if age == 18 %}
{% if age != 18 %}
{% if age > 18 %}
{% if age < 18 %}
{% if age >= 18 %}
{% if age <= 18 %}

8. Equality

html
{% if name == "Aman" %}
    <p>Welcome Aman</p>
{% endif %}

If:

text
name = Aman

the message appears.

9. Not Equal

html
{% if name != "Aman" %}
    <p>You are not Aman.</p>
{% endif %}

10. and

You can combine conditions.

html
{% if age >= 18 and age <= 25 %}
    <p>Young adult</p>
{% endif %}

This requires both conditions to be true.

11. or

html
{% if course == "CSE" or course == "IT" %}
    <p>Computer-related course</p>
{% endif %}

Only one condition needs to be true.

12. not

You can negate a condition:

html
{% if not logged_in %}
    <p>Please login.</p>
{% endif %}

We'll use this extensively when we study authentication.

13. Combining Conditions

Example:

html
{% if age >= 18 and course == "CSE" %}
    <p>Eligible</p>
{% else %}
    <p>Not eligible</p>
{% endif %}

Suppose:

text
age = 21
course = CSE

Output:

text
Eligible

14. Important: Don't Write Python Syntax

A common mistake is trying:

html
{% if age >= 18: %}

Don't add the Python colon.

Correct:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}

Similarly, don't write:

html
{% for student in students: %}

Correct:

html
{% for student in students %}

DTL has its own syntax.

15. for Loop

Now let's learn loops.

Basic syntax:

html
{% for item in items %}
    ...
{% endfor %}

Example:

html
{% for student in students %}
    <p>{{ student }}</p>
{% endfor %}

16. Complete Loop Example

View

python
def students(request):

    students = [
        'Aman',
        'Rahul',
        'Rohit'
    ]

    return render(
        request,
        'students.html',
        {'students': students}
    )

Template

html
<h1>Students</h1>

{% for student in students %}
    <p>{{ student }}</p>
{% endfor %}

Output:

text
Students

Aman
Rahul
Rohit

17. How the Loop Works

Django takes:

python
students = [
    'Aman',
    'Rahul',
    'Rohit'
]

and effectively does:

text
student = Aman
    ↓
<p>Aman</p>

student = Rahul
    ↓
<p>Rahul</p>

student = Rohit
    ↓
<p>Rohit</p>

The HTML inside the loop is rendered once for every item.

18. Looping Through Dictionaries

Suppose:

python
student = {
    'name': 'Aman',
    'age': 21
}

You can loop through dictionary items using:

html
{% for key, value in student.items %}
    <p>{{ key }}: {{ value }}</p>
{% endfor %}

Output:

text
name: Aman
age: 21

19. Looping Through Model-Like Objects

Suppose later your view retrieves:

python
students = Student.objects.all()

Then:

html
{% for student in students %}
    <p>{{ student.name }}</p>
{% endfor %}

can display every student's name.

This is how templates become connected to databases.

20. forloop.counter

Django provides special variables inside a for loop.

One of the most important is:

text
forloop.counter

It starts at 1.

Example:

html
{% for student in students %}
    <p>{{ forloop.counter }}. {{ student }}</p>
{% endfor %}

Output:

text
1. Aman
2. Rahul
3. Rohit

21. forloop.counter0

This starts at 0.

html
{% for student in students %}
    <p>{{ forloop.counter0 }} - {{ student }}</p>
{% endfor %}

Output:

text
0 - Aman
1 - Rahul
2 - Rohit

22. forloop.revcounter

This counts backwards starting from the total number of items.

For:

text
Aman
Rahul
Rohit

you get:

text
3
2
1

Example:

html
{% for student in students %}
    {{ forloop.revcounter }} - {{ student }}
{% endfor %}

23. forloop.revcounter0

This starts at:

text
length - 1

For three items:

text
2
1
0

24. forloop.first

This tells you whether the current iteration is the first one.

Example:

html
{% for student in students %}
    {% if forloop.first %}
        <strong>First Student: {{ student }}</strong>
    {% else %}
        <p>{{ student }}</p>
    {% endif %}
{% endfor %}

Only the first student gets the special formatting.

25. forloop.last

Similarly:

html
{% if forloop.last %}

is true during the final iteration.

Example:

html
{% for student in students %}
    <p>{{ student }}</p>

    {% if not forloop.last %}
        <hr>
    {% endif %}
{% endfor %}

This displays a separator between items but not after the last one.

26. forloop.parentloop

This is useful with nested loops.

Suppose:

html
{% for course in courses %}
    {% for student in course.students %}
        ...
    {% endfor %}
{% endfor %}

Inside the inner loop:

text
forloop

refers to the inner loop.

To access the outer loop's loop information, Django provides:

text
forloop.parentloop

This is an advanced concept, but useful for difficult viva questions.

27. empty

Suppose the list is empty:

python
students = []

Instead of writing a separate if, Django provides:

html
{% for student in students %}
    <p>{{ student }}</p>
{% empty %}
    <p>No students found.</p>
{% endfor %}

If the list contains students, they are displayed.

If it is empty:

text
No students found.

28. Why Is {% empty %} Useful?

Without empty, you might write:

html
{% if students %}
    {% for student in students %}
        <p>{{ student }}</p>
    {% endfor %}
{% else %}
    <p>No students found.</p>
{% endif %}

This works.

But:

html
{% for student in students %}
    <p>{{ student }}</p>
{% empty %}
    <p>No students found.</p>
{% endfor %}

is cleaner for this particular situation.

29. Loop With Objects

Suppose the view sends:

python
students = [
    {
        'name': 'Aman',
        'age': 21
    },
    {
        'name': 'Rahul',
        'age': 22
    }
]

Template:

html
{% for student in students %}
    <h3>{{ student.name }}</h3>
    <p>Age: {{ student.age }}</p>
{% endfor %}

Output:

text
Aman
Age: 21

Rahul
Age: 22

30. Combining for and if

This is extremely common.

html
{% for student in students %}
    {% if student.age >= 18 %}
        <p>{{ student.name }} is an adult.</p>
    {% endif %}
{% endfor %}

This means:

text
For every student:
    if age >= 18:
        display student

31. Example — Display Only CSE Students

View:

python
students = [
    {'name': 'Aman', 'course': 'CSE'},
    {'name': 'Rahul', 'course': 'ECE'},
    {'name': 'Rohit', 'course': 'CSE'}
]

Template:

html
{% for student in students %}
    {% if student.course == "CSE" %}
        <p>{{ student.name }}</p>
    {% endif %}
{% endfor %}

Output:

text
Aman
Rohit

32. Example — Numbered Student List

html
<ol>
{% for student in students %}
    <li>
        {{ forloop.counter }}. {{ student.name }}
    </li>
{% endfor %}
</ol>

Output conceptually:

text
1. Aman
2. Rahul
3. Rohit

33. Nested Loops

Suppose:

python
departments = [
    {
        'name': 'CSE',
        'students': ['Aman', 'Rahul']
    },
    {
        'name': 'ECE',
        'students': ['Rohit', 'Raj']
    }
]

Template:

html
{% for department in departments %}

    <h2>{{ department.name }}</h2>

    {% for student in department.students %}
        <p>{{ student }}</p>
    {% endfor %}

{% endfor %}

Output:

text
CSE
Aman
Rahul

ECE
Rohit
Raj

34. Nested Loop Mental Model

Think:

text
CSE
 ├── Aman
 └── Rahul

ECE
 ├── Rohit
 └── Raj

Outer loop:

html
{% for department in departments %}

Inner loop:

html
{% for student in department.students %}

35. forloop.counter in Nested Loops

Be careful.

Inside:

html
{% for department in departments %}
    {% for student in department.students %}
        {{ forloop.counter }}
    {% endfor %}
{% endfor %}

forloop.counter refers to the inner loop's counter.

If you need the outer loop counter:

html
{{ forloop.parentloop.counter }}

36. Example

html
{% for department in departments %}

    <h2>
        Department {{ forloop.counter }}:
        {{ department.name }}
    </h2>

    {% for student in department.students %}
        <p>
            {{ forloop.parentloop.counter }}.
            {{ forloop.counter }}.
            {{ student }}
        </p>
    {% endfor %}

{% endfor %}

The outer and inner counters are separate.

37. Important DTL Truthiness

Conditions can evaluate values as true/false.

For example:

html
{% if students %}

can be useful for checking whether a collection contains data.

Similarly:

html
{% if name %}

can check whether name has a usable non-empty value.

This is commonly used in templates.

38. Example — Login Message

Later, when you learn authentication, you'll see code like:

html
{% if user.is_authenticated %}
    <p>Welcome, {{ user.username }}</p>
{% else %}
    <p>Please login.</p>
{% endif %}

This is a real-world use of if.

39. and, or, not

Remember:

html
{% if condition1 and condition2 %}
html
{% if condition1 or condition2 %}
html
{% if not condition %}

Example:

html
{% if age >= 18 and has_id %}
    <p>Allowed</p>
{% endif %}

40. Important DTL Limitation

Don't assume you can perform arbitrary complex Python expressions inside an if.

For example, don't treat:

html
{% if complex_python_expression %}

as if it were a normal Python environment.

The template language intentionally provides a restricted set of operations.

If complex business logic is required, prepare the result in the view and send it through context.

41. Better Design

Instead of making the template perform complicated logic:

text
Template
   ↓
Huge business logic

prefer:

text
View
   ↓
Calculate/prepare data
   ↓
Context
   ↓
Template
   ↓
Display

Example:

View:

python
is_eligible = age >= 18 and marks >= 50

return render(
    request,
    'result.html',
    {'is_eligible': is_eligible}
)

Template:

html
{% if is_eligible %}
    <p>Eligible</p>
{% else %}
    <p>Not eligible</p>
{% endif %}

This keeps the template simple.

42. Common Mistake — Missing endif

Wrong:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}
    <p>Adult</p>

Correct:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}
    <p>Adult</p>
{% endif %}

43. Common Mistake — Missing endfor

Wrong:

html
{% for student in students %}
    <p>{{ student }}</p>

Correct:

html
{% for student in students %}
    <p>{{ student }}</p>
{% endfor %}

44. Common Mistake — Using {{ }} for Conditions

Wrong:

html
{{ if age >= 18 }}

Correct:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}

Remember:

text
{{ }} → variable
{% %} → tag

45. Common Mistake — Python Colon

Wrong:

html
{% if age >= 18: %}

Correct:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}

Wrong:

html
{% for student in students: %}

Correct:

html
{% for student in students %}

46. Common Mistake — Wrong End Tag

Wrong:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}
    Adult
{% endfor %}

if must end with:

html
{% endif %}

A for must end with:

html
{% endfor %}

47. Viva Questions

Q1. What is a template tag?

A template tag is Django Template Language syntax used to perform operations or control template rendering.

Q2. What is the syntax of an if tag?

html
{% if condition %}
    ...
{% endif %}

Q3. What is the syntax of a for loop?

html
{% for item in items %}
    ...
{% endfor %}

Q4. What does forloop.counter do?

It provides the current loop iteration number starting from 1.

Q5. What does forloop.counter0 do?

It provides the current iteration number starting from 0.

48. Viva — forloop.first and last

Q:

What is forloop.first?

It is true during the first iteration of a Django template for loop.

Q:

What is forloop.last?

It is true during the last iteration.

49. Viva — {% empty %}

Q:

What does {% empty %} do?

Answer:

It provides alternative template content when a Django for loop has no items to iterate over.

Example:

html
{% for student in students %}
    {{ student }}
{% empty %}
    No students found.
{% endfor %}

50. Coding Question

Requirement:

Display "Adult" if age is 18 or more, otherwise display "Minor".

Answer:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}
    Adult
{% else %}
    Minor
{% endif %}

51. Coding Question

Requirement:

Display every student's name.

html
{% for student in students %}
    <p>{{ student.name }}</p>
{% endfor %}

52. Coding Question

Requirement:

Display:

text
1. Aman
2. Rahul
3. Rohit

Answer:

html
{% for student in students %}
    <p>
        {{ forloop.counter }}. {{ student }}
    </p>
{% endfor %}

53. Coding Question

Requirement:

Display "No students found" if the list is empty.

html
{% for student in students %}
    <p>{{ student }}</p>
{% empty %}
    <p>No students found.</p>
{% endfor %}

54. Coding Question — Conditional Loop

Display only students who are 18 or older.

html
{% for student in students %}
    {% if student.age >= 18 %}
        <p>{{ student.name }}</p>
    {% endif %}
{% endfor %}

55. Predict the Output

Context:

python
{
    'age': 20
}

Template:

html
{% if age >= 18 %}
    Adult
{% else %}
    Minor
{% endif %}

Output:

text
Adult

56. Predict the Output

Context:

python
{
    'students': ['Aman', 'Rahul', 'Rohit']
}

Template:

html
{% for student in students %}
    {{ forloop.counter }} - {{ student }}
{% endfor %}

Output:

text
1 - Aman
2 - Rahul
3 - Rohit

57. Predict the Output

Context:

python
{
    'students': []
}

Template:

html
{% for student in students %}
    {{ student }}
{% empty %}
    No students
{% endfor %}

Output:

text
No students

⭐ Module 14 Cheat Sheet

If:

html
{% if condition %}
{% endif %}

If/else:

html
{% if condition %}
{% else %}
{% endif %}

Multiple conditions:

html
{% if condition1 %}
{% elif condition2 %}
{% else %}
{% endif %}

Loop:

html
{% for item in items %}
{% endfor %}

Empty loop:

html
{% for item in items %}
{% empty %}
{% endfor %}

Loop information:

text
forloop.counter       → 1, 2, 3...
forloop.counter0      → 0, 1, 2...
forloop.revcounter    → n, ..., 1
forloop.revcounter0   → n-1, ..., 0
forloop.first         → True on first iteration
forloop.last          → True on last iteration

Nested loops:

text
forloop.parentloop

Operators:

text
==  !=  >  <  >=  <=
and  or  not

🧠 The Core Pattern You Must Memorize

When displaying one value:

html
{{ name }}

When making a decision:

html
{% if condition %}
{% endif %}

When repeating something:

html
{% for item in items %}
{% endfor %}

Think:

text
{{ }} → DATA
{% %} → LOGIC

🎯 Module 14 Exam-Level Challenge

Given this view:

python
def students(request):

    students = [
        {
            'name': 'Aman',
            'age': 21,
            'course': 'CSE'
        },
        {
            'name': 'Rahul',
            'age': 17,
            'course': 'ECE'
        },
        {
            'name': 'Rohit',
            'age': 22,
            'course': 'CSE'
        }
    ]

    return render(
        request,
        'students.html',
        {'students': students}
    )

Write a template that:

  1. Displays every student's number.
  2. Displays their name and course.
  3. Displays "Adult" if age ≥ 18, otherwise "Minor".
  4. Displays "CSE Student" only for CSE students.
  5. Displays "No students found" if the list is empty.

A correct solution would combine for + forloop.counter + if/else + empty.

Once you can solve that, you are ready for the next level.

Next → Module 15: Template Filters in Depth

We'll properly master filters such as:

text
upper
lower
title
length
default
truncatechars
join
date
add
floatformat
cut

and learn how to combine filters, pass filter arguments, format dates/numbers, and solve filter-based coding/viva questions.

Module 15
Template Filters in Depth

Module 15 — Django Template Filters in Depth

Now we'll properly master Django Template Filters.

You already know:

html
{{ name }}

A filter lets you modify or transform the value before displaying it.

For example:

html
{{ name|upper }}

If:

text
name = "aman"

the output is:

text
AMAN

1. What Is a Template Filter?

A template filter takes a value and transforms it.

Syntax:

html
{{ value|filter }}

Think of it as:

text
value
  ↓
filter
  ↓
modified value

Example:

html
{{ name|upper }}
text
aman
 ↓
upper
 ↓
AMAN

2. Why Do We Need Filters?

Suppose the view gives:

python
name = "aman"

You could change it in Python:

python
name = name.upper()

But sometimes the transformation is purely for presentation.

Instead, the template can handle it:

html
{{ name|upper }}

This keeps simple presentation formatting inside the template.

3. The Pipe |

The pipe character:

text
|

is used to apply a filter.

Example:

html
{{ name|upper }}

Read this as:

Take name and apply the upper filter.

4. upper

Converts text to uppercase.

html
{{ name|upper }}

If:

text
name = "Aman"

output:

text
AMAN

5. lower

Converts text to lowercase.

html
{{ name|lower }}

If:

text
name = "DJANGO"

output:

text
django

6. title

Converts words to title case.

html
{{ sentence|title }}

If:

text
hello django world

output:

text
Hello Django World

7. capfirst

capfirst capitalizes the first character.

html
{{ name|capfirst }}

For:

text
aman

output:

text
Aman

8. length

Returns the length of a value.

html
{{ name|length }}

If:

text
name = Aman

output:

text
4

For a list:

html
{{ students|length }}

If:

python
students = ['Aman', 'Rahul', 'Rohit']

output:

text
3

9. default

This is one of the most useful filters.

Syntax:

html
{{ value|default:"fallback" }}

Example:

html
{{ name|default:"Guest" }}

If:

text
name = ""

output:

text
Guest

10. default_if_none

There is an important difference between:

text
default

and:

text
default_if_none

default_if_none only replaces the value when it is actually None.

Example:

html
{{ name|default_if_none:"Guest" }}

If:

python
name = None

output:

text
Guest

But it doesn't have exactly the same behavior as default for other false/empty values.

11. default vs default_if_none

Remember:

text
default
    ↓
fallback for empty/false-ish values

default_if_none
    ↓
fallback specifically for None

This is a good viva question.

12. Filter Arguments

Some filters accept arguments.

Example:

html
{{ name|default:"Guest" }}

Here:

text
default

is the filter and:

text
"Guest"

is its argument.

Another:

html
{{ text|truncatechars:20 }}

13. truncatechars

This filter shortens text.

Example:

html
{{ description|truncatechars:20 }}

It limits the rendered text to the specified number of characters, including the ellipsis when truncation occurs.

Useful for:

  • blog previews
  • product descriptions
  • summaries
  • cards

14. Example

Suppose:

python
description = "Django is a high level Python web framework."

Template:

html
<p>{{ description|truncatechars:20 }}</p>

Django produces a shortened version with an ellipsis when necessary.

You don't need to memorize the exact output for every string; understand the purpose.

15. wordcount

The:

html
{{ text|wordcount }}

filter returns the number of words.

For:

text
"Django is powerful"

output:

text
3

16. join

Suppose your view sends:

python
subjects = [
    'Python',
    'Django',
    'SQL'
]

Template:

html
{{ subjects|join:", " }}

Output:

text
Python, Django, SQL

The argument:

text
", "

specifies what should be placed between elements.

17. Different Join Separators

You can write:

html
{{ subjects|join:" | " }}

Output:

text
Python | Django | SQL

Or:

html
{{ subjects|join:" - " }}

Output:

text
Python - Django - SQL

18. add

The add filter attempts to add its argument to the value.

Example:

html
{{ age|add:"1" }}

If:

text
age = 21

it can produce:

text
22

It can also concatenate compatible values, so don't think of it as exclusively numeric addition.

19. cut

cut removes all occurrences of a specified string.

Example:

html
{{ name|cut:" " }}

If:

text
name = "Aman Ranjan"

the spaces are removed:

text
AmanRanjan

20. slugify

slugify converts text into a slug-like format.

Example:

html
{{ title|slugify }}

If:

text
title = "Django Web Development"

it can produce:

text
django-web-development

This is useful when creating readable URL slugs.

21. first

For a list:

html
{{ students|first }}

returns the first item.

If:

python
students = ['Aman', 'Rahul', 'Rohit']

output:

text
Aman

22. last

Similarly:

html
{{ students|last }}

returns:

text
Rohit

23. random

The random filter returns a randomly selected item from a sequence.

Example:

html
{{ students|random }}

If:

python
students = ['Aman', 'Rahul', 'Rohit']

the result can be one of those values.

Because it is random, the output isn't predictable.

24. length on a String vs List

The same filter can work on different types.

String:

text
"Aman"
html
{{ name|length }}

→

text
4

List:

python
['Aman', 'Rahul', 'Rohit']
html
{{ students|length }}

→

text
3

25. Filter Chaining

This is very important.

You can apply multiple filters:

html
{{ name|upper|length }}

Suppose:

text
name = aman

Processing:

text
aman
 ↓ upper
AMAN
 ↓ length
4

Output:

text
4

26. Another Chain

html
{{ name|lower|capfirst }}

Suppose:

text
name = aMAN

First:

text
aMAN
 ↓ lower
aman

then:

text
aman
 ↓ capfirst
Aman

Output:

text
Aman

27. Order Matters

Consider:

html
{{ name|upper|length }}

versus:

html
{{ name|length|upper }}

The first makes sense:

text
name → uppercase → length

The second tries to apply upper to the result of length, which is a number and isn't equivalent.

So:

Filters are applied from left to right.

28. floatformat

This is useful for decimal numbers.

Suppose:

python
price = 125.6789

Template:

html
{{ price|floatformat:2 }}

Output:

text
125.68

It formats the value to approximately two decimal places according to Django's floatformat rules.

29. floatformat:0

Example:

html
{{ price|floatformat:0 }}

For:

text
125.6789

it produces a rounded integer-style representation.

30. date

Suppose the view sends a Python date/datetime value:

python
today

You can format it:

html
{{ today|date:"d-m-Y" }}

Example output:

text
12-09-2026

31. Common Date Format Characters

Some useful Django date-format characters:

text
d → day, 2 digits
m → month, 2 digits
Y → 4-digit year
y → 2-digit year
M → short month name
F → full month name

So:

html
{{ date|date:"d M Y" }}

might produce:

text
12 Sep 2026

And:

html
{{ date|date:"F d, Y" }}

might produce:

text
September 12, 2026

32. time

For a time/datetime value:

html
{{ value|time:"H:i" }}

can display something like:

text
20:30

33. urlencode

urlencode is used to encode values for safe use in URLs.

Example:

html
{{ value|urlencode }}

This becomes useful when constructing URLs from dynamic values.

34. linebreaks

The linebreaks filter can convert plain text line breaks into suitable HTML paragraphs and line breaks.

Example:

html
{{ message|linebreaks }}

Useful when displaying user-entered text where line breaks matter.

35. striptags

This filter removes HTML tags from a string.

Example:

html
{{ content|striptags }}

If content contains HTML markup, the tags are removed from the resulting text.

This can be useful when you need plain-text-like output.

36. safe

As you learned in Module 13:

html
{{ content|safe }}

marks the value as safe for HTML rendering.

Example:

python
content = "<b>Hello</b>"

Without safe, Django normally escapes the markup.

With:

html
{{ content|safe }}

the <b> element can be interpreted as HTML.

⚠️ Security warning

Never blindly apply safe to untrusted user input.

It can create an XSS vulnerability.

37. escape

Django also provides:

html
{{ content|escape }}

which explicitly escapes HTML-sensitive characters.

However, remember that Django templates already autoescape normal variable output by default in typical configurations.

38. Autoescape

Suppose:

python
message = "<script>alert('Hello')</script>"

Template:

html
{{ message }}

Django normally escapes the HTML rather than allowing the supplied markup to execute as HTML.

That's part of Django's security model.

39. safe vs escape

safe escape
Marks content as safe HTML Escapes HTML-sensitive characters
Can allow HTML rendering Prevents HTML from being interpreted as markup
Dangerous for untrusted input Useful for safely displaying text

40. Filter With an Object

Suppose:

python
student = {
    'name': 'aman'
}

Template:

html
{{ student.name|upper }}

Output:

text
AMAN

You can apply filters to resolved values, not just simple variables.

41. Filter With a Model Field

Later, when we work with models, you might have:

html
{{ student.name|title }}

or:

html
{{ product.price|floatformat:2 }}

This is extremely common in real Django applications.

42. Multiple Filters on Model Data

For example:

html
{{ product.name|title|truncatechars:30 }}

Processing:

text
Product name
    ↓
title
    ↓
truncatechars
    ↓
display

43. Important Rule: Filters Don't Change the Original Variable

Suppose:

html
{{ name|upper }}
{{ name }}

If:

text
name = aman

the first outputs:

text
AMAN

and the second still outputs:

text
aman

The filter changes the value for that template expression; it doesn't permanently modify the original context variable.

44. Common Mistake — Wrong Syntax

Wrong:

html
{{ name upper }}

Correct:

html
{{ name|upper }}

The pipe is required.

45. Common Mistake — Wrong Argument Syntax

Wrong:

html
{{ name|default("Guest") }}

That's Python/function-call style.

Correct DTL syntax:

html
{{ name|default:"Guest" }}

46. Common Mistake — Using Python Methods

You might be tempted to write:

html
{{ name.upper() }}

Don't treat DTL like Python.

Use:

html
{{ name|upper }}

This is one of the easiest ways to remember why filters exist.

47. Common Mistake — Assuming Every Filter Exists

Don't invent Python methods inside templates.

For example:

html
{{ name|capitalize }}

is not the standard Django filter name you should use.

Django has specific built-in filter names, such as:

text
capfirst
upper
lower
title

48. Practical Example — Product Page

View:

python
def product(request):

    product = {
        'name': 'gaming laptop',
        'price': 79999.456,
        'description': 'A powerful laptop for gaming and development.'
    }

    return render(
        request,
        'product.html',
        {'product': product}
    )

Template:

html
<h1>{{ product.name|title }}</h1>

<p>₹{{ product.price|floatformat:2 }}</p>

<p>
    {{ product.description|truncatechars:30 }}
</p>

This is a very realistic use of filters.

49. Practical Example — Student List

View:

python
def students(request):

    students = [
        'aman',
        'rahul',
        'rohit'
    ]

    return render(
        request,
        'students.html',
        {'students': students}
    )

Template:

html
<h1>Students</h1>

<p>Total students: {{ students|length }}</p>

<p>First student: {{ students|first|title }}</p>

<p>Last student: {{ students|last|title }}</p>

Output:

text
Total students: 3
First student: Aman
Last student: Rohit

50. Filter Chaining — Exam Question

Given:

python
name = "django"

What is the output of:

html
{{ name|upper|length }}

Answer:

text
6

Because:

text
django
 ↓ upper
DJANGO
 ↓ length
6

51. Exam Question

Given:

python
name = ""

What is:

html
{{ name|default:"Guest" }}

Answer:

text
Guest

52. Exam Question

Given:

python
students = ['Aman', 'Rahul', 'Rohit']

What is:

html
{{ students|length }}

Answer:

text
3

53. Exam Question

Given:

python
students = ['Aman', 'Rahul', 'Rohit']

What is:

html
{{ students|first }}

Answer:

text
Aman

54. Exam Question

Given:

python
subjects = ['Python', 'Django', 'SQL']

What is:

html
{{ subjects|join:", " }}

Answer:

text
Python, Django, SQL

55. Viva Questions

Q1. What is a Django template filter?

A template filter transforms or processes a template value before it is rendered.

Q2. What symbol is used to apply a filter?

The pipe | symbol.

Q3. Can filters be chained?

Yes. Multiple filters can be applied from left to right.

Q4. What does upper do?

Converts text to uppercase.

Q5. What does length do?

Returns the length of a value when applicable.

Q6. What does default do?

Provides a fallback value when the value is empty or false according to the filter's behavior.

56. Viva — default vs default_if_none

Teacher:

What's the difference?

Answer:

default provides its fallback for values that evaluate as false, while default_if_none provides the fallback specifically when the value is None.

57. Viva — Filter Chaining

Teacher:

In what order are filters applied?

Answer:

Filters are applied from left to right.

For:

html
{{ name|upper|length }}

the order is:

text
name
 ↓
upper
 ↓
length

58. Viva — safe

Teacher:

Why can safe be dangerous?

Answer:

Because it marks content as safe HTML. If the content contains untrusted malicious HTML or JavaScript, marking it safe can bypass normal escaping and potentially create an XSS vulnerability.

59. Viva — Template vs Python

Teacher:

Why use {{ name|upper }} instead of name.upper()?

Answer:

Django templates use the Django Template Language rather than arbitrary Python code. The upper template filter is the appropriate DTL mechanism for presentation-level uppercase formatting.

60. ⭐ Filters You Should Memorize

For your college exam, definitely know:

text
upper
lower
title
capfirst
length
default
default_if_none
join
first
last
random
add
cut
slugify
truncatechars
floatformat
date
time
safe
escape
striptags
wordcount
urlencode
linebreaks

You don't necessarily need to memorize every edge case, but you should know the purpose and syntax of these.

{{ name|capfirst }}

Given this view:

python

    student = {
        'name': 'aman ranjan',
        'course': 'computer science',
        'marks': 87.5678,
        'subjects': ['Python', 'Django', 'SQL']
    }

    return render(

    )

Write a template that displays:

text
Name: Aman Ranjan
Course: COMPUTER SCIENCE
Marks: 87.57
Number of subjects: 3

You should use:

  • title
  • upper
  • floatformat

A clean solution is:

html
<h1>Name: {{ student.name|title }}</h1>

<p>Course: {{ student.course|upper }}</p>

<p>Marks: {{ student.marks|floatformat:2 }}</p>

  • Sending complex data from views
