Module 16
Dynamic Templates

Module 16 — Dynamic Templates in Django

Now we move from individual template features to building real dynamic webpages.

So far you know:

  • Views
  • URLs
  • HTTP requests/responses
  • URL parameters
  • Templates
  • DTL variables
  • if/else
  • for loops
  • filters

Now we'll connect all of them.

1. What Is a Dynamic Template?

A static HTML page always displays the same content.

Example:

html
<h1>Welcome Aman</h1>
<p>Computer Science</p>

Every user sees the same thing.

A dynamic template gets data from the Django view and generates the HTML based on that data.

Example:

html
<h1>Welcome {{ name }}</h1>
<p>Course: {{ course }}</p>

If the view sends:

python
{
    'name': 'Aman',
    'course': 'Computer Science'
}

the browser displays:

text
Welcome Aman
Course: Computer Science

If another request sends different data, the same template can display different information.

2. Dynamic Template Flow

The basic flow is:

text
Browser
   ↓
URL
   ↓
View
   ↓
Data
   ↓
Template
   ↓
HTML Response
   ↓
Browser

For example:

text
/student/101/
      ↓
student_detail()
      ↓
Student information
      ↓
student.html
      ↓
HTML

This is one of the most important Django concepts.

3. Passing Multiple Variables

Suppose your view is:

python
from django.shortcuts import render

def home(request):

    name = "Aman"
    age = 21
    course = "Computer Science"

    return render(
        request,
        "home.html",
        {
            "name": name,
            "age": age,
            "course": course
        }
    )

Template:

html
<h1>Hello {{ name }}</h1>

<p>Age: {{ age }}</p>

<p>Course: {{ course }}</p>

The dictionary is called the context.

4. Understanding Context Properly

This:

python
{
    "name": name,
    "age": age,
    "course": course
}

is the context dictionary.

Think of it as a bridge:

text
Python View
     ↓
 context
     ↓
Template

The template can access the keys:

html
{{ name }}
{{ age }}
{{ course }}

5. Passing a Dictionary

Instead of creating separate variables, you can create one dictionary.

python
def student(request):

    student = {
        "name": "Aman",
        "age": 21,
        "course": "Computer Science"
    }

    return render(
        request,
        "student.html",
        {"student": student}
    )

Template:

html
<h1>{{ student.name }}</h1>

<p>Age: {{ student.age }}</p>

<p>Course: {{ student.course }}</p>

Notice:

text
student.name
student.age
student.course

DTL uses dot notation to access dictionary values.

6. Complete Example

views.py

python
from django.shortcuts import render

def student(request):

    student = {
        "name": "Aman",
        "age": 21,
        "course": "Computer Science",
        "city": "Phagwara"
    }

    return render(
        request,
        "student.html",
        {"student": student}
    )

urls.py

python
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path("student/", views.student, name="student"),
]

student.html

html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Student</title>
</head>

<body>

    <h1>{{ student.name }}</h1>

    <p>Age: {{ student.age }}</p>

    <p>Course: {{ student.course }}</p>

    <p>City: {{ student.city }}</p>

</body>
</html>

When the browser visits:

text
/student/

Django executes:

python
student(request)

The view sends the dictionary to the template.

The template generates HTML.

7. Dynamic List

Suppose we want to display multiple students.

View:

python
def students(request):

    students = [
        "Aman",
        "Rahul",
        "Rohit",
        "Karan"
    ]

    return render(
        request,
        "students.html",
        {"students": students}
    )

Template:

html
<h1>Students</h1>

<ul>

{% for student in students %}

    <li>{{ student }}</li>

{% endfor %}

</ul>

Output:

text
Students

• Aman
• Rahul
• Rohit
• Karan

8. Dynamic List of Dictionaries

This is much more important.

View:

python
def students(request):

    students = [
        {
            "name": "Aman",
            "age": 21,
            "course": "CSE"
        },
        {
            "name": "Rahul",
            "age": 22,
            "course": "IT"
        },
        {
            "name": "Rohit",
            "age": 20,
            "course": "CSE"
        }
    ]

    return render(
        request,
        "students.html",
        {"students": students}
    )

Template:

html
{% for student in students %}

    <h2>{{ student.name }}</h2>

    <p>Age: {{ student.age }}</p>

    <p>Course: {{ student.course }}</p>

{% endfor %}

This pattern appears constantly in Django applications.

9. Dynamic HTML Table

We can make the same data into a table.

html
<table border="1">

    <tr>
        <th>Name</th>
        <th>Age</th>
        <th>Course</th>
    </tr>

    {% for student in students %}

    <tr>
        <td>{{ student.name }}</td>
        <td>{{ student.age }}</td>
        <td>{{ student.course }}</td>
    </tr>

    {% endfor %}

</table>

The number of rows is automatically determined by the data.

If there are 3 students → 3 rows.

If there are 100 students → 100 rows.

That's what makes the page dynamic.

10. Dynamic Conditions

Suppose:

python
students = [
    {
        "name": "Aman",
        "marks": 85
    },
    {
        "name": "Rahul",
        "marks": 42
    }
]

Template:

html
{% for student in students %}

    <h3>{{ student.name }}</h3>

    <p>Marks: {{ student.marks }}</p>

    {% if student.marks >= 50 %}
        <p>Result: Pass</p>
    {% else %}
        <p>Result: Fail</p>
    {% endif %}

{% endfor %}

Output:

text
Aman
Marks: 85
Result: Pass

Rahul
Marks: 42
Result: Fail

11. Combining Loops + Conditions + Filters

This is the type of question that can appear in a coding exam.

html
{% for student in students %}

    <h2>{{ student.name|title }}</h2>

    <p>Marks: {{ student.marks|floatformat:2 }}</p>

    {% if student.marks >= 50 %}
        <p>PASS</p>
    {% else %}
        <p>FAIL</p>
    {% endif %}

{% empty %}

    <p>No students found.</p>

{% endfor %}

Here we're using:

text
for
if
else
empty
filters
variables

all together.

12. Dynamic URL Parameters + Templates

Now let's connect URL parameters with templates.

Suppose:

python
path(
    "student/<int:id>/",
    views.student_detail
)

View:

python
def student_detail(request, id):

    return render(
        request,
        "student_detail.html",
        {"student_id": id}
    )

Template:

html
<h1>Student Details</h1>

<p>Student ID: {{ student_id }}</p>

Visiting:

text
/student/101/

gives:

text
Student ID: 101

Visiting:

text
/student/205/

gives:

text
Student ID: 205

Same template, different data.

13. URL Parameter Can Be Used to Select Data

Suppose:

python
students = {
    101: {
        "name": "Aman",
        "course": "CSE"
    },
    102: {
        "name": "Rahul",
        "course": "IT"
    }
}

View:

python
def student_detail(request, id):

    student = students.get(id)

    return render(
        request,
        "student_detail.html",
        {"student": student}
    )

URL:

python
path(
    "student/<int:id>/",
    views.student_detail
)

Now:

text
/student/101/

selects:

python
{
    "name": "Aman",
    "course": "CSE"
}

while:

text
/student/102/

selects:

python
{
    "name": "Rahul",
    "course": "IT"
}

14. Handling Missing Data

What if:

text
/student/999/

doesn't exist?

Our:

python
student = students.get(id)

returns:

python
None

We can handle this in the template:

html
{% if student %}

    <h1>{{ student.name }}</h1>
    <p>{{ student.course }}</p>

{% else %}

    <h1>Student not found</h1>

{% endif %}

Later, when we use models, we'll learn the much better:

python
get_object_or_404()

approach.

15. Dynamic Navigation

Templates can also generate links dynamically.

Suppose we have:

python
path(
    "about/",
    views.about,
    name="about"
)

Instead of hardcoding:

html
<a href="/about/">About</a>

use:

html
<a href="{% url 'about' %}">About</a>

This is called URL reversing.

16. Dynamic URL With Parameters

Suppose:

python
path(
    "student/<int:id>/",
    views.student_detail,
    name="student_detail"
)

Template:

html
<a href="{% url 'student_detail' id=student.id %}">
    View Student
</a>

If:

text
student.id = 101

Django generates:

text
/student/101/

This is much better than manually constructing URLs.

17. Dynamic Student List With Links

View:

python
def students(request):

    students = [
        {
            "id": 101,
            "name": "Aman"
        },
        {
            "id": 102,
            "name": "Rahul"
        }
    ]

    return render(
        request,
        "students.html",
        {"students": students}
    )

Template:

html
{% for student in students %}

    <h2>{{ student.name }}</h2>

    <a href="{% url 'student_detail' id=student.id %}">
        View Details
    </a>

{% endfor %}

This creates a dynamic list where every student has a different URL.

18. Nested Data

Consider:

python
student = {
    "name": "Aman",
    "address": {
        "city": "Phagwara",
        "state": "Punjab"
    }
}

Template:

html
<p>{{ student.name }}</p>

<p>{{ student.address.city }}</p>

<p>{{ student.address.state }}</p>

DTL supports nested access through dot notation.

19. List Inside Dictionary

Example:

python
student = {
    "name": "Aman",
    "skills": [
        "Python",
        "Django",
        "SQL"
    ]
}

Template:

html
<h1>{{ student.name }}</h1>

<ul>

{% for skill in student.skills %}

    <li>{{ skill }}</li>

{% endfor %}

</ul>

Output:

text
Aman

• Python
• Django
• SQL

20. Dictionary Inside a List

Example:

python
products = [
    {
        "name": "Laptop",
        "price": 70000
    },
    {
        "name": "Phone",
        "price": 30000
    }
]

Template:

html
{% for product in products %}

    <h2>{{ product.name }}</h2>
    <p>₹{{ product.price }}</p>

{% endfor %}

Again, this is extremely common.

21. Dynamic Page Based on User

Suppose the view receives:

python
def profile(request):

    user = {
        "name": "Aman",
        "is_admin": True
    }

    return render(
        request,
        "profile.html",
        {"user": user}
    )

Template:

html
<h1>Welcome {{ user.name }}</h1>

{% if user.is_admin %}
    <p>Administrator Panel</p>
{% else %}
    <p>User Dashboard</p>
{% endif %}

The same template can render different interfaces based on data.

22. Dynamic Template ≠ Dynamic Database

This is an important distinction.

A template can be dynamic even without a database.

For example:

python
students = [
    "Aman",
    "Rahul"
]

is dynamic template data.

Later we'll connect templates to actual database records through:

text
Model → ORM → View → Template

That is where Django becomes a complete database-driven application.

23. The Full MVT Flow

At this stage, you should understand this architecture:

text
                 Browser
                    │
                    │ Request
                    ▼
                  URL
                    │
                    ▼
                  View
                    │
             ┌──────┴──────┐
             │             │
             ▼             ▼
           Model        Business Logic
             │
             ▼
          Database
             │
             ▼
            Data
             │
             └──────┐
                    ▼
                 Template
                    │
                    ▼
                  HTML
                    │
                    │ Response
                    ▼
                 Browser

Don't worry if the Model → Database part isn't fully clear yet.

We'll cover it extensively in Unit V.

24. View Should Prepare Data

A very important Django principle:

Don't put complicated application logic in the template.

Bad approach:

html
{% if student.marks > 50 and student.age > 18 and ... %}

with huge amounts of business logic.

Better:

python
is_eligible = ...

Then:

html
{% if is_eligible %}
    Eligible
{% endif %}

Templates should primarily handle presentation.

25. View + Template Responsibility

A useful exam answer:

View

Responsible for:

  • Receiving request
  • Application/business logic
  • Getting data
  • Preparing context
  • Selecting template
  • Returning response

Template

Responsible for:

  • Displaying data
  • HTML structure
  • Simple conditions
  • Loops
  • Presentation formatting

26. Complete Dynamic Student Example

Let's combine everything.

views.py

python
from django.shortcuts import render

def students(request):

    students = [
        {
            "id": 101,
            "name": "aman ranjan",
            "course": "computer science",
            "marks": 87.56
        },
        {
            "id": 102,
            "name": "rahul kumar",
            "course": "information technology",
            "marks": 42.50
        },
        {
            "id": 103,
            "name": "rohit sharma",
            "course": "computer science",
            "marks": 91.25
        }
    ]

    return render(
        request,
        "students.html",
        {"students": students}
    )

urls.py

python
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "students/",
        views.students,
        name="students"
    ),
]

students.html

html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>

<head>
    <title>Students</title>
</head>

<body>

<h1>Student List</h1>

{% for student in students %}

    <div>

        <h2>{{ student.name|title }}</h2>

        <p>
            Course: {{ student.course|upper }}
        </p>

        <p>
            Marks: {{ student.marks|floatformat:2 }}
        </p>

        {% if student.marks >= 50 %}
            <p>Result: PASS</p>
        {% else %}
            <p>Result: FAIL</p>
        {% endif %}

    </div>

{% empty %}

    <p>No students available.</p>

{% endfor %}

</body>

</html>

View

27. Dynamic Template Coding Question

Question

Create a Django view that sends three products to a template.

Each product should contain:

  • name
  • price
  • category

Display them in an HTML table.

Solution

python
def products(request):

    products = [
        {
            "name": "Laptop",
            "price": 70000,
            "category": "Electronics"
        },
        {
            "name": "Mouse",
            "price": 1000,
            "category": "Accessories"
        },
        {
            "name": "Keyboard",
            "price": 2000,
            "category": "Accessories"
        }
    ]

    return render(
        request,
        "products.html",
        {"products": products}
    )

Template:

html
<table border="1">

<tr>
    <th>Name</th>
    <th>Price</th>
    <th>Category</th>
</tr>

{% for product in products %}

<tr>
    <td>{{ product.name }}</td>
    <td>₹{{ product.price }}</td>
    <td>{{ product.category }}</td>
</tr>

{% empty %}

<tr>
    <td colspan="3">No products available</td>
</tr>

{% endfor %}

</table>

28. Common Viva Questions

Q1. What is a dynamic template?

A template whose displayed content changes according to data supplied by the view.

Q2. How does a view send data to a template?

Using the context dictionary passed to render().

python
return render(
    request,
    "home.html",
    {"name": "Aman"}
)

Q3. What is context?

Context is the collection of data passed from a view to a template, commonly represented as a dictionary.

Q4. Can a template receive a list?

Yes.

python
{"students": students}

Q5. Can a template receive dictionaries?

Yes.

html
{{ student.name }}

Q6. Can templates contain loops?

Yes, using the {% for %} tag.

Q7. Can templates contain conditions?

Yes, using {% if %}, {% elif %}, and {% else %}.

Q8. Can URL parameters be passed to templates?

Yes. The view receives the URL parameter and can pass it through the context.

Q9. Should complex business logic be written in templates?

No. Complex logic should generally be handled in the view/model layer, while templates should focus on presentation.

Q10. Can dynamic templates work without a database?

Yes. Data can come from Python variables, lists, dictionaries, APIs, files, etc. A database is not required.

⭐ Module 16 Must Remember

The most important pattern is:

python
def view(request):

    data = ...

    return render(
        request,
        "template.html",
        {"data": data}
    )

Then:

html
{{ data }}

or:

html
{% for item in data %}
    {{ item }}
{% endfor %}

or:

html
{% if data %}
    ...
{% endif %}

And with nested data:

html
{{ student.name }}
{{ student.address.city }}
{{ student.skills }}

The core idea is:

View prepares the data → Context carries the data → Template displays the data.

Module 17
Template Inheritance

Module 17 — Template Inheritance in Django

Template inheritance is one of the most important Django template concepts.

It solves a very common problem:

What if every page of our website has the same navbar, footer, CSS, and overall layout?

Instead of copying the same HTML into every file, we create one base template and let other templates inherit from it.

1. The Problem: Repeating HTML

Imagine your website has:

text
Home
About
Students
Contact

Every page needs:

html
<html>
<head>
    ...
</head>

<body>

    <nav>
        Home | About | Students | Contact
    </nav>

    <!-- page-specific content -->

    <footer>
        Copyright 2026
    </footer>

</body>
</html>

Without inheritance, you might copy this entire structure into:

text
home.html
about.html
students.html
contact.html

This is bad.

Why?

If you change the navbar, you'd have to change it in four files.

2. Template Inheritance Solution

Create one:

text
base.html

It contains the common structure.

Then:

text
home.html
about.html
students.html

inherit from it.

Conceptually:

text
                base.html
                    │
       ┌────────────┼────────────┐
       ↓            ↓            ↓
   home.html    about.html   students.html

The child templates only provide the content that changes.

3. base.html

Let's create:

text
templates/
└── base.html

Basic example:

html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>

<head>
    <title>My Website</title>
</head>

<body>

    <nav>
        Home | About | Students
    </nav>

    <main>
        <!-- changing content goes here -->
    </main>

    <footer>
        Copyright 2026
    </footer>

</body>

</html>

But how do we tell Django:

"The content inside <main> should be different for every page?"

We use blocks.

4. {% block %}

A block defines an area that child templates can replace.

Change the <main> section:

html
<main>

    {% block content %}

    {% endblock %}

</main>

Complete:

html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>

<head>
    <title>My Website</title>
</head>

<body>

    <nav>
        Home | About | Students
    </nav>

    <main>

        {% block content %}
        {% endblock %}

    </main>

    <footer>
        Copyright 2026
    </footer>

</body>

</html>

Now content is a block.

5. Creating a Child Template

Suppose we create:

text
home.html

At the top:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

This tells Django:

Use base.html as the parent template.

Then we define the content block:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block content %}

<h1>Welcome to Home Page</h1>

<p>This is the home page.</p>

{% endblock %}

That's it.

6. What Does Django Actually Generate?

You wrote:

base.html

html
<nav>
    Home | About | Students
</nav>

{% block content %}
{% endblock %}

<footer>
    Copyright 2026
</footer>

home.html

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block content %}

<h1>Welcome</h1>

{% endblock %}

Django conceptually combines them into:

html
<nav>
    Home | About | Students
</nav>

<h1>Welcome</h1>

<footer>
    Copyright 2026
</footer>

So the child template supplies the block content while inheriting the surrounding structure.

7. Important Syntax

Parent:

html
{% block content %}
{% endblock %}

Child:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block content %}
    Page content
{% endblock %}

Memorize this pattern.

8. extends

The:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

tag establishes template inheritance.

Usually, it should appear at or near the beginning of the child template.

Example:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block content %}
    <h1>About Us</h1>
{% endblock %}

9. Multiple Blocks

You aren't limited to one block.

For example:

html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>

<head>

    <title>
        {% block title %}
            My Website
        {% endblock %}
    </title>

</head>

<body>

    <header>
        {% block header %}
        {% endblock %}
    </header>

    <main>
        {% block content %}
        {% endblock %}
    </main>

    <footer>
        {% block footer %}
        {% endblock %}
    </footer>

</body>

</html>

Now the child can customize each block.

10. Child Template With Multiple Blocks

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block title %}
    Home
{% endblock %}

{% block content %}

    <h1>Welcome to Home</h1>
    <p>This is the home page.</p>

{% endblock %}

The header and footer blocks remain unchanged if they have no replacement.

11. Real Website Structure

A common Django project might look like:

text
templates/
│
├── base.html
│
├── home.html
│
├── about.html
│
└── students/
    ├── list.html
    └── detail.html

base.html:

html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>

<head>

    <title>
        {% block title %}
            College Website
        {% endblock %}
    </title>

</head>

<body>

    <nav>
        <a href="/">Home</a>
        <a href="/about/">About</a>
        <a href="/students/">Students</a>
    </nav>

    <hr>

    {% block content %}
    {% endblock %}

    <hr>

    <footer>
        College Website
    </footer>

</body>

</html>

12. Home Page

home.html:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block title %}
    Home
{% endblock %}

{% block content %}

    <h1>Welcome</h1>

    <p>Welcome to our college website.</p>

{% endblock %}

13. About Page

about.html:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block title %}
    About
{% endblock %}

{% block content %}

    <h1>About Us</h1>

    <p>This is our college website.</p>

{% endblock %}

Notice how we don't repeat:

html
<html>
<head>
<body>
<nav>
<footer>

That's the whole purpose of inheritance.

14. View Functions

Home:

python
from django.shortcuts import render

def home(request):
    return render(request, "home.html")

About:

python
def about(request):
    return render(request, "about.html")

URLs:

python
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path("", views.home, name="home"),
    path("about/", views.about, name="about"),
]

15. Complete Flow

When the user visits:

text
/about/

Django:

text
URL
 ↓
views.about
 ↓
render(request, "about.html")
 ↓
about.html
 ↓
extends base.html
 ↓
content block inserted
 ↓
final HTML response

16. Passing Dynamic Data With Inheritance

Inheritance doesn't stop you from passing context.

View:

python
def student(request):

    student = {
        "name": "Aman",
        "course": "Computer Science"
    }

    return render(
        request,
        "student.html",
        {"student": student}
    )

Child:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block title %}
    Student
{% endblock %}

{% block content %}

    <h1>{{ student.name }}</h1>

    <p>{{ student.course }}</p>

{% endblock %}

So we can combine:

text
Inheritance
+
Variables
+
Loops
+
Conditions
+
Filters

17. Template Inheritance With a Loop

Suppose the view sends:

python
students = [
    {"name": "Aman", "marks": 85},
    {"name": "Rahul", "marks": 45},
]

Child template:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block title %}
    Students
{% endblock %}

{% block content %}

<h1>Students</h1>

{% for student in students %}

    <h2>{{ student.name }}</h2>

    <p>Marks: {{ student.marks }}</p>

    {% if student.marks >= 50 %}
        <p>PASS</p>
    {% else %}
        <p>FAIL</p>
    {% endif %}

{% endfor %}

{% endblock %}

This is a very realistic Django pattern.

18. {% include %}

Another important template feature is:

html
{% include "navbar.html" %}

include allows you to reuse a separate template fragment.

For example:

text
templates/
├── base.html
├── navbar.html
└── footer.html

navbar.html:

html
<nav>

    <a href="/">Home</a>
    <a href="/about/">About</a>
    <a href="/students/">Students</a>

</nav>

footer.html:

html
<footer>
    Copyright 2026
</footer>

Then:

html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>

<body>

    {% include "navbar.html" %}

    {% block content %}
    {% endblock %}

    {% include "footer.html" %}

</body>

</html>

19. extends vs include

This is a very common viva question.

{% extends %}

Used for:

Template inheritance / parent-child page structure.

Example:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% include %}

Used for:

Reusing a smaller template fragment.

Example:

html
{% include "navbar.html" %}

Think:

text
extends → entire page layout

include → reusable component/fragment

20. When Should You Use include?

Good examples:

text
navbar
footer
sidebar
login form
alert message
product card
student card
pagination

For example:

html
{% include "components/student_card.html" %}

21. Passing Context to an Include

Suppose:

html
{% include "student_card.html" with student=student %}

The included template can use:

html
<h2>{{ student.name }}</h2>

This is useful when rendering reusable components with different data.

22. only

You can restrict the context passed to an included template:

html
{% include "student_card.html" with student=student only %}

only means the included template receives only the explicitly supplied context rather than inheriting the surrounding context.

This is useful for making reusable components more predictable.

23. {% block %} vs {% include %}

Don't confuse these.

Block

Defines an area that a child template can override:

html
{% block content %}
{% endblock %}

Include

Directly inserts another template fragment:

html
{% include "navbar.html" %}

24. block.super

This is a more advanced inheritance concept.

Suppose base.html contains:

html
{% block content %}

<p>Default content</p>

{% endblock %}

Child:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block content %}

{{ block.super }}

<p>Additional content</p>

{% endblock %}

block.super means:

Include the parent's block content here.

So the child gets:

text
Default content
Additional content

instead of completely replacing the parent block.

25. Why Is Template Inheritance Useful?

1. Avoids duplication

You don't repeat navbar/footer.

2. Easier maintenance

Change the navbar once.

3. Consistent design

All pages use the same layout.

4. Cleaner templates

Child templates contain mostly page-specific content.

5. Scalable

Works well when a website has many pages.

26. Common Mistake — Wrong Block Name

Parent:

html
{% block content %}
{% endblock %}

Child:

html
{% block body %}
    Hello
{% endblock %}

This doesn't override the content block.

The names must match:

html
{% block content %}

and:

html
{% block content %}

27. Common Mistake — Forgetting extends

Wrong:

html
{% block content %}
    Hello
{% endblock %}

if the intention is to inherit from base.html.

Correct:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block content %}
    Hello
{% endblock %}

28. Common Mistake — Wrong Template Path

If:

text
templates/
└── base.html

use:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

If:

text
templates/
└── students/
    └── base.html

use:

html
{% extends "students/base.html" %}

The path is relative to the template search locations.

29. Common Mistake — Putting Page Content Outside Blocks

Suppose:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

<h1>Hello</h1>

{% block content %}
    Welcome
{% endblock %}

The normal pattern is to put child-specific content inside defined blocks.

Better:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block content %}
    <h1>Hello</h1>
    <p>Welcome</p>
{% endblock %}

30. Common Mistake — Thinking extends Copies a File Literally

Conceptually, inheritance means Django uses the parent structure and resolves the child's blocks.

It's better to think:

text
Parent layout
+
Child block overrides
=
Rendered template

rather than imagining simple text-file copying.

31. Exam Question

Question:

Create a base.html with:

  • title block
  • content block
  • footer

Then create home.html using inheritance.

Answer:

base.html:

html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>

<head>

    <title>
        {% block title %}
            Website
        {% endblock %}
    </title>

</head>

<body>

    {% block content %}
    {% endblock %}

    <footer>
        Copyright 2026
    </footer>

</body>

</html>

home.html:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block title %}
    Home
{% endblock %}

{% block content %}

    <h1>Welcome Home</h1>
    <p>This is the home page.</p>

{% endblock %}

32. Viva Questions

Q1. What is template inheritance?

Template inheritance allows a child template to reuse a parent template's common structure and override specific blocks.

Q2. Which tag is used for inheritance?

{% extends %}.

Q3. Which tag defines replaceable sections?

{% block %}.

Q4. What is base.html?

A parent template containing common layout elements such as navigation, footer, CSS references, and blocks for page-specific content.

Q5. What is {% include %}?

It inserts another template into the current template and is commonly used for reusable template fragments.

Q6. Difference between extends and include?

extends establishes parent-child template inheritance, while include inserts a reusable template fragment.

Q7. What happens if a child doesn't override a block?

The parent block's content is used.

Q8. What is block.super?

It allows a child block to include the content defined by its parent block.

Q9. Can a base template have multiple blocks?

Yes.

Q10. Can dynamic data be used in inherited templates?

Yes. Context passed by the view is available to the relevant templates and blocks.

33. ⭐ The Pattern You Must Memorize

base.html

html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>

<head>

    <title>
        {% block title %}
        {% endblock %}
    </title>

</head>

<body>

    <nav>
        Navbar
    </nav>

    {% block content %}
    {% endblock %}

    <footer>
        Footer
    </footer>

</body>

</html>

Child:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block title %}
    Home
{% endblock %}

{% block content %}

    <h1>Home Page</h1>

{% endblock %}

If you can write this from memory, you know the core of template inheritance.

34. 🔥 Combined Real-World Structure

A clean Django template system might look like:

text
templates/
│
├── base.html
│
├── components/
│   ├── navbar.html
│   ├── footer.html
│   └── student_card.html
│
├── home.html
├── about.html
│
└── students/
    ├── list.html
    └── detail.html

base.html:

html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>

<head>

    <title>
        {% block title %}
            College
        {% endblock %}
    </title>

</head>

<body>

    {% include "components/navbar.html" %}

    <main>

        {% block content %}
        {% endblock %}

    </main>

    {% include "components/footer.html" %}

</body>

</html>

Then every page can simply do:

html
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block title %}
    Students
{% endblock %}

{% block content %}

    <h1>Student List</h1>

    {% for student in students %}

        {% include "components/student_card.html" %}

    {% endfor %}

{% endblock %}

This is much closer to how a real Django project is organized.

🧠 Module 17 Summary

Remember these four concepts:

text
{% extends %}
      ↓
Parent-child relationship
text
{% block %}
      ↓
Replaceable section
text
{% include %}
      ↓
Reusable template component
text
{{ block.super }}
      ↓
Keep parent's block content

The most important architecture is:

text
                 base.html
                /         \
               /           \
          home.html      students.html
                              |
                              ↓
                         student_card

One-line viva answer:

Django template inheritance allows multiple child templates to reuse a common base layout while overriding specific blocks, reducing duplication and improving maintainability.

Module 18
Debugging Django

Module 18 — Debugging Django

Now we start an extremely practical topic: Debugging.

In a Django project, knowing how to write code is only half the skill.

You also need to know:

When my code doesn't work, how do I find exactly what is wrong?

This is what debugging means.

1. What Is Debugging?

Debugging is the process of:

  1. Finding an error/problem
  2. Understanding why it happened
  3. Locating the problematic code
  4. Fixing it
  5. Testing again

Example:

You visit:

text
/students/

and Django shows:

text
TemplateDoesNotExist

Debugging means determining:

Which template is Django looking for, where is it searching, and why can't it find it?

2. Error vs Bug

These terms are related but different.

Error

A problem that prevents code from working correctly.

Example:

python
print(name

Missing ) → syntax error.

Bug

The program runs but behaves incorrectly.

Example:

python
price = 100
quantity = 5

total = price + quantity

The program runs, but the correct calculation should be:

python
total = price * quantity

So:

Error = problem in execution/code.
Bug = incorrect behavior or result.

3. Django Debug Mode

Open:

text
settings.py

You'll find:

python
DEBUG = True

During development, Django gives detailed error information when something goes wrong.

For example:

text
TemplateDoesNotExist at /students/

and below it you'll get a traceback showing where the error occurred.

4. Why Is DEBUG=True Useful?

Because Django can show:

  • Exception type
  • Error message
  • File name
  • Line number
  • Code around the error
  • Traceback
  • Request information
  • Django/Python information

This makes debugging much easier.

5. ⚠️ Never Use DEBUG=True in Production

Suppose your production website crashes.

If:

python
DEBUG = True

Django can expose sensitive internal information through the detailed error page.

Therefore:

python
DEBUG = False

should normally be used in production.

This is both an exam question and an important security concept.

6. Reading a Django Error Page

Suppose Django displays:

text
TemplateDoesNotExist at /students/

students/list.html

Don't panic.

Read the error from top to bottom.

The important information is:

text
Exception:
TemplateDoesNotExist

Message:
students/list.html

This immediately tells you:

Django couldn't find the requested template.

7. Traceback

A traceback shows the chain of function calls that led to the error.

For example:

text
Traceback

File ".../urls.py", line 10
    path("students/", views.students)

File ".../views.py", line 15
    return render(...)

TemplateDoesNotExist

The most useful part is usually the last exception shown, along with the file/line information around where it occurred.

8. Debugging Strategy

When Django gives an error, follow this sequence:

text
1. Read exception type
        ↓
2. Read error message
        ↓
3. Find file and line number
        ↓
4. Inspect surrounding code
        ↓
5. Check related configuration
        ↓
6. Fix
        ↓
7. Run again

Don't randomly change multiple files.

9. Error #1 — SyntaxError

Example:

python
def home(request)
    return HttpResponse("Hello")

There's a missing :.

Python reports something similar to:

text
SyntaxError: expected ':'

Correct:

python
def home(request):
    return HttpResponse("Hello")

10. Syntax Errors in Templates

For example:

html
{% if user %}
    Hello

You forgot:

html
{% endif %}

Correct:

html
{% if user %}
    Hello
{% endif %}

Template syntax errors can appear when Django compiles the template.

11. Error #2 — NameError

Example:

python
def home(request):
    return HttpResponse(message)

But message was never defined.

You may get:

text
NameError: name 'message' is not defined

Correct:

python
def home(request):
    message = "Hello"
    return HttpResponse(message)

12. Error #3 — ImportError

Suppose:

python
from django.http import HttpRespons

The actual class is:

python
HttpResponse

You may get an import-related error.

Correct:

python
from django.http import HttpResponse

Common causes:

  • Typo in import
  • Wrong module
  • Missing package
  • Circular imports in more advanced projects

13. Error #4 — ModuleNotFoundError

Example:

python
import some_package

but the package isn't installed.

Python may report:

text
ModuleNotFoundError

For third-party packages, check the active virtual environment and installation.

For Django itself:

bash
python -m django --version

14. Error #5 — TemplateDoesNotExist

This is one of the most common Django beginner errors.

Suppose your view says:

python
return render(request, "home.html")

but Django can't find it.

You may see:

text
TemplateDoesNotExist at /
home.html

15. Why Does TemplateDoesNotExist Happen?

Common reasons:

Reason 1 — Wrong folder

You might have:

text
templates/
    home.htm

but requested:

text
home.html

Reason 2 — Wrong filename

python
render(request, "home.html")

but file is:

text
homepage.html

Reason 3 — App not installed

If using app-level templates:

python
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    "students",
]

must include the app.

Reason 4 — Wrong path

Suppose:

text
students/
└── templates/
    └── students/
        └── home.html

Then:

python
render(request, "students/home.html")

not:

python
render(request, "home.html")

16. Correct App Template Structure

Recommended:

text
students/
│
├── templates/
│   └── students/
│       └── home.html
│
├── views.py
└── ...

Then:

python
return render(
    request,
    "students/home.html"
)

The extra students/ directory helps avoid template-name collisions between apps.

17. Error #6 — NoReverseMatch

This is another very important Django error.

Suppose URL:

python
path(
    "student/<int:id>/",
    views.student_detail,
    name="student_detail"
)

But template says:

html
<a href="{% url 'student_detail' %}">
    Student
</a>

Django needs the id parameter.

You might get:

text
NoReverseMatch

18. Fixing NoReverseMatch

Provide the required parameter:

html
<a href="{% url 'student_detail' id=101 %}">
    Student
</a>

Or dynamically:

html
<a href="{% url 'student_detail' id=student.id %}">
    Student
</a>

19. NoReverseMatch Common Causes

Wrong URL name

URL:

python
name="student_detail"

Template:

html
{% url 'student' %}

Wrong.

Missing parameter

URL:

python
path(
    "student/<int:id>/",
    views.student_detail,
    name="student_detail"
)

Template:

html
{% url 'student_detail' %}

Missing id.

Wrong parameter name

URL:

python
<int:id>

Template:

html
{% url 'student_detail' student_id=101 %}

Wrong keyword.

Use:

html
{% url 'student_detail' id=101 %}

20. Error #7 — ViewDoesNotExist

Suppose:

python
path(
    "home/",
    views.hom
)

but the actual function is:

python
def home(request):

Django can't find the specified view.

Correct:

python
path(
    "home/",
    views.home
)

21. Error #8 — AttributeError

Example:

python
student = {
    "name": "Aman"
}

print(student.name)

A dictionary doesn't provide that access pattern in normal Python.

You'd use:

python
student["name"]

or in a Django template:

html
{{ student.name }}

A Python error may look like:

text
AttributeError

22. Error #9 — TypeError

Example:

python
age = 20

print(age + " years")

Python cannot add an integer and string directly.

You'll get a TypeError.

Correct:

python
print(str(age) + " years")

or use an f-string:

python
print(f"{age} years")

23. Error #10 — DoesNotExist

This becomes especially important when we start using models.

Suppose:

python
student = Student.objects.get(id=100)

If no matching student exists, Django raises something like:

text
Student.DoesNotExist

Later, you'll learn the cleaner solution:

python
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404

student = get_object_or_404(Student, id=100)

which converts the missing object into an HTTP 404 response.

24. Error #11 — OperationalError

You may encounter database errors such as:

text
django.db.utils.OperationalError

Common causes can include:

  • Database configuration problems
  • Missing database table
  • Migration not applied
  • Database connection failure

For example, if you create a model but haven't applied migrations, you may encounter a missing-table problem.

We'll understand this much better in the Models/Migrations modules.

25. Error #12 — 404 Page Not Found

Suppose your URL configuration contains:

python
path("students/", views.students)

but you visit:

text
/student/

Notice:

text
students/

vs:

text
student/

Django doesn't find a matching URL and returns:

text
404 Not Found

26. URL 404 vs Object 404

Very important distinction.

URL doesn't exist:

text
/students/abc/

doesn't match your URL pattern.

That's a URL routing 404.

URL exists but object doesn't:

text
/student/999/

matches:

python
<int:id>

but student 999 doesn't exist.

That's an object/data 404.

These are different problems even though both result in HTTP 404.

27. Error #13 — CSRF Error

You'll encounter this in the Forms module.

A POST form may produce:

text
403 Forbidden
CSRF verification failed

Often this means the template doesn't contain the required CSRF token.

Typical Django form:

html
<form method="POST">

    {% csrf_token %}

    ...
    
</form>

We'll study CSRF properly in Unit IV.

28. Error #14 — Port Already in Use

Suppose you start:

bash
python manage.py runserver

but another process is already using port 8000.

You can use another port:

bash
python manage.py runserver 8001

Then visit:

text
http://127.0.0.1:8001/

29. Error #15 — Wrong Virtual Environment

Suppose Django was installed inside:

text
venv

but VS Code is using another Python interpreter.

You might see:

text
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'django'

even though you installed Django.

Check:

bash
python -m django --version

and verify that the correct virtual environment/interpreter is active.

30. Django Debug Toolbar vs Django Debug Mode

Don't confuse:

text
DEBUG = True

with a separate debugging tool such as Django Debug Toolbar.

DEBUG=True is a Django setting controlling development behavior and error reporting.

A debug toolbar is an additional development package/tool used for inspecting things such as:

  • SQL queries
  • request information
  • templates
  • performance

For your syllabus, the important concept is primarily:

python
DEBUG = True

31. Using print() for Debugging

A beginner-friendly technique:

python
def home(request):

    name = "Aman"

    print(name)

    return render(
        request,
        "home.html",
        {"name": name}
    )

The value appears in the terminal running Django.

You can inspect:

python
print(request.method)
print(request.GET)
print(request.POST)

during development.

32. Better Debugging With breakpoint()

Python provides:

python
breakpoint()

Example:

python
def student(request):

    students = ["Aman", "Rahul"]

    breakpoint()

    return render(
        request,
        "students.html",
        {"students": students}
    )

Execution pauses at that point when using a suitable debugger/terminal environment.

You can inspect variables.

This is more advanced than print() debugging.

33. Debugging in VS Code

VS Code provides a debugger where you can:

  • Set breakpoints
  • Run code step-by-step
  • Inspect variables
  • Watch expressions
  • See the call stack

A breakpoint is a point where program execution pauses so you can inspect what's happening.

34. Example Debugging Process

Suppose:

python
def student(request):

    student = {
        "name": "Aman",
        "age": 21
    }

    return render(
        request,
        "students/detail.html",
        {"student": student}
    )

You get:

text
TemplateDoesNotExist
students/detail.html

Step 1

Read exception:

text
TemplateDoesNotExist

Step 2

Read requested path:

text
students/detail.html

Step 3

Check filesystem:

text
students/
└── templates/
    └── students/
        └── detail.html

If instead you have:

text
students/
└── templates/
    └── detail.html

the requested path is wrong for that structure.

Step 4

Fix either the path or template location.

Step 5

Reload.

That's systematic debugging.

35. Don't Change Everything at Once

A common beginner mistake is:

"It doesn't work, so I'll change views.py, urls.py, settings.py, and HTML simultaneously."

Don't.

Instead:

text
Error
 ↓
Identify exact error
 ↓
Identify responsible layer
 ↓
Change minimum necessary code
 ↓
Test

36. Identify the Layer

Django applications can be thought of as layers:

text
Browser
   ↓
URL
   ↓
View
   ↓
Model/Database
   ↓
Template
   ↓
Response

If the error is:

text
NoReverseMatch

look first at:

text
URLs + template URL tag

If:

text
TemplateDoesNotExist

look at:

text
Template path + settings + installed app

If:

text
DoesNotExist

look at:

text
Database query/object retrieval

This saves enormous time.

37. Error Diagnosis Table

Error Usually means
SyntaxError Invalid Python syntax
NameError Variable/name doesn't exist
ImportError Import problem
ModuleNotFoundError Module/package can't be found
TemplateDoesNotExist Template can't be found
NoReverseMatch URL reversing failed
ViewDoesNotExist Referenced view can't be found
AttributeError Object doesn't have requested attribute
TypeError Wrong/incompatible type operation
DoesNotExist Requested model object doesn't exist
OperationalError Database/SQL-related operational issue
404 URL/resource not found
403 Permission/CSRF/access forbidden
500 Server-side application error

38. ⭐ Very Important: Read the Last Exception

Suppose the traceback contains:

text
File ...
File ...
File ...
File ...

TemplateDoesNotExist

Don't get overwhelmed by the entire traceback.

Start with:

What exception occurred?

Then:

What message accompanies it?

Then:

Which line in my code triggered it?

39. Example Viva Question

Teacher:

What is debugging?

Answer:

Debugging is the systematic process of identifying, locating, analyzing, and fixing errors or unexpected behavior in a program.

40. Viva Question

Teacher:

What is DEBUG in Django?

Answer:

DEBUG is a Django setting that controls development debugging behavior. When DEBUG=True, Django provides detailed error information. It should not be enabled in production.

41. Viva Question

Teacher:

Why shouldn't DEBUG=True be used in production?

Answer:

Because detailed error pages can expose sensitive application and environment information.

42. Viva Question

Teacher:

What is TemplateDoesNotExist?

Answer:

It occurs when Django cannot locate the template requested by the application.

43. Viva Question

Teacher:

What is NoReverseMatch?

Answer:

It occurs when Django cannot construct a URL from a named URL pattern, commonly because the URL name or required parameters are incorrect or missing.

44. Viva Question

Teacher:

What is a traceback?

Answer:

A traceback is a report showing the sequence of function calls that led to an exception, along with information about where the error occurred.

45. Viva Question

Teacher:

Difference between 404 and 500?

Answer:

A 404 indicates that the requested resource or URL was not found, while a 500 indicates an unexpected server-side error occurred while processing the request.

46. Viva Question

Teacher:

How can you debug a variable in a Django view?

Answer:

During development, I can use print() statements, Python's breakpoint(), or an IDE debugger to inspect the variable and program execution.

47. Coding Question

Question:

This code gives an error:

python
def home(request):
    return render(request, "home.html")

The file actually exists at:

text
students/templates/students/home.html

What should you change?

Answer:

python
def home(request):
    return render(request, "students/home.html")

assuming the app is correctly installed and template discovery is configured.

48. Coding Question

Given:

python
path(
    "student/<int:id>/",
    views.student_detail,
    name="student_detail"
)

This template causes NoReverseMatch:

html
<a href="{% url 'student_detail' %}">
    Student
</a>

Fix it.

Answer:

html
<a href="{% url 'student_detail' id=101 %}">
    Student
</a>

Or dynamically:

html
<a href="{% url 'student_detail' id=student.id %}">
    Student
</a>

49. Coding Question

Find the error:

python
def home(request)
    return HttpResponse("Hello")

Answer:

Missing colon:

python
def home(request):
    return HttpResponse("Hello")

50. Coding Question

Find the error:

python
from django.http import HttpRespons

Answer:

The class name is:

python
HttpResponse

Correct:

python
from django.http import HttpResponse

51. Debugging Checklist ⭐

Whenever your Django application isn't working:

1. Check terminal

Look for:

text
Exception
Error
Traceback

2. Check browser

Look at:

text
404
403
500

3. Read the exception

For example:

text
TemplateDoesNotExist

4. Check exact line

Don't just read the filename.

5. Check spelling

Especially:

text
URLs
view names
template names
variable names
imports

6. Check configuration

Especially:

text
INSTALLED_APPS
TEMPLATES
DATABASES
URL patterns

7. Test again

Don't assume the fix worked until you reload/test.

52. ⭐ Master Debugging Flow

Memorize this:

text
                    ERROR
                      ↓
             Read exception type
                      ↓
             Read error message
                      ↓
             Find file + line
                      ↓
              Identify Django layer
                      ↓
             Check relevant code
                      ↓
                 Fix it
                      ↓
                  Test again

This is much better than randomly modifying code.

Module 19
Testing in Django

Module 19 — Testing in Django

Now we move to Testing, the final topic of Unit III.

So far, we've learned how to:

text
URLs → Views → Templates → Dynamic Data → Debugging

But how do we know that our application actually works correctly?

That's where testing comes in.

1. What Is Software Testing?

Software testing is the process of checking whether software behaves as expected.

Suppose we create:

python
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

We expect:

text
add(2, 3) → 5

A test verifies that assumption.

In Django, we can automatically test:

  • Views
  • URLs
  • Templates
  • Models
  • Forms
  • Authentication
  • HTTP responses
  • Application logic

2. Why Do We Need Testing?

Imagine your Django application has:

text
100 views
500 URLs
50 forms
20 models

You cannot manually check every feature every time you modify the application.

Suppose you change the login system.

It might accidentally break:

text
Registration
Profile
Dashboard
Logout

Automated tests help detect these regressions.

3. What Is a Test?

A test generally follows:

text
Arrange
   ↓
Act
   ↓
Assert

Arrange

Prepare the required data.

Act

Perform the operation.

Assert

Check whether the result is what you expected.

Example:

python
result = add(2, 3)

self.assertEqual(result, 5)

Here:

text
Act → add(2, 3)
Assert → result == 5

4. What Is Unit Testing?

Unit testing tests a small, isolated part of an application.

For example:

python
def calculate_total(price, quantity):
    return price * quantity

We could test this function independently.

python
self.assertEqual(
    calculate_total(100, 5),
    500
)

The goal is to verify individual units of behavior.

5. Django Testing Framework

Django provides built-in support for testing.

A newly created Django app normally contains:

text
students/
├── admin.py
├── apps.py
├── models.py
├── tests.py
├── views.py
└── ...

The default:

text
tests.py

is where you can begin writing tests.

Django's testing system is built on Python's unittest framework.

6. Basic Django Test

Suppose our views.py contains:

python
from django.http import HttpResponse

def home(request):
    return HttpResponse("Hello Django")

We can write:

python
from django.test import TestCase

class HomeTest(TestCase):

    def test_home(self):
        response = self.client.get("/")

        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)

Let's understand every line.

7. TestCase

python
from django.test import TestCase

TestCase provides Django-specific testing functionality.

Then:

python
class HomeTest(TestCase):

creates a test class.

It inherits from Django's TestCase.

8. Test Method

Inside the class:

python
def test_home(self):

This is a test method.

Django's test discovery looks for methods whose names begin with:

text
test

So:

python
def test_home(self):

is detected as a test.

9. Django Test Client

This is extremely important:

python
self.client

Django provides a test client that can simulate requests to your application.

For example:

python
response = self.client.get("/")

This behaves conceptually like a browser making a GET request.

You don't need to manually open Chrome.

10. GET Request Test

Example:

python
response = self.client.get("/")

This sends a GET request to:

text
/

Then we can inspect:

python
response.status_code

If the page works:

text
200

11. assertEqual

We can write:

python
self.assertEqual(
    response.status_code,
    200
)

This means:

Assert that the response status code equals 200.

If it is:

text
200

the test passes.

If it is:

text
404

the test fails.

12. Complete Example

views.py

python
from django.http import HttpResponse

def home(request):
    return HttpResponse("Hello Django")

urls.py

python
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path("", views.home, name="home"),
]

tests.py

python
from django.test import TestCase

class HomeTest(TestCase):

    def test_home(self):
        response = self.client.get("/")

        self.assertEqual(
            response.status_code,
            200
        )

Run:

bash
python manage.py test

13. Running Tests

The main command is:

bash
python manage.py test

Django searches for tests and runs them.

You might see:

text
Creating test database...
.
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 1 test

OK

The . indicates a passing test.

14. What Is the Test Database?

When Django tests interact with the database, Django creates a separate test database.

This prevents normal development data from being modified by tests.

Conceptually:

text
Normal Database
      │
      │ protected
      ↓
Test Database
      │
      ↓
Tests run here
      │
      ↓
Test database is removed

This is an important Django testing feature.

15. Why Not Use the Real Database?

Imagine your database contains:

text
1000 students

A test might create:

text
Student: Test Student

If tests used your real database, they could modify or delete real data.

Therefore Django isolates testing using a test database.

16. Testing Response Content

Suppose:

python
def home(request):
    return HttpResponse("Hello Django")

We can test whether the response contains the expected text:

python
self.assertContains(
    response,
    "Hello Django"
)

So:

python
def test_home_content(self):

    response = self.client.get("/")

    self.assertContains(
        response,
        "Hello Django"
    )

17. assertContains

This is very useful for Django views.

It checks whether the response contains the specified content.

Example:

python
self.assertContains(
    response,
    "Welcome"
)

If the response contains:

text
Welcome to Django

the test passes.

18. Testing Status Codes

Common examples:

python
self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)

For a missing URL:

python
response = self.client.get("/does-not-exist/")
self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 404)

You can test expected HTTP behavior.

19. Testing Templates

Suppose your view:

python
def home(request):

    return render(
        request,
        "home.html"
    )

You can check whether the correct template was used:

python
self.assertTemplateUsed(
    response,
    "home.html"
)

Complete:

python
def test_home_template(self):

    response = self.client.get("/")

    self.assertTemplateUsed(
        response,
        "home.html"
    )

20. Testing Multiple Things

A good test can check several related expectations.

python
def test_home(self):

    response = self.client.get("/")

    self.assertEqual(
        response.status_code,
        200
    )

    self.assertTemplateUsed(
        response,
        "home.html"
    )

    self.assertContains(
        response,
        "Welcome"
    )

This checks:

text
HTTP status
+
Template
+
Content

21. Testing URL Names

Suppose:

python
path(
    "students/",
    views.students,
    name="students"
)

You can use Django's URL reversing system in tests.

For example:

python
from django.urls import reverse

url = reverse("students")

response = self.client.get(url)

Then:

python
self.assertEqual(
    response.status_code,
    200
)

This is often better than hardcoding:

python
"/students/"

because if the URL path changes but its name remains the same, the test doesn't need to change.

22. reverse() in Tests

Example:

python
url = reverse("home")
response = self.client.get(url)

If:

python
path(
    "",
    views.home,
    name="home"
)

then:

text
reverse("home")

returns:

text
/

23. Testing Dynamic URLs

Suppose:

python
path(
    "student/<int:id>/",
    views.student_detail,
    name="student_detail"
)

Use:

python
url = reverse(
    "student_detail",
    kwargs={"id": 101}
)

response = self.client.get(url)

Django generates:

text
/student/101/

Then:

python
self.assertEqual(
    response.status_code,
    200
)

24. Testing POST Requests

The test client can also send POST requests.

Example:

python
response = self.client.post(
    "/students/",
    {
        "name": "Aman",
        "age": 21
    }
)

This simulates submitting a form.

The general syntax is:

python
self.client.post(
    url,
    data
)

25. GET vs POST Testing

GET

python
response = self.client.get("/students/")

POST

python
response = self.client.post(
    "/students/",
    {"name": "Aman"}
)

The test client supports both.

26. Testing Redirects

Suppose a successful POST redirects to:

text
/students/

You might test:

python
response = self.client.post(
    "/students/create/",
    {"name": "Aman"}
)

self.assertRedirects(
    response,
    "/students/"
)

assertRedirects() checks redirect behavior.

27. Why Test Redirects?

Imagine you create a student.

Expected:

text
POST form
   ↓
student created
   ↓
redirect
   ↓
student list

If the redirect breaks, the user experience breaks.

Testing ensures the expected navigation occurs.

28. Testing a View With Context

Suppose:

python
def home(request):

    return render(
        request,
        "home.html",
        {"name": "Aman"}
    )

You can inspect:

python
response.context["name"]

For example:

python
self.assertEqual(
    response.context["name"],
    "Aman"
)

This verifies that the expected context was provided.

29. Testing a Model

We'll learn models in detail later, but here's the basic idea.

Suppose:

python
from django.db import models

class Student(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)

A test might create:

python
student = Student.objects.create(
    name="Aman"
)

Then:

python
self.assertEqual(
    student.name,
    "Aman"
)

This tests model behavior/database interaction.

30. setUp()

Suppose many tests need the same data.

Instead of creating the data repeatedly:

python
def test_one(self):
    ...

def test_two(self):
    ...

def test_three(self):
    ...

you can use:

python
def setUp(self):
    ...

Example:

python
class StudentTest(TestCase):

    def setUp(self):

        self.student = Student.objects.create(
            name="Aman"
        )

    def test_student_name(self):

        self.assertEqual(
            self.student.name,
            "Aman"
        )

setUp() runs before each test method.

31. Why setUp() Is Useful

Suppose you have 10 tests and all require:

text
Student
Course
Teacher

You can prepare the common test data in setUp().

This avoids duplication.

32. Important: Tests Are Independent

A good test should generally not depend on another test having run first.

For example:

text
test_create_student
        ↓
test_delete_student

You shouldn't assume test_create_student always runs first.

Each test should establish the state it needs.

Django's TestCase helps isolate database state between tests.

33. Test Naming

Good:

python
def test_home_page_loads(self):
python
def test_student_creation(self):
python
def test_invalid_login(self):

Bad:

python
def check(self):

The test discovery convention is important.

34. Testing Invalid Behavior

Don't only test successful cases.

Suppose:

text
Valid ID → 200
Invalid ID → 404

Test both.

Example:

python
def test_invalid_student(self):

    response = self.client.get(
        "/student/999/"
    )

    self.assertEqual(
        response.status_code,
        404
    )

This is called testing an edge/error case.

35. Positive vs Negative Tests

Positive test

Tests expected valid behavior.

text
Valid request
→ 200

Negative test

Tests invalid/unexpected input.

text
Invalid request
→ 400/404/etc.

Both are important.

36. What Is Regression Testing?

Suppose your login system worked yesterday.

You modify the registration system.

After the modification, login accidentally breaks.

A test that previously passed now fails.

This helps detect a regression.

So:

Regression testing checks that previously working functionality continues to work after changes.

Automated tests are particularly valuable for this.

37. Test-Driven Development

You may hear the term TDD.

TDD stands for:

Test-Driven Development.

The simplified cycle is:

text
Write failing test
       ↓
Write code
       ↓
Make test pass
       ↓
Refactor
       ↓
Repeat

This is a development methodology.

You don't need to use TDD for every Django project, but understand the concept for viva.

38. Complete Example — Testing a Home Page

views.py

python
from django.shortcuts import render

def home(request):

    return render(
        request,
        "home.html",
        {
            "name": "Aman"
        }
    )

urls.py

python
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path(
        "",
        views.home,
        name="home"
    ),
]

tests.py

python
from django.test import TestCase
from django.urls import reverse


class HomeTest(TestCase):

    def test_home_page(self):

        url = reverse("home")

        response = self.client.get(url)

        self.assertEqual(
            response.status_code,
            200
        )

        self.assertTemplateUsed(
            response,
            "home.html"
        )

        self.assertContains(
            response,
            "Aman"
        )

This is a very good beginner Django test.

39. Understanding the Test

Let's break it down.

Step 1

python
url = reverse("home")

Gets the URL using its name.

Step 2

python
response = self.client.get(url)

Simulates a GET request.

Step 3

python
self.assertEqual(
    response.status_code,
    200
)

Checks that the page loaded successfully.

Step 4

python
self.assertTemplateUsed(
    response,
    "home.html"
)

Checks the template.

Step 5

python
self.assertContains(
    response,
    "Aman"
)

Checks the content.

40. Running a Specific App's Tests

You can run:

bash
python manage.py test students

This tells Django to run tests associated with the students app.

You can also run a particular test module/class/method using Django's test-label syntax.

For example:

bash
python manage.py test students.tests.HomeTest

or:

bash
python manage.py test students.tests.HomeTest.test_home_page

This is useful when you have many tests.

41. Test Output

A successful test run may look approximately like:

text
Creating test database...
.
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Ran 1 test

OK
Destroying test database...

If a test fails, Django provides information about:

  • Which test failed
  • Expected result
  • Actual result
  • Traceback

Then you debug the failing test/code.

42. Common Testing Mistakes

Mistake 1

Forgetting:

python
from django.test import TestCase

Mistake 2

Naming test method incorrectly:

python
def home_test(self):

Instead use:

python
def test_home(self):

Mistake 3

Using incorrect URL:

python
self.client.get("/wrong/")

when the actual URL is:

text
/students/

Mistake 4

Expecting the wrong status:

python
self.assertEqual(
    response.status_code,
    404
)

when the view should return 200.

Mistake 5

Testing only successful cases.

Always consider invalid input and failure scenarios.

43. Important Assertions to Know

For your syllabus and viva, know these:

assertEqual

python
self.assertEqual(actual, expected)

Checks equality.

assertContains

python
self.assertContains(response, "Hello")

Checks response content.

assertTemplateUsed

python
self.assertTemplateUsed(
    response,
    "home.html"
)

Checks template usage.

assertRedirects

python
self.assertRedirects(
    response,
    "/students/"
)

Checks redirects.

44. Other Useful Assertions

Python/Django tests also provide many other assertions, including:

python
self.assertTrue(value)
self.assertFalse(value)
self.assertIsNone(value)
self.assertIsNotNone(value)
self.assertIn(item, collection)
self.assertNotEqual(a, b)

You don't need to memorize every assertion, but understand that Django tests build on Python's testing framework.

45. Viva Questions

Q1. What is software testing?

Software testing is the process of verifying that software behaves according to its expected requirements.

Q2. Why do we test Django applications?

To verify correctness, detect bugs, prevent regressions, and ensure that application features continue to work after changes.

Q3. What is TestCase?

django.test.TestCase is a Django testing class that provides a test environment and database isolation for tests.

Q4. How do you run Django tests?

bash
python manage.py test

Q5. What is Django test client?

It is a Python interface provided by Django for simulating HTTP requests to an application without using a real browser.

Q6. How do you send a GET request?

python
self.client.get("/")

Q7. How do you send a POST request?

python
self.client.post(
    "/students/",
    data
)

46. Viva — Test Database

Teacher:

Does Django testing use the normal database?

Answer:

Django creates a separate test database for database-related tests, helping prevent tests from modifying normal application data.

47. Viva — setUp()

Teacher:

What is setUp()?

Answer:

setUp() is a method used to prepare common test data or state before each test method runs.

48. Viva — Regression

Teacher:

What is regression testing?

Answer:

Regression testing verifies that existing functionality continues to work after code changes.

49. Viva — Test Discovery

Teacher:

How does Django find tests?

Answer:

Django's test runner discovers tests according to Python/Django test discovery conventions, including test modules and test methods whose names begin with test.

Test a redirect:

def test_create_student_redirect(self):

54. ⭐ Testing Strategy for a Django Application

For a typical Django project, you might test:

text
              Django Application
                     │
       ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
       ↓             ↓             ↓
      URLs          Views        Models
       │             │             │
       ↓             ↓             ↓
    Routing       Responses      Database
       │             │             │
       └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                     ↓
                   Forms
                     ↓
              Authentication

For example:

URL tests

text
Does /students/ resolve correctly?

View tests

text
Does the view return 200?

Template tests

text
Is students.html rendered?

Content tests

text
Does the response contain the student's name?

Model tests

text
Can a Student be created correctly?

Form tests

text
Does invalid input get rejected?

Authentication tests

text
Can a logged-in user access the dashboard?
