Module 22
Form Validation

Module 22 — Form Validation in Django

This module is very important for coding questions and viva, because teachers often ask:

  • How does Django validate form data?
  • What is cleaned_data?
  • Difference between clean_<field>() and clean().
  • How do you create custom validation?
  • How do you validate two fields together?
  • How do you display validation errors?
  • How do min_length, max_length, min_value, etc. work?

1. What is Form Validation?

Form validation means checking whether the data entered by the user is:

  1. Present when required
  2. Of the correct type
  3. Within allowed limits
  4. In the correct format
  5. Logically valid according to our application's rules

For example, suppose we have:

python
class StudentForm(forms.Form):
    name = forms.CharField()
    age = forms.IntegerField()
    email = forms.EmailField()

A user might enter:

text
Name: Aman
Age: abc
Email: hello

The form should reject this data.

Django automatically performs many basic validations for us.

2. The Most Important Line: is_valid()

When a form receives submitted data:

python
form = StudentForm(request.POST)

we check:

python
if form.is_valid():

Example:

python
def student_form(request):

    if request.method == "POST":
        form = StudentForm(request.POST)

        if form.is_valid():
            print("Valid data")
        else:
            print("Invalid data")

    else:
        form = StudentForm()

    return render(request, "student_form.html", {"form": form})

Important

is_valid() does much more than simply return True or False.

It triggers Django's validation process.

Conceptually:

text
request.POST
     ↓
Bound Form
     ↓
form.is_valid()
     ↓
Validation
     ↓
Valid? ─────── No ──→ form.errors
   │
  Yes
   ↓
form.cleaned_data

3. What is cleaned_data?

After successful validation:

python
form.cleaned_data

contains the cleaned and converted data.

Example:

python
class StudentForm(forms.Form):
    name = forms.CharField()
    age = forms.IntegerField()

User submits:

text
name = "Aman"
age = "21"

Notice that HTTP form data arrives essentially as strings.

Django converts the age into an integer.

After:

python
form.is_valid()

we can do:

python
form.cleaned_data["name"]

Result:

text
Aman

and:

python
form.cleaned_data["age"]

Result:

python
21

which is an integer.

Very important rule

Do not use:

python
form.cleaned_data

before:

python
form.is_valid()

Correct:

python
if form.is_valid():
    age = form.cleaned_data["age"]

4. Built-in Validation

Django fields already provide many validators.

For example:

python
class StudentForm(forms.Form):
    name = forms.CharField(
        min_length=3,
        max_length=30
    )

    age = forms.IntegerField(
        min_value=18,
        max_value=60
    )

    email = forms.EmailField()

Django automatically checks:

Name

text
Minimum 3 characters
Maximum 30 characters

Age

text
Minimum 18
Maximum 60

Email

Checks whether the value has a valid email format.

5. required

By default, Django form fields are required.

For example:

python
name = forms.CharField()

means the user cannot leave it empty.

You can explicitly write:

python
name = forms.CharField(required=True)

Both mean essentially the same thing.

Making a field optional

python
phone = forms.CharField(required=False)

Now the user may leave the phone field empty.

Example:

python
class StudentForm(forms.Form):
    name = forms.CharField()
    phone = forms.CharField(required=False)

Here:

text
name → required
phone → optional

Viva question

Q: What is the default value of required?

Answer:

text
True

6. min_length

Used with fields such as CharField.

python
username = forms.CharField(min_length=5)

This means:

text
username must contain at least 5 characters

For example:

text
abc       ❌
aman      ❌
aman123   ✅

7. max_length

python
username = forms.CharField(max_length=20)

Maximum 20 characters are allowed.

You can combine them:

python
username = forms.CharField(
    min_length=5,
    max_length=20
)

8. min_value

Used for numeric fields.

python
age = forms.IntegerField(min_value=18)

Allowed:

text
18
19
20
...

Rejected:

text
17
16
10

9. max_value

python
age = forms.IntegerField(max_value=60)

So:

text
18 → valid
40 → valid
60 → valid
61 → invalid

Combine both:

python
age = forms.IntegerField(
    min_value=18,
    max_value=60
)

10. Email Validation

Django provides:

python
forms.EmailField()

Example:

python
email = forms.EmailField()

This provides built-in email validation.

For example:

text
aman@gmail.com       ✅
student@example.com  ✅
hello               ❌
abc@                ❌

11. ChoiceField Validation

Suppose we only allow:

python
COURSES = [
    ("cse", "Computer Science"),
    ("ece", "Electronics"),
    ("me", "Mechanical"),
]

Form:

python
class StudentForm(forms.Form):

    course = forms.ChoiceField(
        choices=COURSES
    )

The first value is what is submitted:

text
cse

The second value is displayed:

text
Computer Science

Django also validates that the submitted choice belongs to the allowed choices.

12. BooleanField

Example:

python
agree = forms.BooleanField()

The user must check the checkbox.

You can make it optional:

python
agree = forms.BooleanField(required=False)

13. Validation Errors

Suppose:

python
class StudentForm(forms.Form):
    age = forms.IntegerField(min_value=18)

User enters:

text
15

Then:

python
form.is_valid()

returns:

python
False

The errors are available through:

python
form.errors

You can inspect:

python
print(form.errors)

14. Displaying Errors in Template

Suppose we have:

html
<form method="POST">
    {% csrf_token %}

    {{ form.as_p }}

    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

Django automatically displays field errors when the bound form is invalid.

You can also explicitly display them:

html
{{ form.name.errors }}

For age:

html
{{ form.age.errors }}

Or all errors:

html
{{ form.errors }}

15. Field-Level Custom Validation

Now we reach one of the most important topics.

Suppose Django's built-in validators are not enough.

For example:

Student name should not contain numbers.

We can create custom validation.

16. clean_<field>()

For validating a specific field, use:

python
clean_<fieldname>()

For example:

python
clean_name()

Complete example:

python
from django import forms

class StudentForm(forms.Form):

    name = forms.CharField()
    age = forms.IntegerField()

    def clean_name(self):
        name = self.cleaned_data["name"]

        if any(char.isdigit() for char in name):
            raise forms.ValidationError(
                "Name should not contain numbers."
            )

        return name

Let's understand this carefully.

17. How clean_name() Works

Suppose user enters:

text
Aman123

Django first performs the normal validation for the field.

Then Django calls:

python
clean_name()

Inside:

python
name = self.cleaned_data["name"]

we get the already cleaned name.

Then:

python
if any(char.isdigit() for char in name):

checks whether any character is a digit.

If yes:

python
raise forms.ValidationError(
    "Name should not contain numbers."
)

The form becomes invalid.

If everything is fine:

python
return name

The returned value becomes the cleaned value for that field.

18. Why Must We Return the Value?

This is a common viva/coding question.

Correct:

python
def clean_name(self):
    name = self.cleaned_data["name"]

    if len(name) < 3:
        raise forms.ValidationError("Too short")

    return name

The return is important because Django uses the returned value as the cleaned value.

You can even modify it:

python
def clean_name(self):
    name = self.cleaned_data["name"]
    return name.strip().title()

So:

text
"  aman ranjan  "

can become:

text
"Aman Ranjan"

19. Another clean_<field>() Example

Suppose username cannot contain spaces.

python
class RegisterForm(forms.Form):

    username = forms.CharField()

    def clean_username(self):
        username = self.cleaned_data["username"]

        if " " in username:
            raise forms.ValidationError(
                "Username cannot contain spaces."
            )

        return username

20. Password Validation Example

Suppose password must contain at least one digit.

python
class RegisterForm(forms.Form):

    password = forms.CharField(
        widget=forms.PasswordInput
    )

    def clean_password(self):
        password = self.cleaned_data["password"]

        if not any(char.isdigit() for char in password):
            raise forms.ValidationError(
                "Password must contain at least one digit."
            )

        return password

21. clean() — Cross-Field Validation

This is another very important viva question.

Use:

python
clean()

when validation depends on multiple fields together.

For example:

text
Password
Confirm Password

We need to compare both.

22. Password Confirmation Example

python
from django import forms

class RegisterForm(forms.Form):

    password = forms.CharField(
        widget=forms.PasswordInput
    )

    confirm_password = forms.CharField(
        widget=forms.PasswordInput
    )

    def clean(self):
        cleaned_data = super().clean()

        password = cleaned_data.get("password")
        confirm_password = cleaned_data.get("confirm_password")

        if password and confirm_password:
            if password != confirm_password:
                raise forms.ValidationError(
                    "Passwords do not match."
                )

        return cleaned_data

23. Why super().clean()?

This line:

python
cleaned_data = super().clean()

calls Django's parent implementation of clean().

It gives us the cleaned field data that has already passed field-level validation.

Then:

python
password = cleaned_data.get("password")

gets the password.

And:

python
confirm_password = cleaned_data.get("confirm_password")

gets the confirmation.

Then:

python
if password != confirm_password:

compares them.

24. clean_<field>() vs clean()

This is extremely important for viva.

Method Purpose
clean_name() Validate one specific field
clean_email() Validate one specific field
clean_age() Validate one specific field
clean() Validate multiple fields together

Easy rule

One field → clean_<field>()
Multiple fields → clean()

25. Example: Age Validation

Built-in validation:

python
age = forms.IntegerField(
    min_value=18,
    max_value=60
)

This is preferable when the rule is simple.

But suppose:

Students under 18 cannot register for a particular course.

Now validation depends on both:

text
age
course

So we use:

python
def clean(self):

Example:

python
class StudentForm(forms.Form):

    age = forms.IntegerField()
    course = forms.ChoiceField(
        choices=[
            ("cse", "CSE"),
            ("mba", "MBA")
        ]
    )

    def clean(self):
        cleaned_data = super().clean()

        age = cleaned_data.get("age")
        course = cleaned_data.get("course")

        if age is not None and course == "mba" and age < 18:
            raise forms.ValidationError(
                "Student must be at least 18 for MBA."
            )

        return cleaned_data

26. add_error()

Sometimes you want to add an error to a specific field.

Django provides:

python
self.add_error()

Example:

python
class StudentForm(forms.Form):

    age = forms.IntegerField()

    def clean(self):
        cleaned_data = super().clean()

        age = cleaned_data.get("age")

        if age is not None and age < 18:
            self.add_error(
                "age",
                "Student must be at least 18."
            )

        return cleaned_data

Now the error belongs specifically to:

text
age

rather than being a non-field/form-wide error.

27. ValidationError

Import:

python
from django import forms

Then:

python
raise forms.ValidationError("Invalid data")

You can also import it directly:

python
from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError

Then:

python
raise ValidationError("Invalid data")

Both approaches are commonly seen.

28. Field Error vs Non-Field Error

Suppose we have:

python
password
confirm_password

and they don't match.

This error doesn't belong naturally to only one field.

Using:

python
raise forms.ValidationError(
    "Passwords do not match."
)

creates a non-field/form-level error.

In the template, you can display:

html
{{ form.non_field_errors }}

29. Using add_error() Instead

If you want the error associated with a specific field:

python
self.add_error(
    "confirm_password",
    "Passwords do not match."
)

Now the error appears against:

text
confirm_password

This can make the UI clearer.

30. Complete Validation Example

Let's build a realistic registration form.

python
from django import forms


class RegisterForm(forms.Form):

    username = forms.CharField(
        min_length=5,
        max_length=20
    )

    email = forms.EmailField()

    age = forms.IntegerField(
        min_value=18,
        max_value=60
    )

    password = forms.CharField(
        min_length=8,
        widget=forms.PasswordInput
    )

    confirm_password = forms.CharField(
        widget=forms.PasswordInput
    )

    def clean_username(self):
        username = self.cleaned_data["username"]

        if " " in username:
            raise forms.ValidationError(
                "Username cannot contain spaces."
            )

        return username

    def clean_password(self):
        password = self.cleaned_data["password"]

        if not any(char.isdigit() for char in password):
            raise forms.ValidationError(
                "Password must contain at least one digit."
            )

        return password

    def clean(self):
        cleaned_data = super().clean()

        password = cleaned_data.get("password")
        confirm_password = cleaned_data.get("confirm_password")

        if password and confirm_password:
            if password != confirm_password:
                self.add_error(
                    "confirm_password",
                    "Passwords do not match."
                )

        return cleaned_data

This one form demonstrates:

  • min_length
  • max_length
  • EmailField
  • min_value
  • max_value
  • PasswordInput
  • clean_<field>()
  • clean()
  • custom validation
  • ValidationError
  • add_error()

31. Validation Pipeline — Very Important

You should understand what happens internally.

Suppose:

python
form = RegisterForm(request.POST)

Then:

python
form.is_valid()

starts the validation process.

Conceptually:

text
             request.POST
                  ↓
             Bound Form
                  ↓
             is_valid()
                  ↓
        Field-level processing
                  ↓
      Field type/required checks
                  ↓
          Built-in validators
                  ↓
        clean_<field>() methods
                  ↓
             clean()
                  ↓
          Validation complete
             ↙          ↘
          valid         invalid
            ↓              ↓
    cleaned_data       form.errors

This flow is worth remembering for viva.

32. What Happens When Validation Fails?

Suppose:

python
age = forms.IntegerField(min_value=18)

User enters:

text
15

Then:

python
form.is_valid()

returns:

python
False

and:

python
form.errors

contains the error.

Therefore:

python
if form.is_valid():
    # process data
else:
    # display form again with errors

33. Important: Don't Process Invalid Data

Bad:

python
form = StudentForm(request.POST)

name = form.cleaned_data["name"]

Why bad?

Because validation has not happened.

Correct:

python
form = StudentForm(request.POST)

if form.is_valid():
    name = form.cleaned_data["name"]

34. Complete View + Form + Template

forms.py

python
from django import forms


class StudentForm(forms.Form):

    name = forms.CharField(
        min_length=3,
        max_length=30
    )

    age = forms.IntegerField(
        min_value=18,
        max_value=60
    )

    email = forms.EmailField()

    def clean_name(self):
        name = self.cleaned_data["name"]

        if any(char.isdigit() for char in name):
            raise forms.ValidationError(
                "Name cannot contain numbers."
            )

        return name

views.py

python
from django.shortcuts import render
from .forms import StudentForm


def student_form(request):

    if request.method == "POST":

        form = StudentForm(request.POST)

        if form.is_valid():

            name = form.cleaned_data["name"]
            age = form.cleaned_data["age"]
            email = form.cleaned_data["email"]

            return render(
                request,
                "success.html",
                {
                    "name": name,
                    "age": age,
                    "email": email
                }
            )

    else:

        form = StudentForm()

    return render(
        request,
        "student_form.html",
        {"form": form}
    )

student_form.html

html
<h1>Student Registration</h1>

<form method="POST">

    {% csrf_token %}

    {{ form.as_p }}

    <button type="submit">
        Register
    </button>

</form>

If validation fails, Django renders the same form again with errors.

35. Built-in vs Custom Validation

Built-in validation

Use:

python
age = forms.IntegerField(
    min_value=18,
    max_value=60
)

when Django already provides the rule.

Custom validation

Use:

python
def clean_age(self):

when your application's specific rule isn't covered by built-in field options.

Example:

python
def clean_age(self):
    age = self.cleaned_data["age"]

    if age % 2 != 0:
        raise forms.ValidationError(
            "Age must be an even number."
        )

    return age

36. Common Mistakes

Mistake 1

Using:

python
clean_data

instead of:

python
cleaned_data

Correct:

python
self.cleaned_data

Mistake 2

Using cleaned data before validation:

python
form.cleaned_data

Correct:

python
if form.is_valid():
    form.cleaned_data

Mistake 3

Forgetting return:

python
def clean_name(self):
    name = self.cleaned_data["name"]

    if len(name) < 3:
        raise forms.ValidationError("Too short")

Better:

python
def clean_name(self):
    name = self.cleaned_data["name"]

    if len(name) < 3:
        raise forms.ValidationError("Too short")

    return name

Mistake 4

Using clean() for a single-field rule unnecessarily.

For:

Username cannot contain spaces.

Prefer:

python
def clean_username(self):

not:

python
def clean(self):

Mistake 5

Forgetting:

python
super().clean()

when writing a custom clean().

Use:

python
cleaned_data = super().clean()

Mistake 6

Using:

python
request.POST

incorrectly.

Correct:

python
form = StudentForm(request.POST)

Mistake 7

Forgetting CSRF protection in a POST template:

html
{% csrf_token %}

37. clean_<field>() vs Validator Functions

Django also supports validators.

Example:

python
from django.core.validators import MinValueValidator

You can define:

python
age = forms.IntegerField(
    validators=[MinValueValidator(18)]
)

This is useful when you want a reusable validation rule.

For simple field-specific logic, clean_<field>() is often easier to understand.

38. Very Important Viva Questions

Q1. What is form validation?

Answer:

Form validation is the process of checking whether submitted form data is present, correctly formatted, type-correct, within allowed limits, and satisfies application-specific rules.

Q2. What does is_valid() do?

Answer:

is_valid() runs the form's validation process and returns True if the submitted data is valid, otherwise False.

Q3. What is cleaned_data?

Answer:

cleaned_data is a dictionary containing validated and cleaned form data after successful form validation.

Q4. When is cleaned_data available?

Answer:

It should be accessed after form.is_valid() has been called.

Q5. What is clean_<field>()?

Answer:

It is a custom validation method used to validate or transform a specific form field.

Example:

python
def clean_email(self):
    ...

Q6. What is clean()?

Answer:

clean() is used for form-wide or cross-field validation when the validation rule depends on multiple fields.

Q7. Difference between clean_name() and clean()?

Answer:

text
clean_name() → validates name only
clean()      → validates multiple fields/form-wide rules

Q8. What is ValidationError?

Answer:

ValidationError is raised when submitted data does not satisfy a validation rule.

Example:

python
raise forms.ValidationError("Invalid name")

Q9. What is add_error()?

Answer:

add_error() manually adds a validation error to a particular form field.

Example:

python
self.add_error("age", "Age is invalid.")

Q10. Why do we use super().clean()?

Answer:

It calls Django's parent clean() implementation and provides the cleaned data needed for further form-wide validation.

Q11. What does required=False mean?

Answer:

It makes a form field optional.

Q12. What is min_length?

Answer:

It specifies the minimum number of characters allowed for a field.

Q13. What is min_value?

Answer:

It specifies the minimum numeric value accepted by a field.

Q14. Does is_valid() return cleaned data?

No.

It returns:

python
True

or:

python
False

The cleaned data is accessed through:

python
form.cleaned_data

39. Coding Questions You Should Be Able to Write

Question 1

Create a form with:

  • Name: minimum 3 characters
  • Age: 18–60
  • Email: valid email

Answer:

python
class StudentForm(forms.Form):

    name = forms.CharField(
        min_length=3
    )

    age = forms.IntegerField(
        min_value=18,
        max_value=60
    )

    email = forms.EmailField()

Question 2

Create custom validation so that a username cannot contain spaces.

python
def clean_username(self):
    username = self.cleaned_data["username"]

    if " " in username:
        raise forms.ValidationError(
            "Username cannot contain spaces."
        )

    return username

Question 3

Validate password confirmation.

python
def clean(self):
    cleaned_data = super().clean()

    password = cleaned_data.get("password")
    confirm = cleaned_data.get("confirm_password")

    if password != confirm:
        raise forms.ValidationError(
            "Passwords do not match."
        )

    return cleaned_data

40. The Most Important Things to Memorize

If you have limited time before an exam, remember these:

Built-in validation

python
required=True
required=False
min_length=3
max_length=20
min_value=18
max_value=60

Validation

python
if form.is_valid():

Cleaned data

python
form.cleaned_data

Field-specific validation

python
def clean_name(self):
    value = self.cleaned_data["name"]

    # validation

    return value

Form-wide validation

python
def clean(self):
    cleaned_data = super().clean()

    # cross-field validation

    return cleaned_data

Error

python
raise forms.ValidationError("Invalid data")

Field-specific error

python
self.add_error(
    "field_name",
    "Error message"
)

Module 22 Summary

The complete concept is:

text
User submits form
       ↓
request.POST
       ↓
Form(request.POST)
       ↓
form.is_valid()
       ↓
Built-in validation
       ↓
clean_<field>()
       ↓
clean()
       ↓
 ┌───────────────┐
 │               │
Valid          Invalid
 │               │
 ↓               ↓
cleaned_data   form.errors

And the golden rule is:

Use built-in field options for simple validation, clean_<field>() for one-field custom validation, and clean() for validation involving multiple fields.

Next → Module 23: CSRF & CSRF Protection We'll cover exactly why {% csrf_token %} is required, how CSRF attacks work, Django's CSRF middleware/token mechanism, common CSRF errors, AJAX/POST considerations, and the viva questions around CSRF.

Module 23
CSRF & CSRF Protection

Module 23 — CSRF & CSRF Protection in Django

CSRF is a very important Django security topic and is commonly asked in viva/interviews.

By the end of this module, you should be able to explain:

  • What CSRF means
  • What a CSRF attack is
  • Why Django uses CSRF protection
  • What {% csrf_token %} does
  • What CsrfViewMiddleware does
  • Why CSRF is mainly relevant to state-changing requests
  • How to fix a CSRF verification error
  • CSRF vs XSS vs authentication
  • How CSRF works with forms and AJAX

1. What is CSRF?

CSRF stands for:

Cross-Site Request Forgery

It is a web security attack where an attacker tricks a user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a website where the user is already authenticated.

The important idea is:

The request comes from the victim's browser, and the browser may automatically include the user's authentication credentials, such as cookies.

2. Simple Real-Life Example

Imagine you are logged into:

text
bank.com

Your browser has a login/session cookie.

Now you visit an attacker's website:

text
evil.com

The attacker tries to make your browser send a request to:

text
bank.com/transfer/

If the bank doesn't verify that the request genuinely came from its own form/site, the request could potentially be accepted using your existing authentication.

So:

text
Victim logged in
       ↓
Browser has authentication cookie
       ↓
Victim visits malicious website
       ↓
Malicious website causes request
       ↓
Browser sends request to target site
       ↓
Target site may think request is legitimate

That's the basic CSRF problem.

3. Why Is CSRF Possible?

The important concept is automatic browser credentials.

For example, session authentication commonly uses cookies.

Suppose:

text
Browser
   |
   | Cookie: sessionid=abc123
   ↓
example.com

The browser can automatically send the cookie when making a request to that domain.

The server therefore knows:

"This request belongs to the logged-in user."

But that doesn't necessarily prove:

"The user intentionally submitted this particular action."

That's the gap CSRF protection addresses.

4. What Does Django Do?

Django provides built-in CSRF protection.

You normally see this in a POST form:

html
<form method="POST">

    {% csrf_token %}

    {{ form.as_p }}

    <button type="submit">
        Submit
    </button>

</form>

The important line is:

django
{% csrf_token %}

5. What Is {% csrf_token %}?

It is a Django template tag that inserts a CSRF token into the HTML form.

Conceptually, the rendered HTML contains something like:

html
<input type="hidden"
       name="csrfmiddlewaretoken"
       value="some-secret-token">

The exact token value is generated/handled by Django.

So when the form is submitted:

text
POST request
   ↓
Form data
   +
CSRF token
   ↓
Django
   ↓
CSRF verification

6. Why Do We Need the Token?

The idea is that an attacker shouldn't be able to obtain the valid CSRF token from the target website's page because of browser security restrictions.

Therefore:

text
Legitimate form
      ↓
Contains valid CSRF token
      ↓
Django accepts request

Whereas an attacker's forged request generally won't contain the valid token:

text
Malicious request
      ↓
Missing/invalid CSRF token
      ↓
Django rejects request

7. CSRF Token Is NOT a Password

A common misconception is:

"CSRF token is the user's password."

No.

It is a security value used to verify that a request is coming through an expected interaction with the site.

Think of it as:

text
Authentication
→ Who are you?

CSRF protection
→ Did this state-changing request come through an expected trusted flow?

These solve different problems.

8. Django's CSRF Middleware

Django normally enables CSRF protection through middleware.

In settings.py, you'll see:

python
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware',
    'django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware',
    'django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware',
    'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware',
    ...
]

The important line is:

python
'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware',

This middleware performs CSRF checks.

9. Two Things You Must Remember

For a normal Django POST form, remember:

In the template:

django
{% csrf_token %}

In settings.py:

python
'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware',

The middleware is normally included in a newly created Django project.

10. Complete Example

Suppose we have:

forms.py

python
from django import forms


class StudentForm(forms.Form):
    name = forms.CharField()
    age = forms.IntegerField()

views.py

python
from django.shortcuts import render
from .forms import StudentForm


def student_form(request):

    if request.method == "POST":

        form = StudentForm(request.POST)

        if form.is_valid():
            return render(
                request,
                "success.html"
            )

    else:
        form = StudentForm()

    return render(
        request,
        "student_form.html",
        {"form": form}
    )

student_form.html

html
<form method="POST">

    {% csrf_token %}

    {{ form.as_p }}

    <button type="submit">
        Submit
    </button>

</form>

This is the standard pattern.

11. What Happens If We Forget {% csrf_token %}?

Suppose we write:

html
<form method="POST">

    {{ form.as_p }}

    <button type="submit">
        Submit
    </button>

</form>

Notice:

django
{% csrf_token %}

is missing.

When the POST request reaches Django, CSRF verification can fail.

You may see an error such as:

text
403 Forbidden
CSRF verification failed. Request aborted.

The exact error page/details depend on Django configuration and environment.

12. Why 403?

HTTP status:

text
403 Forbidden

means:

The server understood the request but refuses to authorize/process it.

CSRF verification failure is commonly returned as a 403 response.

This is different from:

text
404 → resource/URL not found
500 → server-side error
400 → bad request
403 → forbidden

13. CSRF and GET vs POST

This is important.

CSRF protection is primarily concerned with unsafe/state-changing HTTP methods, such as:

text
POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE

A normal GET request should generally be safe and should not change server state.

For example:

text
GET /products/

should retrieve products.

Whereas:

text
POST /delete-account/

changes state.

Therefore, CSRF protection is especially important for the second type.

14. Should GET Change Data?

Ideally, no.

Bad design:

text
GET /delete-student/10/

because simply visiting a URL could perform a destructive action.

Better:

text
POST /delete-student/10/

with CSRF protection.

General principle:

GET should be safe/read-only; state-changing operations should use appropriate non-safe methods and CSRF protection where applicable.

15. CSRF Token in a Form

Consider:

html
<form method="POST">

    {% csrf_token %}

    <input type="text" name="name">

    <button type="submit">
        Save
    </button>

</form>

When Django renders the page:

text
{% csrf_token %}
        ↓
Django generates/inserts CSRF token
        ↓
Browser receives form
        ↓
User submits form
        ↓
POST + CSRF information
        ↓
Django verifies it

16. CSRF Cookie

Django also uses a CSRF cookie as part of its CSRF protection mechanism.

Conceptually:

text
Browser
   |
   | CSRF cookie
   ↓
Django

The exact mechanics are more sophisticated than simply "put a token in the form."

For a normal HTML form, the practical rule you need to remember is:

django
{% csrf_token %}

17. csrf_token vs csrfmiddlewaretoken

You may encounter both terms.

Template tag:

django
{% csrf_token %}

This is what you write in the Django template.

Django renders a hidden form field containing the token, commonly named:

text
csrfmiddlewaretoken

So:

text
{% csrf_token %}
       ↓
hidden input
       ↓
csrfmiddlewaretoken

18. CSRF with Django Forms

Django Forms do not automatically mean that CSRF is handled by the form itself.

You still need:

django
{% csrf_token %}

in a POST HTML form.

For example:

html
<form method="POST">

    {% csrf_token %}

    {{ form.as_p }}

    <button type="submit">
        Submit
    </button>

</form>

Remember:

{{ form.as_p }} renders the form fields, but {% csrf_token %} is a separate Django template tag.

19. Common CSRF Error

You submit your form and see:

text
Forbidden (403)
CSRF verification failed.
Request aborted.

First check:

1. Is the form POST?

html
<form method="POST">

2. Did you add:

django
{% csrf_token %}

3. Is CSRF middleware enabled?

python
'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware',

4. Are you submitting to the expected URL/domain?

5. Is the browser accepting cookies as expected?

20. Don't Disable CSRF Just to Fix an Error

You might find:

python
from django.views.decorators.csrf import csrf_exempt

and:

python
@csrf_exempt
def my_view(request):
    ...

This disables CSRF checking for that view.

Important

Do not use this as your first solution to:

"My form gives a CSRF error."

Instead, find out why the legitimate request is failing.

Disabling protection unnecessarily creates a security risk.

21. What Does @csrf_exempt Do?

Example:

python
from django.views.decorators.csrf import csrf_exempt


@csrf_exempt
def my_view(request):
    return HttpResponse("Hello")

It tells Django to exempt this view from normal CSRF protection.

This may be appropriate for certain carefully designed endpoints, but it should be used deliberately.

Viva question

Q: What is csrf_exempt?

Answer:

csrf_exempt is a Django decorator that disables CSRF validation for a particular view.

22. CSRF vs Authentication

These are different.

Authentication

Answers:

Who is the user?

Example:

text
Login username/password
Session
Authentication cookie

CSRF protection

Answers roughly:

Is this state-changing request properly authorized by the site's CSRF mechanism?

So:

text
Authentication ≠ CSRF protection

You can be authenticated and still be vulnerable to CSRF if the application doesn't properly protect state-changing requests.

23. CSRF vs XSS

Another common viva question.

CSRF

Attacker tricks a victim's browser into making an unwanted request.

text
Attacker
   ↓
tricks browser
   ↓
target website

XSS

Attacker gets malicious JavaScript/content executed in another user's browser in the context of a vulnerable website.

text
Malicious script
       ↓
victim's browser
       ↓
runs in website context

Simple distinction:

CSRF tricks the browser into making a request.
XSS executes malicious script in the victim's browser.

24. CSRF vs SQL Injection

These are also completely different.

CSRF

Targets request authenticity/state-changing actions.

SQL Injection

Targets database queries by injecting malicious SQL input.

text
CSRF → HTTP request security

SQL Injection → Database query security

Django's ORM helps reduce SQL injection risks when used properly, while CSRF middleware addresses CSRF.

25. CSRF with AJAX

Suppose JavaScript sends:

javascript
fetch("/students/", {
    method: "POST",
    body: ...
});

You can't simply assume that because it's AJAX, CSRF doesn't apply.

For Django-protected POST requests, you need to send the CSRF token appropriately.

A common approach is to read the CSRF token from the cookie and send it in the request header.

Conceptually:

text
AJAX POST
   +
X-CSRFToken header
   ↓
Django CSRF validation

For example, using fetch:

javascript
fetch("/students/", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
        "X-CSRFToken": csrftoken,
        "Content-Type": "application/json"
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(data)
});

The exact implementation of obtaining csrftoken depends on how your Django app is configured.

For your syllabus, remember the key concept:

AJAX POST requests also need CSRF protection when Django's CSRF checks apply.

26. CSRF with @ensure_csrf_cookie

Django provides:

python
from django.views.decorators.csrf import ensure_csrf_cookie

and:

python
@ensure_csrf_cookie
def my_view(request):
    ...

This can be used when you need Django to ensure that a CSRF cookie is sent to the client.

This becomes more relevant in JavaScript/AJAX applications.

For a normal Django HTML form, you usually don't need to manually use it.

27. CSRF Trusted Origins

Sometimes you may deploy Django across different trusted origins.

Django provides:

python
CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS

in settings.py.

Example conceptually:

python
CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = [
    "https://example.com",
]

This is useful when Django needs to trust requests originating from specific origins.

Important

Don't randomly add domains to this list.

Only add origins you actually trust.

28. CSRF Failure View

Django provides a CSRF failure mechanism.

You can configure a custom CSRF failure view using:

python
CSRF_FAILURE_VIEW

For example:

python
CSRF_FAILURE_VIEW = "students.views.csrf_failure"

and:

python
def csrf_failure(request, reason=""):
    return render(
        request,
        "csrf_failure.html"
    )

This is an advanced concept, but it is useful for viva.

29. Complete Secure Form Pattern

For almost every basic Django POST form, remember this:

Template

html
<form method="POST">

    {% csrf_token %}

    {{ form.as_p }}

    <button type="submit">
        Submit
    </button>

</form>

View

python
def student_form(request):

    if request.method == "POST":

        form = StudentForm(request.POST)

        if form.is_valid():

            # Process valid data

            return redirect("success")

    else:

        form = StudentForm()

    return render(
        request,
        "student_form.html",
        {"form": form}
    )

This gives you:

text
POST
 +
Django Form
 +
Validation
 +
CSRF
 +
Redirect

We'll connect these concepts even more in the next module.

30. Common Mistakes

Mistake 1 — Forgetting CSRF token

Wrong:

html
<form method="POST">
    {{ form.as_p }}
</form>

Correct:

html
<form method="POST">
    {% csrf_token %}
    {{ form.as_p }}
</form>

Mistake 2 — Thinking CSRF is only for login

Wrong.

CSRF protection applies to many state-changing operations:

text
Create
Update
Delete
Change password
Change email
Transfer money
Submit data

Mistake 3 — Thinking HTTPS replaces CSRF

HTTPS protects data in transit.

CSRF protection addresses a different threat.

Therefore:

text
HTTPS ≠ CSRF protection

A site should generally use HTTPS and appropriate CSRF protection.

Mistake 4 — Using csrf_exempt everywhere

Don't do this:

python
@csrf_exempt
def every_view(request):

just to make errors disappear.

It removes an important security defense.

31. Viva Masterclass

Q1. What is CSRF?

CSRF stands for Cross-Site Request Forgery. It is an attack in which an attacker tricks a user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a website where the user is authenticated.

Q2. How does Django protect against CSRF?

Django provides built-in CSRF protection using CSRF tokens and CsrfViewMiddleware.

Q3. What is {% csrf_token %}?

It is a Django template tag that inserts CSRF protection information into a form so Django can verify the request.

Q4. Where should {% csrf_token %} be used?

For a normal Django POST form:

html
<form method="POST">
    {% csrf_token %}
</form>

Q5. What happens if CSRF validation fails?

Typically Django returns:

text
403 Forbidden

with a CSRF verification failure.

Q6. What is CsrfViewMiddleware?

It is Django middleware that performs CSRF protection checks on applicable requests.

Q7. What is csrf_exempt?

A decorator that exempts a view from Django's normal CSRF protection.

Q8. Is CSRF the same as XSS?

No.

text
CSRF → tricks browser into making unwanted requests

XSS → executes malicious script in browser

Q9. Is CSRF the same as authentication?

No.

text
Authentication → identifies/authenticates the user

CSRF protection → helps verify legitimate state-changing requests

Q10. Does a POST request automatically become secure?

No.

POST does not automatically provide security.

You need appropriate measures such as:

text
HTTPS
+
CSRF protection
+
validation
+
authentication/authorization

depending on the application.

32. Exam Answer: "Explain CSRF in Django"

If your teacher asks this as a 5-mark question, you can write:

CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) is a web security attack in which an attacker tricks an authenticated user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a website. Django provides built-in CSRF protection using a CSRF token and CsrfViewMiddleware. In a Django POST form, the {% csrf_token %} template tag is added inside the form. Django verifies the CSRF information when the request is submitted. If the verification fails, Django generally returns a 403 Forbidden response. CSRF protection is especially important for state-changing requests such as POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. It is different from authentication and XSS protection.

33. Must Remember

Memorize these:

text
CSRF
↓
Cross-Site Request Forgery
django
{% csrf_token %}
python
'django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware',
python
@csrf_exempt

And remember:

text
CSRF → request forgery
XSS → malicious script
Authentication → identity
HTTPS → encrypted transport

One-line rule

For a normal Django POST form, put {% csrf_token %} inside the <form> and keep Django's CSRF middleware enabled.

Module 23 Complete ✅

Next → Module 24: POST Redirect Pattern

There we'll learn the important POST → Redirect → GET (PRG) pattern, why refreshing a submitted form can cause duplicate submissions, how redirect() works, how to redirect using named URLs, and how Django forms, validation, CSRF and redirects fit together in a complete submission flow.

Module 24
POST Redirect Pattern (PRG)

Module 24 — POST Redirect Pattern (PRG)

This module is short but very important in practical Django development and viva.

The main concept is:

After successfully processing a POST request, redirect the user to another page instead of directly rendering the response.

This pattern is called:

POST → Redirect → GET (PRG)

1. The Problem With Directly Rendering After POST

Suppose we have a student registration form.

User submits:

text
Name: Aman
Age: 21

Browser sends:

text
POST /students/register/

Your Django view processes the data:

python
if request.method == "POST":
    form = StudentForm(request.POST)

    if form.is_valid():
        # Save/process data

Now suppose you do:

python
return render(request, "success.html")

The browser is currently displaying the response to the POST request.

If the user presses:

text
F5 / Refresh

the browser may ask:

"Resubmit the form?"

Because the current page came from a POST request.

This can potentially cause the same operation to happen again.

For example:

text
POST
↓
Create student
↓
Success page
↓
Refresh
↓
POST again
↓
Create student again

That could result in duplicate data.

2. The Solution: Redirect

Instead of:

python
return render(request, "success.html")

use:

python
return redirect("success")

Now the flow becomes:

text
POST
 ↓
Process data
 ↓
Redirect
 ↓
GET
 ↓
Success page

This is:

POST → Redirect → GET

3. Why Is This Called PRG?

PRG stands for:

text
P → POST
R → Redirect
G → GET

So:

text
POST request
      ↓
Process submitted data
      ↓
HTTP Redirect
      ↓
GET request
      ↓
Display result

The browser's final page is now the result of a GET request.

Therefore, refreshing the page normally repeats the GET rather than resubmitting the original POST.

4. Basic Django Example

python
from django.shortcuts import render, redirect


def student_form(request):

    if request.method == "POST":

        form = StudentForm(request.POST)

        if form.is_valid():

            # Process data

            return redirect("success")

    else:
        form = StudentForm()

    return render(
        request,
        "student_form.html",
        {"form": form}
    )

The important line is:

python
return redirect("success")

5. Where Does "success" Come From?

Usually from a named URL.

For example:

python
path(
    "success/",
    views.success,
    name="success"
)

Then:

python
return redirect("success")

Django finds the URL whose name is:

text
success

and redirects the browser there.

6. The Success View

python
def success(request):
    return render(
        request,
        "success.html"
    )

Complete flow:

text
POST /students/register/
             ↓
       student_form()
             ↓
        form.is_valid()
             ↓
           valid
             ↓
    redirect("success")
             ↓
GET /students/success/
             ↓
        success()
             ↓
       success.html

7. redirect() vs render()

This is a common viva question.

render()

python
return render(
    request,
    "success.html"
)

renders a template directly.

Conceptually:

text
View
 ↓
Template
 ↓
HTTP response

redirect()

python
return redirect("success")

tells the browser to go to another URL.

Conceptually:

text
View
 ↓
Redirect response
 ↓
Browser makes GET request
 ↓
New view

8. Important Difference

render() redirect()
Renders a template Sends browser to another URL
Usually returns the page directly Causes a new request
Doesn't change the browser URL to another route by itself Browser URL changes
Useful for displaying a page Useful after successful POST/action

9. Why Not Just Render the Success Page?

Consider:

python
if form.is_valid():

    form.save()

    return render(
        request,
        "success.html"
    )

The browser's current request is still:

text
POST

Then refresh can potentially repeat the POST.

Better:

python
if form.is_valid():

    form.save()

    return redirect("success")

Now:

text
POST
 ↓
save
 ↓
redirect
 ↓
GET
 ↓
success page

10. PRG Is Especially Useful for Database Operations

Suppose:

python
Student.objects.create(
    name="Aman"
)

If the POST gets accidentally repeated, you could create another student.

Similarly:

text
POST /create-order/
POST /payment/
POST /register/
POST /comment/
POST /contact/

are actions where duplicate submissions can be problematic.

PRG is therefore widely used after successful form submissions.

11. Redirect With URL Name

Recommended:

python
return redirect("success")

with:

python
path(
    "success/",
    views.success,
    name="success"
)

This is better than hardcoding the URL:

python
return redirect("/students/success/")

Why?

Because if the URL changes later:

python
path(
    "registration-complete/",
    views.success,
    name="success"
)

your Python code can still use:

python
redirect("success")

12. Redirect to Another View

You can also redirect using a view name:

python
return redirect("home")

provided that:

python
path(
    "",
    views.home,
    name="home"
)

exists.

13. Redirect With Parameters

Suppose your URL is:

python
path(
    "student/<int:id>/",
    views.student_detail,
    name="student_detail"
)

You can redirect with the parameter:

python
return redirect(
    "student_detail",
    id=10
)

Django resolves it to something like:

text
/student/10/

This is similar to URL reversing.

14. Redirect Using reverse()

You can also do:

python
from django.urls import reverse
from django.shortcuts import redirect

Then:

python
return redirect(
    reverse("success")
)

But normally:

python
return redirect("success")

is simpler.

Django's redirect() can resolve a named URL for you.

15. PRG With a Django Form

Let's combine what we've learned.

forms.py

python
from django import forms


class StudentForm(forms.Form):

    name = forms.CharField(
        min_length=3
    )

    age = forms.IntegerField(
        min_value=18,
        max_value=60
    )

views.py

python
from django.shortcuts import render, redirect
from .forms import StudentForm


def student_form(request):

    if request.method == "POST":

        form = StudentForm(request.POST)

        if form.is_valid():

            name = form.cleaned_data["name"]
            age = form.cleaned_data["age"]

            # Process/save data here

            return redirect("success")

    else:

        form = StudentForm()

    return render(
        request,
        "student_form.html",
        {"form": form}
    )


def success(request):

    return render(
        request,
        "success.html"
    )

urls.py

python
from django.urls import path
from . import views


urlpatterns = [

    path(
        "register/",
        views.student_form,
        name="student_form"
    ),

    path(
        "success/",
        views.success,
        name="success"
    ),
]

Template

html
<form method="POST">

    {% csrf_token %}

    {{ form.as_p }}

    <button type="submit">
        Register
    </button>

</form>

16. What Happens When Form Is Invalid?

This is very important.

Suppose user submits:

text
Name: A
Age: 12

Validation fails.

The view does:

python
if form.is_valid():
    return redirect("success")

Since:

python
form.is_valid()

is False, Django does not redirect.

It reaches:

python
return render(
    request,
    "student_form.html",
    {"form": form}
)

The form is displayed again with errors.

So the complete behavior is:

text
POST
 ↓
Validation
 ↓
 ┌─────────────┐
 │             │
Valid        Invalid
 │             │
 ↓             ↓
Redirect     Render form
 │             +
 ↓           errors
GET
 ↓
Success

This is the standard pattern.

17. Why Don't We Redirect When Validation Fails?

Because we want to preserve the submitted form and its errors.

Suppose:

text
Age = 15

and minimum age is 18.

We want the user to see:

text
Age
15

❌ Ensure this value is greater than or equal to 18.

If we redirected immediately, we'd need another mechanism to preserve the errors/data.

So the usual pattern is:

text
Invalid POST → render form with errors
Valid POST → redirect

18. PRG + CSRF + Validation

Now you can connect Modules 21–24.

A secure form flow looks like:

text
User opens form
       ↓
GET
       ↓
Django renders form
       ↓
User fills form
       ↓
POST
       ↓
CSRF verification
       ↓
Form validation
       ↓
 ┌──────────────┐
 │              │
Invalid       Valid
 │              │
 ↓              ↓
Show errors   Process data
               ↓
            Redirect
               ↓
              GET
               ↓
          Success page

This is an extremely useful mental model.

19. POST Redirect vs Redirect After Every POST

Not every POST necessarily has to use PRG.

The important principle is:

After a successful state-changing POST, redirecting is generally a good practice when the next page represents the result of that operation.

For example:

text
Create student → redirect to student detail
Update student → redirect to student detail
Delete student → redirect to student list
Submit registration → redirect to success/dashboard

20. Redirect After Create

Example:

python
def create_student(request):

    if request.method == "POST":

        form = StudentForm(request.POST)

        if form.is_valid():

            student = Student.objects.create(
                name=form.cleaned_data["name"]
            )

            return redirect(
                "student_detail",
                id=student.id
            )

    else:
        form = StudentForm()

    return render(
        request,
        "create_student.html",
        {"form": form}
    )

Flow:

text
POST
 ↓
Create student
 ↓
Redirect to student detail
 ↓
GET student detail

21. Redirect After Delete

Example:

python
def delete_student(request, id):

    if request.method == "POST":

        student = get_object_or_404(
            Student,
            id=id
        )

        student.delete()

        return redirect("student_list")

Flow:

text
POST /student/10/delete/
          ↓
      Delete student
          ↓
redirect("student_list")
          ↓
GET /students/

This is a very common Django pattern.

22. HTTP Redirect Status

A redirect is represented by an HTTP 3xx response.

For example:

text
302 Found

is commonly used for redirects.

Django's:

python
redirect()

creates an appropriate redirect response.

You generally don't need to manually construct the HTTP response for ordinary redirects.

23. Common Mistake: Calling render() Instead of redirect()

Bad after successful POST:

python
if form.is_valid():

    form.save()

    return render(
        request,
        "success.html"
    )

Better:

python
if form.is_valid():

    form.save()

    return redirect("success")

24. Common Mistake: Redirect Before Processing

Wrong:

python
if request.method == "POST":

    return redirect("success")

    form.save()

Why?

Because:

python
return

immediately exits the function.

Therefore this:

python
form.save()

will never execute.

Correct:

python
if form.is_valid():

    form.save()

    return redirect("success")

25. Common Mistake: No Named URL

If you write:

python
return redirect("success")

but don't have:

python
name="success"

Django may raise:

text
NoReverseMatch

So make sure:

python
path(
    "success/",
    views.success,
    name="success"
)

exists.

26. redirect() vs reverse()

This is a useful viva distinction.

reverse()

Builds a URL string.

python
reverse("success")

might produce:

text
/success/

redirect()

Returns an HTTP redirect response.

python
redirect("success")

tells the browser to navigate to that URL.

Simple rule:

text
reverse()  → creates URL
redirect() → redirects browser

27. Viva Questions

Q1. What is PRG?

PRG stands for Post-Redirect-Get. It is a web design pattern where a successful POST request is followed by a redirect, and the browser then makes a GET request to display the result.

Q2. Why is PRG used?

It prevents the final page from being directly associated with the POST submission, reducing accidental duplicate submissions when the user refreshes the page.

Q3. What function is used for redirecting in Django?

python
redirect()

Q4. Difference between render() and redirect()?

render() generates a response using a template, while redirect() sends a redirect response causing the browser to make a new request to another URL.

Q5. What happens when validation fails?

The form is normally rendered again with its validation errors rather than redirecting to the success page.

Q6. Why use named URLs with redirect()?

Named URLs avoid hardcoding URL paths and make the application easier to maintain when URL patterns change.

Q7. Can redirect() accept URL parameters?

Yes.

python
return redirect(
    "student_detail",
    id=10
)

Q8. What happens when the user refreshes after PRG?

The browser refreshes the final GET request instead of normally resubmitting the original POST.

28. Exam Question

"Explain POST-Redirect-GET pattern in Django."

A good answer:

POST-Redirect-GET (PRG) is a web design pattern used after successful form submission. First, the client sends a POST request containing form data. Django validates and processes the data. Instead of directly rendering the success page for the POST request, Django returns a redirect using redirect(). The browser then sends a new GET request to the redirected URL. This prevents the success page from being directly associated with the POST request and helps avoid accidental duplicate form submissions when the page is refreshed.

29. Must-Memorize Code

This pattern is worth memorizing exactly:

python
def student_form(request):

    if request.method == "POST":

        form = StudentForm(request.POST)

        if form.is_valid():

            # Process data

            return redirect("success")

    else:

        form = StudentForm()

    return render(
        request,
        "student_form.html",
        {"form": form}
    )

And:

python
path(
    "success/",
    views.success,
    name="success"
)

Remember this:

text
POST
 ↓
Validate
 ↓
Valid?
 ├── No → Render form + errors
 │
 └── Yes
       ↓
   Process/save
       ↓
    redirect()
       ↓
      GET
       ↓
   Success page

Golden rule:

Invalid POST → render the form again.
Successful POST → process the data → redirect.

This connects directly with everything we've learned:

text
Forms
 +
Validation
 +
CSRF
 +
POST
 +
Redirect
 =
Proper Django form submission

Module 25
Databases & Django Models

Module 25 — Databases & Django Models

This is a major Django module because from here we move from forms and HTTP into database-backed applications.

You will learn:

  • What a database is
  • Tables, rows, columns
  • SQL vs ORM
  • What a Django model is
  • models.py

  • How Django converts models into database tables

1. Why Do We Need a Database?

So far, we've worked with data like:

python
students = [
    {"name": "Aman", "age": 21},
    {"name": "Rahul", "age": 22},
]

But where is this data stored?

It's only in Python memory.

If the Django server stops:

text
Server stops
    ↓
Python memory cleared
    ↓
Data lost

We need persistent storage.

That's where a database comes in.

text
Django application
       ↓
   Database
       ↓
Persistent data

2. What Is a Database?

A database is an organized collection of data that can be stored, retrieved, updated, and deleted efficiently.

For example, a college application might store:

text
Students
Courses
Teachers
Departments
Marks
Attendance

3. What Is a Database Table?

A relational database stores data in tables.

Imagine a Student table:

id name age email
1 Aman 21 [aman@gmail.com](mailto:aman@gmail.com)
2 Rahul 22 [rahul@gmail.com](mailto:rahul@gmail.com)
3 Priya 20 [priya@gmail.com](mailto:priya@gmail.com)

The table consists of:

  • Columns → properties/fields
  • Rows → individual records

4. Column

A column represents a particular type of information.

For example:

text
id
name
age
email

In Django, these correspond to model fields.

5. Row

A row represents one record.

For example:

text
1 | Aman | 21 | aman@gmail.com

is one student record.

In Django, this eventually corresponds to a model instance.

6. Primary Key

A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table.

Example:

id name age
1 Aman 21
2 Rahul 22
3 Priya 20

Here:

text
id

is the primary key.

It should uniquely identify a record.

7. Why Is id Important?

Suppose we want to retrieve Aman.

We can identify him using:

text
id = 1

For example:

text
/student/1/

This connects to the URL parameter concepts we learned earlier.

8. What Database Does Django Use by Default?

A new Django project normally uses:

SQLite

In settings.py, you'll see something similar to:

python
DATABASES = {
    "default": {
        "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.sqlite3",
        "NAME": BASE_DIR / "db.sqlite3",
    }
}

SQLite is lightweight and stores the database in a file.

The file is usually:

text
db.sqlite3

9. Other Databases Django Supports

Django can work with databases such as:

text
SQLite
PostgreSQL
MySQL
MariaDB
Oracle

For learning and small development projects, SQLite is very convenient.

For larger production systems, PostgreSQL is a common choice.

10. What Is a Django Model?

Now the most important definition:

A Django model is a Python class that represents data and describes the structure of a database table.

For example:

python
class Student(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    age = models.IntegerField()
    email = models.EmailField()

This Python class describes a Student table.

Conceptually:

text
Python Model
      ↓
Database Table

11. Where Do We Define Models?

Inside:

text
students/models.py

A newly created Django app already contains:

python
from django.db import models

We define our model there.

12. Creating Your First Model

Suppose we want to store students.

Open:

text
students/models.py

Write:

python
from django.db import models


class Student(models.Model):

    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)

    age = models.IntegerField()

    email = models.EmailField()

That's our first Django model.

13. Understanding the Code

Let's break it down.

Import

python
from django.db import models

This imports Django's model/database functionality.

Class

python
class Student(models.Model):

We're creating a Python class called:

text
Student

It inherits from:

text
models.Model

This tells Django:

This class is a Django database model.

Name field

python
name = models.CharField(max_length=100)

This creates a text field.

max_length=100 means the maximum length is 100 characters.

Age

python
age = models.IntegerField()

Stores integer values.

Email

python
email = models.EmailField()

Stores email-like text and provides Django-level field validation behavior.

14. Model → Table

Our model:

python
class Student(models.Model):

    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    age = models.IntegerField()
    email = models.EmailField()

conceptually becomes a table similar to:

id name age email
1 Aman 21 [aman@gmail.com](mailto:aman@gmail.com)
2 Rahul 22 [rahul@gmail.com](mailto:rahul@gmail.com)

Notice something:

We didn't define:

python
id

yet Django normally creates an automatic primary-key field if you don't explicitly define one.

15. Automatic Primary Key

When you define:

python
class Student(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)

Django automatically adds a primary key unless you've configured a different primary key.

In modern Django versions, the exact automatically generated field type can depend on your configuration/default settings, but conceptually you should remember:

Django automatically provides a primary key when you don't define one.

You can access it using:

python
student.pk

or commonly:

python
student.id

when the automatically created field is named id.

16. pk vs id

Suppose:

python
student = Student.objects.get(...)

You can access:

python
student.id

And Django also provides:

python
student.pk

pk means:

Primary Key

The advantage of pk is that it works regardless of what the actual primary-key field is called.

17. Model Fields

Django provides many field types.

Some important ones:

Django field Typical purpose
CharField Short text
TextField Long text
IntegerField Integer
FloatField Floating-point number
DecimalField Precise decimal values
BooleanField True/False
EmailField Email address
DateField Date
DateTimeField Date + time
TimeField Time
URLField URL
FileField File upload
ImageField Image upload
ForeignKey Relationship to another model

We'll study relationships in depth later.

18. CharField

Used for relatively short strings.

python
name = models.CharField(max_length=100)

You must normally specify max_length for CharField.

Example:

python
username = models.CharField(max_length=50)

19. TextField

Used for larger amounts of text.

Example:

python
description = models.TextField()

Good for:

text
Blog posts
Descriptions
Comments
Long messages

20. IntegerField

python
age = models.IntegerField()

Stores integers:

text
18
21
100
-5

21. FloatField

python
rating = models.FloatField()

Can store floating-point numbers.

Example:

text
4.5
3.14
9.8

For financial values, DecimalField is generally preferable because decimal precision matters.

22. DecimalField

Example:

python
price = models.DecimalField(
    max_digits=10,
    decimal_places=2
)

Meaning:

text
max_digits = total digits
decimal_places = digits after decimal

For:

text
99999.99

there are:

text
7 total digits
2 decimal places

So this would fit:

python
models.DecimalField(
    max_digits=7,
    decimal_places=2
)

23. BooleanField

Used for true/false values.

python
is_active = models.BooleanField(default=True)

Possible values:

text
True
False

24. DateField

python
birth_date = models.DateField()

Stores a date.

Example:

text
2004-08-15

25. DateTimeField

python
created_at = models.DateTimeField()

Stores:

text
date + time

You may often see:

python
created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

This automatically sets the value when the object is first created.

We'll study field options in much more detail in the next module.

26. Field Options

Fields can have additional options.

Example:

python
name = models.CharField(
    max_length=100,
    null=True,
    blank=True
)

Some important options:

text
null
blank
default
unique
primary_key

Don't try to memorize all of them yet; we'll cover them properly in Module 26 — Model Fields.

For now, understand that field definitions contain:

text
Field type
+
Field options

27. Model vs Database Table

This distinction is very important.

Model

Python class:

python
class Student(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)

Table

Database representation:

text
Student table
--------------------
id
name
age
email

So:

text
Django Model
     ↓
Database Table

28. Model Object vs Database Row

Similarly:

Model instance

python
student = Student(
    name="Aman",
    age=21,
    email="aman@gmail.com"
)

Database row

Eventually:

id name age email
1 Aman 21 [aman@gmail.com](mailto:aman@gmail.com)

Therefore:

text
Model class     → Table
Model instance  → Row
Model field     → Column

This is an excellent viva answer.

29. What Is ORM?

ORM stands for:

Object-Relational Mapping

Django provides an ORM that allows us to interact with the database using Python objects and methods instead of writing SQL for every operation.

For example, instead of SQL:

sql
SELECT * FROM students;

you can use Django ORM:

python
Student.objects.all()

30. Why Is ORM Useful?

Without ORM, you might write SQL:

sql
SELECT * FROM students
WHERE age > 18;

With Django ORM:

python
Student.objects.filter(age__gt=18)

The ORM translates the Python-style operation into database-specific SQL.

Conceptually:

text
Python code
    ↓
Django ORM
    ↓
SQL
    ↓
Database

We'll study ORM deeply in Module 28 onward.

31. Do We Need to Write SQL?

Not necessarily.

For many common operations, Django ORM allows you to work with:

python
Student.objects.all()
Student.objects.get(...)
Student.objects.filter(...)
Student.objects.create(...)

rather than manually writing SQL.

However, understanding basic SQL is still useful.

32. Creating a Model Does NOT Immediately Create the Table

This is extremely important.

Suppose you write:

python
class Student(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)

The database table isn't simply created just because you saved models.py.

You need Django's migration system.

33. First: Register the App

Before using migrations, make sure the app is in:

python
INSTALLED_APPS

For example:

python
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...
    "students",
]

Without registering the app, Django won't properly include its models in the project.

34. makemigrations

Run:

bash
python manage.py makemigrations

Django detects model changes and creates migration files describing those changes.

Conceptually:

text
models.py
   ↓
makemigrations
   ↓
migration file

For example:

text
students/
└── migrations/
    ├── __init__.py
    └── 0001_initial.py

35. migrate

Then run:

bash
python manage.py migrate

This applies migrations to the database.

Conceptually:

text
Migration files
      ↓
python manage.py migrate
      ↓
Database tables

36. makemigrations vs migrate

This is a must-know viva question.

Command Purpose
makemigrations Creates migration files from model changes
migrate Applies migrations to the database

Easy way to remember:

text
makemigrations
→ Make instructions

migrate
→ Apply instructions

37. Complete Process

Suppose we create:

python
class Student(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)
    age = models.IntegerField()

Then:

Step 1

Save models.py.

Step 2

Run:

bash
python manage.py makemigrations

Step 3

Run:

bash
python manage.py migrate

Now Django creates/updates the database schema.

38. What Is a Migration?

A migration is a versioned set of database schema changes generated from changes to Django models.

Suppose initially:

python
class Student(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)

Later you add:

python
age = models.IntegerField()

Run:

bash
python manage.py makemigrations

Django creates another migration describing:

text
Add age field to Student

Then:

bash
python manage.py migrate

applies it.

We'll study migrations deeply in Module 27.

39. Django's Database Flow

You should understand this complete flow:

text
models.py
    ↓
Python Model
    ↓
makemigrations
    ↓
Migration File
    ↓
migrate
    ↓
Database Schema
    ↓
Database Table

Then when the application runs:

text
View
 ↓
Django ORM
 ↓
Database
 ↓
Model objects
 ↓
Template

Earlier we learned:

text
Model
View
Template

Now we can understand the database connection.

text
             Django
               |
       ┌───────┴────────┐
       ↓                ↓

       |                |

More accurately:

text
Browser
   ↓

   ↓

Suppose database contains:

id name age
1 Aman 21

The view can retrieve them:

python
def students(request):

The template:

html

text
Students

Aman - 21
Rahul - 22

Notice how our previous knowledge of dynamic templates now connects with models.

42. Model Data Can Be Passed to Templates

The model object retrieved through ORM can be placed into context:

python

django

So:

text

43. Creating a Model Object

You can create an object in Python:

python
student = Student(
    name="Aman",
    age=21,
    email="aman@gmail.com"
)

At this point, the object has been created in Python memory.

To save it to the database:

python

Then it is persisted.

44. save()

Example:

python
student = Student(
    name="Aman",

student.save()

text
Student object

45. objects

You will frequently see:

This is Django's model manager, commonly used to perform database queries.

For example:
